docs.title: modeling-api
docs.text:
Guided mode for analysts · exact control for data scientists · honest uncertainty · one safe platform

v0.5: workflows, governance, explorers, mmm-framework and statsmodels

Workflows connect these items into one versioned graph that you can schedule: unit-root tests, differencing decisions, AR/MA order searches, rolling-origin backtests against naive forecasts, model selection and governance. Governance policies apply null tests to each model. The model must be better than the same model fitted on shuffled results. It must also give no credit to fake noise drivers. A second person approves the model, and the platform makes an evidence pack.

Version 0.5 also adds:

  • Data and Model Explorers
  • mmm-framework marketing-mix models with budget optimisation
  • twelve statsmodels time-series models
  • an About card on everything, with Help me choose

What's new in 0.5.

docs.title: Trustworthy models,from spreadsheet to endpoint.
docs.text:
modeling-api fits Bayesian and classical models of data that has named dimensions (market × channel × week, store × product × day, household × trip). The models answer questions in the units that your business uses. An analyst uploads a spreadsheet and gets a report, a sanity scorecard and instant what-if sliders. A data scientist writes a small spec or some lines of Python and gets the same model behind a versioned endpoint. Each call uses the same fitted preprocessing again, exactly.

Full analyses (tests, decisions, models and benchmarks) run as versioned workflows. A model goes live only after it is better than shuffled data, fake drivers and a naive forecast. Each run occurs in a new sandbox, and each result tells how sure it is.

Your first MMM in Guided mode Quickstart for data scientists What's new in 0.5

docs.title: Two ways in, one model
docs.text: The two groups edit the same ModelSpec. Each Guided screen has View as YAML. The changes of an expert come back to Guided mode with no loss. Who it is for, and who it is not for.

docs.title: Analysts
docs.text:
Upload → report → scenario in minutes, with honest uncertainty.

  • Select what you want to learn. Answer questions such as "which column is revenue?". The platform suggests the answer and tells you why.
  • Tell what you already believe ("TV returns 1.5 to 4 per euro"), or enter a lift test.
  • Read a report in plain words. A sanity scorecard tells you if you can trust it.
  • Move the what-if sliders. Your browser gives the answers. The range stays honest when some channels move at the same time. "Run exact" asks the full model.
  • Share a live chart, or put the model in a Google Sheet.
  • If you are not sure which model to use, use Help me choose. It asks some questions and explains its recommendations. Each option has an About card in plain words.

Your first analysis in Guided mode

docs.title: Data scientists
docs.text:
Any PyMC, scikit-learn or forecasting model. The same preprocessing, exactly. Endpoints in one click.

  • A PyMC model is one build() method. An sklearn model is one estimator(). Built-in marketing-mix, forecasting, demand and choice models are ready to use.
  • Steps learn on the training data only. At score time, the platform replays them and does not fit them again. This applies to forecasts, new markets and counterfactuals.
  • Uncertainty is a primary part of each result: draws, quantiles or intervals. Each one has the aggregations that are valid for it.
  • Promote a version to an endpoint through the scorecard gate. Copy a snippet for Python, TypeScript, curl, R, Apps Script or a notebook.
  • Automate the statistics with workflows of tests, branches, searches, backtests and governance checks. Run them live from mapi workflows run --watch or api.workflows.

Quickstart: zero to first model · Workflow cookbook

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    D["Your data<br/>CSV · Parquet · MFF ·<br/>Meridian"] --> I["Sandboxed ingest<br/>checked, profiled,<br/>dims and roles"]
    Q["Guided answers<br/>or a YAML spec"] --> V{{"Static checks<br/>before any compute"}}
    I --> V
    V --> F["Fit in a fresh sandbox<br/>preprocessing learned<br/>on train only"]
    F --> B[("Signed bundle<br/>states · posterior ·<br/>scorecard · grids")]
    W["Workflow<br/>tests → decisions →<br/>search → backtest"] -.-> F
    B --> R["Report, explorers,<br/>what-if, budget plans"]
    B --> G{{"Governance<br/>null tests · benchmarks ·<br/>second-person approval"}}
    G --> E["Endpoint<br/>gated on the scorecard<br/>and the validation"]
    E --> S["Sheets · BI embeds ·<br/>webhooks ·<br/>Python, TS, R"]
  1. Your data stays labelled. The upload becomes an xr.Dataset with named dims, roles and units. No later part of the process uses the position of the data.
  2. Mistakes fail early. Examples are a spec that leaks the holdout, a forecast past the limit of the model, or a market that the model did not see. You get typed errors before any compute.
  3. The fit learns, and the score replays. Each preprocessing step stores what it learned. Thus a forecast or a new market goes through exactly the same transformations. Then the result goes back into your units.
  4. The platform checks results two times. It compares the outputs with the checksums of the storage, and it signs them. The scorecard checks convergence, holdout error and plausibility.
  5. Models must show that they are good. A governance policy applies null tests and benchmarks to each version and records the evidence. If you ask, it waits for a second person. Endpoints can refuse all versions that are not validated.
  6. Other tools connect to an endpoint, not to a file. Promote a better model, and all integrations use it. Roll back with one call.
  7. Full analyses repeat automatically. A workflow runs the tests, decisions, fits and checks again each Monday, or when the data changes. It uses again each step whose inputs did not change.

docs.title: Your first MMM in Guided mode
docs.text:
This section shows the full path of a geo marketing-mix model. The path starts with a spreadsheet of weekly spend and revenue by region. It ends with a budget scenario. The times are from an automated "tester" on a laptop. The platform used almost all of this time. The full path took 135 seconds from upload to scenario.

  1. Choose "Geo marketing mix". Then drop your CSV file on the page. The platform makes a profile of each column in your browser. It suggests which column is revenue and which columns are spend. It also tells why. (5 s)
  2. Say what you believe, if you have beliefs. For example, give an ROI range for each channel, or a lift test. Preview what this means shows it in business units before the fit. (22 s, optional)
  3. Fit the model. The progress shows in plain language. The platform tests the model on weeks that it did not see. Then it fits the model again on all the data. (80 s)
  4. Read the results. You see the ROI and share of each channel with 90% ranges. You also see the sanity scorecard, with the next action for each check. (instant)
  5. Ask "what if". Move search +20%. The change in revenue and its range show immediately. Run exact confirms the result with the full model. (30 s with the exact run and a forecast)
  6. Share it. Put the model live as an endpoint, or share a chart with a link.

The full tutorial, with screenshots · From a spreadsheet to a draft, with curl

Templates: start from the question, not from the model.

Your data: suggested answers, each with its reason.

Beliefs: ROI ranges and lift tests, with a preview in business units.

Results: each number with the range that it can really be in.

Scorecard: can you trust it, and what to do if you cannot.

What if: instant answers from a response curve for each draw.

docs.title: What's new in v0.5
docs.text:
• Workflows that think like a statistician

    Unit roots → differencing → AR/MA orders → rolling-origin backtest → ARIMAX vs naive → select → governance. All of these steps are one versioned YAML graph. The graph has live node status, a cache, schedules and dataset triggers. It has seventeen statistical tests, seven split plans and Diebold-Mariano.

    Workflow cookbook

  • Models must beat noise

    Governance policies have these checks: shuffled-target and placebo-regressor null tests, naive benchmarks, residual whiteness, stability, signs and prior sensitivity. They also have approval by a second person and evidence packs. Endpoints refuse models that are not validated.

    Can you trust this model?

  • Data and Model Explorers

    Before you make a model, see stationarity, cross-correlation with the KPI, STL, VIF and quality warnings. After the fit, see parameters, residual tests, IRF/FEVD, forecasts, backtests and side-by-side comparisons.

    Explore a dataset

  • mmm-framework MMMs and budget plans

    mmm.bayesian pools over geos and products. mmm.frequentist fits in seconds. You get business priors and lift tests. The platform optimises budgets from the posterior with risk objectives.

    Marketing-mix models

  • Twelve statsmodels models

    The models go from SARIMAX to VECM and Markov switching. They have future drivers, prediction intervals, impulse responses and cointegration tests.

    statsmodels models

  • About cards and Help me choose

    Each model, step, node, check and template explains itself in plain words. Eight questions give a ranked shortlist with reasons. Use the web app, mapi choose or api.catalog.recommend().

    Choosing a model

docs.title: See it at work
docs.text:
Workflows: tests, decisions, searches, backtests and governance in one graph, with typed ports. Run monitor: each step, decision and verdict live, with the cost of the run. Governance: checks, evidence and the approval of a second person. Null tests: the real model must be better than the same model fitted on shuffled results. Data Explorer: a plain verdict that tells if each series wanders. Budget plans: mmm-framework plans from the posterior, with the frontier.

Everything that is new in 0.5

docs.title: What came in v0.4
docs.text:
• Guided mode

    Guided mode has four templates (geo marketing mix, weekly forecast, demand by store, customer choice). It finds the roles of columns and has MFF and Meridian presets. You can open drafts as YAML. A lock can keep a project in Guided mode only.

    Tutorial

  • Business priors and lift tests

    A sandbox translates ROI or contribution-share ranges into model priors. A prior-predictive preview shows the result. Experiments go into the likelihood as calibration.

    Guided modelling

  • Sanity scorecard and promotion gate

    The scorecard has checks for convergence, holdout error and coverage, plausibility and data. Each check is in plain words. A pass goes live. A warn needs an audited reason from an admin. The gate blocks a fail.

    The gate

  • What-if, forecasts, counterfactuals

    The sliders use response curves that the platform calculates before, for each posterior draw. Thus the bands stay joint and honest. "Run exact" scores the full model with common random numbers.

    What if…

  • Endpoints, aliases and snippets

    Each use gets a stable alias, with history and rollback. Each endpoint has a frozen input contract with an example call, and score:<alias> tokens. The platform makes code in seven flavours.

    Integrations hub

  • Signed webhooks

    The events are run.*, model.version.ready, endpoint.promoted and score.completed. They are HMAC-signed and go through an SSRF guard. The platform tries them again if they fail, logs them, and can send them again.

    Receive webhooks

  • Embeds and static renders

    Chart links are read-only and expire. Use them in Notion, Slack, Looker Studio or Power BI. The sandbox also renders PNG, SVG or PDF files.

    Embed a chart

  • Google Sheets

    A card on each endpoint makes an Apps Script. The script writes a forecast into a sheet each morning. Its token has a scope of that one endpoint only.

    Connect Sheets

  • Sign-up and the data lifecycle

    Users can make their own workspaces, with e-mail verification and abuse controls. There is a GDPR export and a tenant deletion that purges all stores. There is also a Cloud Armor policy.

    Deleting and exporting data

  • A customer-choice model

    choice.multinomial_logit is a conditional logit with household effects. It has categorical holdout metrics: the log score, Brier, and the hit rate compared with a guess of the favourite each time.

    Use cases

  • Client and CLI for all of it

    api.endpoint("…").score(ds) returns an xarray.Dataset. From a terminal, mapi endpoints, webhooks, plots, guided, priors and tenant do the other tasks.

    The Python client

docs.title: Measured, not promised
docs.text:
We measured these values on an 8-core laptop against the full stack. The fits were real fits in the sandboxed runner. The v0.5 journeys used the data and settings of M3.5 verification:

37–40 sthe canonical workflow: 19 nodes from unit-root tests to governance, through the orchestrator and the sandboxed runner p = 0.7–0.95an ARIMAX fitted on pure noise, compared with 19 fits on shuffled data. The validation fails. Promotion gives NOT_VALIDATED. 0.1 %of the result that a model fitted on real signal gave to three fake noise drivers 26 sa validation with the null tests: 19 fits on shuffled data plus 3 fake drivers 10–16 san mmm-framework budget plan with a 5-point efficient frontier, in the sandbox

These runs found eight defects that unit, integration and mocked-browser tests did not find. We repaired each defect and added a regression test before the release. The v0.4 journey used the data of M3 verification:

The fit used 79 s. 0.08 %the difference between the instant slider and the exact model, for TV at half budget (−454,590 vs −454,241, exact sd 14,003) 0.01 %the difference between "TV off" from the grid and an exact counterfactual run (−1,046,519 vs −1,046,414) 76–81 %of each translated prior is in the 80% ROI range that the analyst gave 0 objectsstay in five buckets after a tenant deletion (285 before). docs.title: Connect it to everything
docs.text:
Integrations: Sheets, BI and webhooks in a few steps. Endpoints: one alias, and each promotion and rollback with its reason. Snippets: Python, TypeScript, curl, R, Apps Script, notebook. Embeds: a read-only chart for a dashboard or a document. You can revoke it at any time. 
geo_mmm = api.endpoint("geo-mmm-prod")
schema = geo_mmm.schema()
print(sorted(schema.snapshot.input_schema.vars))

plan = xr.Dataset(
    {"spend_local": (("market", "channel", "date"), np.array([[[1200.0], [5300.0]]]))},
    coords={"market": ["de"], "channel": ["search", "tv"], "date": ["2025-12-30"]},
)
result = geo_mmm.score(plan, wait=60)  # inline XrJSON in, xr.Dataset out
print(result["revenue_local"].sel(stat="mean").values)

Tutorials · Use cases · The Python client

docs.title: The core idea: fit with preprocessing, score with the same preprocessing
docs.text:
The same pipeline object runs at fit time and at score time. At fit time, each step learns its state from the training data. At score time, it replays that state. Steps that look back in time store a small tail for each group. Thus a forecast sees exactly the history that the model used for the fit.

flowchart LR
    subgraph FIT["Fit (once)"]
        direction LR
        A["Daily spend & revenue<br/>local currency"] --> B["fx_convert<br/>(side table)"]
        B --> C["resample<br/>daily → weekly"]
        C --> S{{"split<br/>last 8 weeks"}}
        S --> D["holidays<br/><i>pinned side table</i>"]
        D --> M["model.fit<br/><i>keeps the fitted history<br/>for carry-over</i>"]
    end
    M --> BUN[("Bundle<br/>states · context tails · posterior<br/>hashes · no pickle")]
    subgraph SCORE["Score (any time)"]
        direction LR
        F["Next quarter's plan<br/>or a new market"] --> G["same steps,<br/><b>replayed</b> state"]
        G --> H["model.score"]
        H --> I["inverse → weekly EUR<br/>summaries · your names"]
    end
    BUN --> G
What you writeWhat the platform doesWhat you get back 
pipeline:
  - {id: to_eur, use: core.fx_convert@^1, with: {vars: [y, spend], table: fx, ...}}
  - {id: weekly, use: core.resample@^1,   with: {dim: time, freq: W-SUN, how: sum}}
  - {id: hols,   use: core.holidays@^1,   with: {table: holidays, along: time}}
model:
  use: mmm.bayesian@^1                 # mmm-framework: scaling and carry-over inside
  settings: {hierarchy: {pool_over: [geo]}, new_levels: hyperprior}
  fit: {mode: evaluate_then_refit}
  1. The platform checks the full spec statically. It checks names, dims, settings and units at each stage. It also checks where the split occurs, and if a step can learn from the holdout (LEAKAGE_RISK).
  2. It fits each stateful step on the training weeks only, and then fits the model. Then it scores the holdout through the same path that a forecast uses and records the metrics.
  3. It fits again on all weeks, so that forecasts start from the latest data. Then it writes a bundle with each state, context tail and hash.
  • Forecasts in weekly EUR, not in "model units". The model reports its own units. The units stop at the weekly resample, because you cannot get daily values back from weekly sums. The output_space (model-owned) and units attributes of the output tell this.
  • A new market that comes from the fitted hyperprior. Its range is honestly wider than the range of a known market.
  • What-if deltas that share their noise with the baseline (common random numbers). Thus the delta shows the change, not the sampling noise.

This is the same model in plain Python, without a server. The test suite runs each snippet on this site:

from mapi_sdk import fit_spec

bundle = fit_spec(spec, data, registry=registry, raw_schema=schema)
print(bundle.metrics.values)  # holdout metrics, in units sold: {'rmse': ..., 'mape': ..., ...}
print(bundle.metrics.n_holdout)  # 48 cells: 3 stores x 2 skus x 8 weeks

from mapi_spec import ErrorCode, MapiError


def try_score(request_yaml: str, payload: xr.Dataset) -> ErrorCode:
    try:
        score_bundle(bundle, request_yaml, payload, registry=registry)
    except MapiError as err:
        print(err.code, "-", err)
        return err.code
    raise AssertionError("expected a typed error")


FORECAST = """
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://quickstart/fruit-demand
mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 4}
"""

# 1. a forecast without next month's promotions: promo is future_required
code_1 = try_score(FORECAST, plan.drop_vars("promo"))

# 2. quantiles are per cell, so "total over all stores" would be a made-up number
code_2 = try_score(FORECAST + "output: {aggregate: {over: [store]}}\n", plan)

# 3. a product outside the fitted range: sku is a fixed dim
code_3 = try_score(FORECAST, plan.assign_coords(sku=["apples", "kiwis"]))

docs.title: Secure by design
docs.text:
The platform can run models and data from persons that it does not trust. The most important controls are not settings that you can forget to set. They are part of how the platform works. The security model tells what each control stops. It also tells what we must still verify in the cloud.

  • A fresh sandbox per run

    Each ingest, fit, score and render runs in its own sandbox (a microVM on Cloud Run Jobs). The sandbox has no secrets. Its only network access is signed URLs to its own objects. The code enforces the placement by trust tier.

  • Tenants never see each other

    Each table has PostgreSQL row-level security. It is pinned for each transaction, and it fails closed. The platform checks roles at each request. Operators manage the platform, but they do not read tenant data.

  • Outputs are claims

    The platform compares the outputs of a run with the hashes and generations of the store. Then it copies the outputs to a location where runs cannot write, and signs them. It makes download links only after it verifies the signature.

  • Integrations that cannot be turned against you

    Webhooks are HMAC-signed. They go through an SSRF guard that pins the checked address. Embed links show only platform recipes and have no credential. You can revoke them. Snippets never contain a secret.

  • Compute you can see and cap

    Quotas are in vCPU-seconds for each token, tenant and platform. Each token that calls an endpoint has a budget. Each run shows a cost. There is a global spend cap and an audited kill switch.

  • No pickle, anywhere

    Bundles are single zarr zips plus JSON sidecars. Native models are skops (allow-listed types) or xgboost JSON. Each file has CRC32C, MD5 and SHA-256 values. The platform verifies them when it reads the file.

docs.title: Run it for many teams
docs.text:
One deployment serves many organisations. Users sign up, or sign in with their own identity provider. They work in the projects where they have a role, and they see the cost of their compute. Operators manage the platform, but they never read the data of a tenant.

Tenants and projects: your role in each project, and the trust tier of each tenant.

Usage: the metered cost of each run, by token and resource class, against each quota.

Your data: a GDPR export, and a deletion that purges all stores.

Administration · Deploy on your laptop or Google Cloud · Roadmap: what comes next

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
Each use case below starts from an item that is ready to use. This item is a Guided template that an analyst can run from a spreadsheet, or a gallery workflow that automates the full analysis. Each use case also has a built-in model. A data scientist can configure, extend or replace this model in a spec. All use cases share the platform: sandboxed runs, the scorecard, governance policies, the explorers, endpoints, snippets, webhooks and embeds.

Use case Start from Model The question it answers Budget planning Guided Geo marketing mix, or the mmm_governed workflow mmm.bayesian (or mmm.frequentist), on mmm-framework What does each channel bring in, and where must the next euro go? Governed forecasting pipeline The ts_readiness_arimax workflow, scheduled ts.sarimax (ARIMAX), checked against naive forecasts Can we publish this forecast each Monday? Can we prove that it is better than a naive forecast? Macro and VAR analysis The var_vecm_cointegration workflow ts.vecm or ts.var (also ts.varmax, ts.dynamic_factor) Do these series move together, and what happens to one when another is shocked? Weekly forecasting Guided Weekly forecast ts.hsgp_trend What will this series do over the next weeks, and how sure are we? Store demand Guided Demand by store tabular.regressor (xgboost, quantiles) How much will each store sell, including a store that opens next month? Customer choice Guided Customer choice choice.multinomial_logit Which product does a shopper pick, and how does a price change shift that?

docs.title: Marketing-mix budget planning
docs.text:
The question. Media spend goes to TV, search and social in some markets. What did each channel add to revenue? What does each euro return now? How do we divide the budget of the next quarter?

The data. One row for each week and market: revenue, spend for each channel, and optional controls (for example, price or distribution). Two years of weekly data is a good start. The platform recognises MFF long tables and Meridian-shaped tables directly.

What you get.

  • Contribution and ROI for each channel and market with 90% ranges, response curves, and a decomposition of revenue into baseline and channels.
  • Beliefs as ROI or share ranges, and lift tests as calibration. A sandbox translates them into model priors, with a preview in business units.
  • What-if sliders whose ranges stay joint when some channels move. "Run exact", counterfactuals with a channel set to off, and forecasts.
  • Budget plans from the model (POST …:optimize, mmm-framework planning). A plan gives the allocation in your bounds, the uplift and the probability that it helps. It also gives the stability of each move and the efficient frontier. A planning tool can call an endpoint for the plan.
  • Proof before the plan. The default marketing-mix policy fits the model again on shuffled sales and with fake noise channels. It checks the effect signs and the holdout error, and records the evidence. The mmm_governed workflow does all of this in one run: collinearity check, fit, policy, report and evidence pack.

Start here. Your first MMM in Guided mode → Priors, lift tests and the scorecard → Optimise a budget. Writing your own MMM spec: the marketing-mix guide and mmm-framework on the platform.

docs.title: Governed forecasting pipeline
docs.text:
The question. Finance publishes a weekly demand forecast. Other teams use it for their plans. Each Monday, Finance must update it with the latest data. The person who approves it must know three things. The data chose the model. The model is better than a naive forecast on weeks that it did not see. The model does not only fit noise.

The data. One weekly KPI with a minimum of two years of history. Also drivers that you know before (prices, promotions, holidays). You upload them as a new dataset version each week.

What you get.

  • The ts_readiness_arimax workflow. A schedule (0 6 * * 1, Europe/Berlin) or a trigger on each new dataset version runs it:
    • ADF, KPSS, Phillips-Perron and Zivot-Andrews decide the differencing.
    • An information-criterion search selects the AR and MA orders.
    • An expanding-window backtest scores ARIMAX against naive and seasonal-naive forecasts. It uses the same folds at 1, 4 and 8 weeks.
    • The workflow keeps the model only if it is better than these forecasts.
  • A governance policy for forecasts that you publish: null tests, benchmarks, residual whiteness and holdout accuracy. It has the approval of a second person and require_validated_for_promotion. Thus the endpoint that the planners call can serve only a validated version. If not, it gives 409 NOT_VALIDATED.
  • A record of the run each week. It has the verdict of each test, each branch with the values that it read and the selected orders. It also has the backtest table, the Diebold-Mariano verdict, the governance evidence and an evidence pack for the auditor. The platform uses unchanged steps again from the cache. Thus a new run costs only what changed.

We captured the canonical run on a laptop, with a weekly KPI that wanders. All four tests say "difference once". The search selects ARIMA(1, 1, 1). On 13 held-out weeks, the model is 25% better than "same as last week". But the record also tells that the one-week advantage over naive is possibly luck. It also tells that two of twenty shuffled fits were equally good. An approval needs this type of honesty (the full output).

Start here. Workflow cookbook: readiness to ARIMAX → Validate models with governance policies → Schedules and triggers → Endpoints and webhooks.

docs.title: Macro and VAR analysis
docs.text:
The question. Some series drive each other. Examples are income and consumption, the prices of close substitutes, or sales, distribution and search interest. Are the series tied together in the long run? If one series gets a shock, how do the others respond, and for how long? Does one series help to predict another?

The data. Two to five series at the same frequency, with one value for each series and period (value(series, quarter)). The ingest reads a wide sheet with the wide mapping. The best length is 50 periods or more.

What you get.

  • The var_vecm_cointegration workflow. A Johansen trace test decides the branch. Tied series get a cointegration-rank search and a VECM on the levels. The workflow differences the series that are not tied. AIC selects the lag order, and the workflow fits a VAR on the changes. Granger tests run on the two branches. The forecast comes from the system that the workflow fitted.
  • Impulse responses with bands and variance decompositions in the Model Explorer. Also the Johansen table, the speed of adjustment (alpha: how fast a gap closes), the long-run relations (beta) and Granger tables.
  • ts.varmax when outside drivers are important. ts.dynamic_factor for many series that move with some common factors. ts.ecm (ARDL bounds test) for one equation with long-run drivers.

We ran the workflow of the cookbook on a laptop with three simulated weekly series (160 weeks). In the data, a and b share one stochastic trend, and c wanders alone. The workflow found exactly that:

johansen  The series share at least one long-run relationship.
          (trace statistic 69.1, rank 1)
tied      took the then arm   {'nodes.johansen.rank': 1}
rank      1
vecm      model://growth/wf-macro-system-vecm@v1
granger   Past values of the driver help predict the result.
          (b -> a, lag 1, p = 0.0015)
forecast  8 weeks: dataset://growth/wf-macro-system-forecast-forecast@v1
skipped   diff, lags, var   (the VAR branch was not needed)

(This is a summary of the node results of the run. The cookbook shows the client calls that read them.)

Start here. Workflow cookbook: VAR/VECM cointegration → statsmodels time-series models → Explore a model: impulse responses.

docs.title: Weekly forecasting
docs.text:
The question. What will the orders, visits, calls or sales be in the next 8 to 26 weeks? What is the range that a planner can use?

The data. One date column and one numeric column, weekly or daily. For a seasonal pattern, the history must have a minimum of two seasons.

What you get.

  • A forecast fan: the median and the 50% and 90% ranges, with the fitted history and the split line. Thus you can see the result of the model on the weeks that it did not see.
  • A holdout check: the error, and how frequently the actual values were in the 90% range.
  • The max_extension of the model declares how far it can forecast. The platform refuses a longer horizon with HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT before any compute.
  • A Google Sheet that gets a new forecast from the endpoint each morning.

Start here. The Guided tutorial (pick Weekly forecast) → Connect Google Sheets → Forecasting and sequential models.

docs.title: Demand by store
docs.text:
The question. How many units will each store sell each week, with the prices, promotions and calendar? How many units will a store sell that the model did not see?

The data. One row for each store and week: units sold, and drivers (for example, price and a promotion flag).

What you get.

  • An xgboost model with calendar features. A low and a high estimate (quantiles) for each store and week, and the importance of each driver.
  • The platform scores new stores by declaration. The policy of the store dim tells if the platform can score a store that the model did not see, and how. The result does not depend on what the model does with an unknown category.
  • An endpoint that a replenishment system can call with the plan for the next week. A webhook when a new fit is ready.

Start here. The Guided tutorial (pick Demand by store) → Tabular models → Endpoints and webhooks → Receive webhooks. The xgb_store_demand conformance fixture runs the same problem end to end in some seconds.

docs.title: Customer choice
docs.text:
The question. On each shopping trip, which product does a household select? How does a change in price or a promotion move the shares?

The data. One row for each trip and product: the product that the household selected, its price and its promotion, if there is one. The row identifies the household and the trip.

What you get.

  • A conditional logit with household effects and Bayesian-bootstrap draws.
  • The holdout hit rate on the last trip of each household. The scorecard compares it, in plain words, with a guess of the most popular product each time.
  • Price and promotion counterfactuals: how the shares move when a price changes.

Start here. The Guided tutorial (pick Customer choice) → Built-in models.

docs.title: Your own model
docs.text: If none of these use cases is correct for you, write your own model. A PyMC model is one build() method, and an sklearn model is one estimator(). The platform does the coordinates, splits, replayed preprocessing, summaries, bundles, endpoints and integrations. Port a model in 15 minutes · Why modeling-api?

docs.title: What's new in 0.5 v0.5
docs.text:
v0.4 made one model easy to fit, read and share. v0.5 makes the full analysis around the model repeatable and trustworthy. A weekly forecast is not "fit an ARIMA and hope" now. It is a versioned workflow. The workflow does these steps:

  1. It tests the series for unit roots.
  2. It decides the differencing.
  3. It searches the AR and MA orders.
  4. It backtests the model on rolling origins against naive forecasts.
  5. It keeps the model only if the model wins.
  6. It checks the model against shuffled data and fake drivers.
  7. It records the evidence.
  8. It waits for the sign-off of a colleague.

The workflow also runs again each Monday morning automatically.

  • Workflows

    A workflow is a versioned YAML graph. It can contain statistical tests, transforms, branches, train/test plans, order searches, model fits, evaluations, governance checks and reports. You get live node status, a cache for unchanged steps, schedules and dataset triggers.

    Workflow cookbook

  • Governance and null tests

    Policies tell which checks a model must pass and who must approve. For example, the model must be better than the same model fitted on shuffled results. It must give no credit to fake noise drivers, and it must be better than naive forecasts. Promotion refuses models that are not validated. Evidence packs are available for auditors.

    Can you trust this model?

  • Data and Model Explorers

    The Data Explorer has thirteen sections, for example profiles, stationarity, cross-correlation with the KPI, STL, VIF and quality warnings. The Model Explorer has eleven sections, for example parameters, residual tests, IRF/FEVD, forecasts, backtests and side-by-side comparisons with Diebold-Mariano tests.

    Explore a dataset · Explore a model

  • mmm-framework marketing-mix models

    mmm.bayesian is national or pooled over geos and products. mmm.frequentist is a ridge model with bootstrap ranges. You also get business priors, lift tests, response curves and budget optimisation with risk objectives and an efficient frontier.

    Marketing-mix models

  • Twelve statsmodels time-series models

    The models are SARIMAX, ARIMA, ETS, Theta, unobserved components, ARDL, error correction, VAR, VECM, VARMAX, dynamic factors and Markov switching. They support future drivers, prediction intervals, impulse responses, Granger and cointegration tests, and panels for each series.

    statsmodels models

  • About cards and Help me choose

    Each model, step, node, check and template has an About card in plain words. The card tells what the item does, when to use it and when not to use it. It also tells what the item needs and what it gives. Help me choose changes eight answers into a ranked shortlist with the reasons.

    Choosing a model

docs.title: For analysts: answers you can defend
docs.text:
• Help me choose. Possibly you do not know if you need an ARIMAX, an exponential smoothing model or a marketing-mix model. Answer a maximum of eight questions, for example "What do you want to do?", "What does your data look like?" and "Do you need a range?". You get the best fits. Each fit has the reasons, the cautions and its About card. You can use Help me choose in the web app, in the terminal (mapi choose) or in Python.
  • Templates that think like a statistician. Start a workflow from the gallery, for example Is my weekly KPI ready to forecast?, Do these series move together?, A governed marketing-mix model or Forecast bake-off. Read the result as a report. Each test has a plain verdict ("The series wanders: consider differencing it."). Each decision shows the numbers that it read. Each comparison says "is possibly luck" or "It is not luck".
  • A model must earn its place. Before a person uses a model, the platform shuffles the results that the model was fitted on. Then it fits the model again, many times. A model that learned something real must be clearly better on the real data. The platform also adds drivers that are pure noise. These drivers must get almost no credit. The null tests explained page shows why this is important, without formulas.
  • Explore before you model. The Data Explorer shows gaps, constant columns, outliers, collinear drivers and series that wander. It also shows which drivers move with the KPI, and at which lag.

docs.title: For data scientists: the statistics, end to end
docs.text:
• A DAG with typed ports. The port types are dataset, test_result, split_plan, model_version, metrics, table, evidence and report. The server validates the DAG statically with JSON pointers before a run starts. Branches use a safe expression language (never eval) and record the values that they read. Alternatives ([diff.data, inputs.data]) take the first input that exists.
  • Seventeen statistical tests. We checked these tests against statsmodels/scipy/arch reference values. The tests are:
    • ADF, KPSS, Phillips-Perron, Zivot-Andrews, Johansen and Engle-Granger
    • Ljung-Box, Jarque-Bera, Breusch-Pagan, White and ARCH-LM
    • Granger, ACF/PACF, seasonal strength, VIF, CUSUM and Chow.
  • Split plans and searches. There are seven split plans: holdout, rolling origin, expanding window, blocked k-fold, purged k-fold, geo holdout and nested. There are ARMA/SARIMA/VAR-lag/cointegration-rank searches and grid searches on backtests. There is also Diebold-Mariano with the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction.
  • Honest backtests. Each candidate and each naive benchmark use the same folds. A gap allows for late data. The backtest scores each horizon separately.
  • Governance with real statistics. Each check gives the value, the threshold and the evidence. The checks change for Bayesian, frequentist and machine-learning models. The checks are:
    • block-permutation tests of the target
    • placebo noise regressors, measured by ablation, and time-shifted placebos
    • out-of-sample skill against naive and seasonal-naive forecasts
    • Ljung-Box whiteness and rolling-window stability
    • prior sensitivity, parametric-bootstrap recovery, R-hat and holdout accuracy.
  • All of it from Python and the terminal. The Python client has api.workflows, api.governance, api.validations, api.explorations, api.models.optimize and api.catalog.recommend. The CLI has mapi workflows run --watch, mapi validate model, mapi approve, mapi explore, mapi optimize and mapi choose.

docs.title: The canonical example, three ways
docs.text:
The cookbook shows each node of the example. This is a short version:

PythonCommand lineHTTP 
from mapi_client import WorkflowEnd, WorkflowEventFrame, WorkflowSnapshot

# create the workflow, or save the file as its next revision when it changed
workflow, revision = api.workflows.upsert(Path("weekly-readiness.yaml"))
run = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest"},  # pinned to a version at start
    params={"drivers": ["price"], "window": 80, "max_p": 2, "max_q": 2},
)
for item in api.workflows.stream_events(run.run_id):  # server-sent events, resumable
    match item:
        case WorkflowSnapshot(run=now):
            print(f"{len(now.nodes)} nodes, {now.status.value}")
        case WorkflowEventFrame(event=e) if e.type.value == "workflow.branch.decided":
            print(f"  {e.node_id}: took the {e.data['arm']} arm")
        case WorkflowEventFrame(event=e) if e.node_id is not None:
            print(f"  {e.node_id}: {e.type.value.rsplit('.', 1)[-1]}")
        case WorkflowEnd(status=status):
            print("run", status.value if status else "ended")

mapi workflows templates                      # the gallery, in plain words
mapi workflows init ts_readiness_arimax --name weekly-readiness   # writes weekly-readiness.yaml
mapi workflows validate weekly-readiness.yaml # checked by the server: pointers to every problem
mapi workflows apply weekly-readiness.yaml -m "first version"     # create, or save a revision
mapi workflows run weekly-readiness \
  --input data=dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest \
  --param 'drivers=["price"]' --param window=104 \
  --watch                                     # live node status; exit 1 if the run fails

api POST /v1/workflows -d "$(jq -Rs '{text: .}' weekly-readiness.yaml)"
api POST "/v1/workflows/$WF/runs" -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" -d '{
  "inputs": {"data": "dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest"},
  "params": {"drivers": ["price"]}}'
curl -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" "$API/v1/workflow-runs/$RUN/events"

The Python walkthrough printed this output on a live local stack. The data was three years of a weekly KPI that wanders, with a price driver. We made the event stream shorter. The run took about two minutes on a laptop. Most of the time was for sandboxed fits.

23 nodes, queued
  adf: queued
  kpss: queued
  …
  adf: succeeded
  kpss: succeeded
  …
  wanders: took the then arm
  seasonal: took the else arm
  sdiff: skipped
  …
  governance: succeeded
  trusted: took the then arm
run succeeded
The series wanders: consider differencing it.
wanders then {'nodes.pp.reject': False, 'nodes.za.reject': False, 'nodes.adf.reject': False, 'nodes.kpss.reject': True}
seasonal else {'nodes.seas.seasonal': False}
trusted then {'nodes.governance.passed': True}
ARIMA(1, 1, 1)
The difference between backtest and naive at horizon 1 is possibly luck.
backtest has the best average error (1.83) and beats every benchmark (the strongest, naive, scored 1.87).
passed
validated
data.quality                 pass    No data problems found (156 periods of history).
convergence                  pass    The fit reported no convergence problems.
baseline.beats_naive         pass    On the 13 held-out periods the model's error is 25% lower than 'same as last period' (the strongest simple benchmark).
holdout.accuracy             pass    On data it was not fitted on, the model's average percentage error is 1.8% (limit 15%).
residuals.whiteness          pass    No pattern is left in the errors (Ljung-Box p = 0.39 at 10 lags).
null.permutation_target      pass    The model did better on held-out data (skill 0.236) than all 20 fits with the drivers price shuffled in blocks of 7 (the result untouched) (p = 0.048).
stability.rolling_params     fail    ar.L1 changes a lot across windows of history (variation 1205%): the relationship may not be stable over time.

This output shows that the platform is honest. It does not flatter the model:

  • All four unit-root tests agree that the series wanders. Thus the workflow differences the series one time.
  • On weeks that it did not see, ARIMAX is 25% better than "same as last week".
  • ARIMAX forecasts better than all twenty fits with the price driver shuffled in time. Thus the driver has real information.
  • But Diebold-Mariano says that the one-week-ahead advantage over naive is possibly luck.
  • The AR coefficient changes across windows of history.

The default forecasting policy uses stability as information only. Thus the version is validated, and the failure stays on the record for the reviewer. A stricter policy makes the failure blocking. Each validation makes its own random shuffles. Thus the p-value of the shuffled-driver test changes a little between validations.

The tests of the documentation run this walkthrough, without changes, against a real server.

docs.title: Upgrading from 0.4
docs.text:
• mmm-framework is the only marketing-mix engine. We removed the earlier marketing-mix plugins. Specs move to mmm.bayesian@^1. They do not have their own scaling and lag steps now, because the model controls scaling, carry-over and units. For budget optimisation, use POST …:optimize (api.models.optimize, mapi optimize). See Marketing-mix models and the Removed section of the CHANGELOG.

  • Contract version 0.2. This version adds:

    • resources: workflow, policy and tenant_policy
    • actions: validate and approve
    • scopes: workflows:write, workflows:run, models:validate and policies:manage
    • the reviewer capability on memberships.

    An API token cannot approve. - Migrations 0011_workflows and 0012_governance. These migrations add workflow and governance tables under forced row-level security. - Promotion can now need validation. If a policy has require_validated_for_promotion, endpoints refuse unvalidated versions with 409 NOT_VALIDATED. The default policies that the platform seeds on first use do not gate promotion. You must turn on this gate yourself. - Client and CLI. All of the items above are new API surface. No existing signature changed. mapi_client exports WorkflowSnapshot, WorkflowEventFrame and WorkflowEnd for the workflow event stream.

docs.title: What is not in 0.5 yet
docs.text:
• mmm.nested and mmm.multivariate (the extensions of mmm-framework) have About cards but no plugin. The multiplicative specification, time-varying effects and price/promotion levers are not available.
  • statsmodels models do not have the counterfactual, simulate or filter score modes. A what-if is a forecast with changed future drivers.
  • evaluate.residuals and model.forecast nodes make tables, not plots.
  • We did not run 0.5 on real Google Cloud or in Docker. See the release notes.

docs.title: Why modeling-api?
docs.text:
Most statistical models that are important to a business start in a notebook. Someone explains them in a slide deck, and then the work stops. To make the models useful, a second project is necessary, and most of it is plumbing. The project must put the models in front of the persons who make decisions. It must keep the models honest after the data changes. It must prove that they learned something real, and let other tools use them.

modeling-api is that second project, done one time, for a specific type of model: Bayesian and classical models of labelled, multi-dimensional data (panels, time series, hierarchies). The preprocessing and uncertainty of these models must stay correct in production. Their analysis must be repeatable and defensible.

docs.title: The problems it solves
docs.text: The problem What usually happens What modeling-api does The preprocessing at score time is not the preprocessing at fit time Someone writes the scaling, lags and currency conversion again in the service. Or they fit them again on the new data, or they forget them Steps store what they learned at fit time and replay it at score time. This includes the look-back tail of each group. Inverse transforms bring answers back to your units (Pipelines) Data is positional Column 7 changes meaning. A new market is "row 12". The lags of a forecast start from the wrong week Data is an xr.Dataset with named dims. Each dim declares what can occur at score time (fixed, extend, new_levels). The platform checks requests against it before any compute (Labelled data) The analysis is only in the head of one person "I ran ADF, it looked non-stationary, so I differenced and tried a few ARIMAs". This occurs one time, by hand, and nobody writes it down A workflow runs the tests and makes the decisions by stated rules. It searches the orders, backtests against naive forecasts and records each value that it read. It runs again on a schedule or when the data changes. It uses the unchanged steps again (Workflows) A model goes live because it looks good The fit looks good, and there is an R² on the training data. Nobody checks if noise can give the same result Governance policies: the model must be better than the same model fitted on shuffled results. It must give no credit to fake noise drivers. It must be better than naive benchmarks out of sample. A second person approves, and endpoints refuse versions that are not validated (Null tests explained) Uncertainty is lost or added incorrectly A point estimate controls a budget decision. Someone adds the 90% quantiles of 40 stores Each output has its representation (draws, quantiles, interval, point, moments). The platform gives only the valid summaries and aggregations (Representations) Each scenario needs the data scientist The analyst asks "what if we move 20% to search?" and waits a week Guided mode has templates, beliefs in business terms and a report in plain language. It has instant what-if sliders over a response curve for each draw, and budget plans from the posterior (Guided mode) To choose a model, you need a statistician The analyst uses the model of the last project, or the model with the most interesting name Each model, step, node and check has an About card in plain words. Help me choose asks some questions and gives a ranked shortlist with reasons (Choosing a model) You find data problems after the model Gaps, a constant driver or a series that wanders show in the residuals one week later The Data Explorer makes a profile of each upload in the sandbox. It shows quality warnings, the stationarity of each series, cross-correlation with the KPI by lag, STL and collinearity (Explore a dataset) Nobody knows if they can trust the model Convergence warnings are in a log that nobody reads A sanity scorecard (convergence, holdout error and coverage, plausibility, data) in plain words, and a promotion gate that uses it (Scorecard) Other tools need the model A Flask app for each model, a shared pickle, or a CSV file in an e-mail each Monday Endpoints with aliases, history and rollback. Scoped tokens, generated snippets, signed webhooks and charts that you can embed (Integrations) Many teams, untrusted code and data One shared server where all code can read all data Tenants with row-level security and a new sandbox for each run. Outputs that the platform verifies against the checksums of the storage and signs. Quotas and a kill switch (Security model)

docs.title: Compared with notebooks and an ad-hoc Flask app
docs.text:
This is the most usual alternative. It is a good alternative for one model and one team.

Notebook + a small web app modeling-api How to start Minutes: you already have the notebook A spec or a build() method. Guided templates and workflow recipes need no code Freedom Any library, any code Any PyMC or scikit-learn model through the plugin contract. Built-in models for MMM (mmm-framework), twelve statsmodels time-series models, forecasting, demand and choice. Your own plugins run now on a deployment that you control (installed into its runner). Upload to a shared deployment comes in v0.6, first for allow-listed teams Preprocessing at score time Someone copies it into the app by hand, or pickles it with the model Declared steps with fitted state that the platform replays exactly. Static checks find leakage Forecasts and new groups The result depends on what the code does with a row or date that it did not see Declared for each dim and checked before compute, with typed errors (UNSEEN_LEVELS, HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT, …) How to repeat the analysis Run the cells again, and hope that the sequence is correct A versioned workflow with typed ports. The platform validates it before it runs. A schedule or new data starts it. It records each decision How to validate the model A holdout number in a slide, if someone asks Null tests, benchmarks, residual checks and stability checks under a versioned policy. The approval of a second person. An evidence pack for the auditor Model versions File names, and a model registry if you set one up Immutable spec revisions, signed bundles, lineage, and endpoints with history and rollback Who can use it Persons who can run the notebook or call the app Analysts in Guided mode. Other apps through endpoints, sheets, BI embeds and webhooks Security It depends on the app. Often there is pickle and an open port Sign-in, roles, scoped tokens, sandboxed runs, no pickle, verified outputs How to operate it You own the server You own the deployment (a laptop, Docker Compose or Google Cloud). It is multi-tenant from the start

Use the notebook when the model is a single analysis that nobody else must call or check. Move to modeling-api when a second person, a second model or a second application needs the model. Also move when someone asks "how do we know this is not noise?".

docs.title: Compared with workflow orchestrators
docs.text:
Airflow, Prefect, Dagster and similar tools are very good when you must run any type of task on a schedule across systems. The workflows of modeling-api are narrower on purpose. They are the statistics of one analysis, not a data pipeline.

General-purpose orchestrator modeling-api workflows A step is Any Python function or container A node from a catalog (51 nodes: 17 statistical tests, transforms, 7 train/test plans, order searches, fits, backtests, comparisons, governance, reports) or a saved sub-workflow Between steps The data that the code sends Typed ports (dataset, test_result, split_plan, model_version, …). The platform checks them before the run starts, with a JSON pointer to each problem Decisions Python if statements Branch conditions in a small, safe expression language (never eval). The run records the values that each condition read Where user data is read The location where the task runs In a new sandbox without network. The orchestrator sees only JSON results Reuse A task cache that you configure The identity of each node is its implementation, its parameters and the content of its inputs. The platform uses unchanged steps again automatically Output The data that the tasks write Verdicts in plain language, a report, governance evidence and a model version that is ready to validate and promote

Use an orchestrator to move data between systems and to call modeling-api. Use a workflow for the analysis. The two tools work well together. For example, an orchestrator uploads the data of the new week, and the dataset trigger runs the workflow.

docs.title: Compared with marketing-mix vendors and libraries
docs.text:
Marketing-mix models are the first domain pack, thus users ask about this comparison most. modeling-api is not a new MMM methodology. It does not compete with the statistics of the established libraries. It is a platform that runs MMMs, applies governance checks to them and puts them in front of planners.

Open-source MMM libraries (for example, Google's Meridian and Meta's Robyn) are very good at the model. But they are libraries, and you run them in a notebook. You must supply the serving, the scenario tools for analysts, the validation, the versions and the access control.

  • The built-in MMMs run on mmm-framework. This is an open-source (Apache-2.0) Bayesian MMM framework on PyMC. Business priors become its ROI priors. Lift tests become its experiment likelihoods. Its planning module optimises budgets from the posterior (MMM guide).
  • The ingest recognises Meridian-shaped tables (time, geo, kpi, <channel>_spend). The Meridian model is not part of the platform, because it needs TensorFlow.
  • The platform does not support Robyn (R).

Managed MMM services usually supply data collection from ad platforms, a methodology, models as a service and planning dashboards. modeling-api does not collect data from ad platforms, and it gives no consulting. But you own the spec, the data and the fitted posterior. You can read each prior and each check. You can run models other than MMM on the same platform, and connect the result to your own tools.

Typical managed MMM service Open-source MMM library modeling-api Data collection from ad platforms Often included No No: upload CSV, Parquet, MFF or Meridian-shaped tables The model The model of the vendor Your model, in code The Bayesian (or fast frequentist) MMM of mmm-framework, national or pooled over geos and products, or your own plugin Priors and calibration Different for each vendor, frequently hidden Your priors, in code Business priors as ROI or share ranges, and lift tests. You can see all of them in the spec Proof that it does not fit noise Not frequently shown You must do it Shuffled-sales and fake-channel null tests, effect signs, holdout accuracy and prior sensitivity, with evidence and the approval of a reviewer Analyst scenarios Dashboards You build them What-if sliders with joint uncertainty, "Run exact", forecasts and counterfactuals Budget optimisation Usually included Library functions optimize runs in the sandbox on mmm-framework planning: bounds, groups, risk objectives (P10, CVaR) and the efficient frontier Other models on the same platform No No Forecasting, macro systems (VAR/VECM), store demand, customer choice, your own Who owns the posterior The vendor You You

docs.title: Compared with generic ML model serving
docs.text:
MLflow, BentoML, KServe, Seldon and the endpoints of the cloud providers are very good at their task. They package a trained model from almost any framework. They serve it with low latency and autoscaling. modeling-api is for a narrower problem, and it makes different trade-offs.

Generic model serving modeling-api Input contract Column or tensor signatures: names and shapes, but no dimensions xr.Dataset with named dims, coordinates, roles, units and a score policy for each dim Preprocessing at score time You must do it. Put it in the artifact, or write it again Declared steps with fitted state that the platform replays exactly. Splits that know the stage, and a context tail for each group New groups and horizons The result depends on what the model does with a row that it did not see Declared for each dim (fixed, extend, new_levels + strategy) and checked before compute Uncertainty Point predictions by default. Intervals are a custom output A primary representation that decides which summaries and aggregations are valid Units of the answer The space that the model used for training Inverted to original units. Each variable records its output space Serialization Native to the framework. Pickle and cloudpickle are usual Zarr zip + JSON, skops or xgboost JSON. The platform rejects pickle on write and on read Promotion Usually manual, or a CI job A sanity scorecard is the gate. When a policy tells so, a governance validation is also a gate. It has null tests and the approval of a second person Latency Milliseconds, warm replicas, autoscaling, GPUs Batch: one sandboxed run for each call (seconds, plus cold start in the cloud). Instant what-if from grids that the platform calculates before. No GPUs and no warm scorers yet Frameworks Almost any PyMC, scikit-learn, xgboost, statsmodels, mmm-framework and hand-written models through the plugin contract Who it is for ML engineers who serve many types of model Statisticians, data scientists, and the analysts and apps that use their models

docs.title: When to use something else
docs.text:
• You need answers from the exact model in less than one second, or thousands of requests each second. Use a model server. modeling-api answers sliders immediately from grids that it calculates before. But an exact score is a sandboxed run.
  • Deep learning or GPU work. The platform does not support it before the scale milestone.
  • General data pipelines (move data between systems, join across databases, call APIs). Use an orchestrator. Workflows are for the statistics of an analysis. They use catalog nodes, and they run without network access.
  • Your model needs the network at run time (an API, a database). Runs have no egress, by design.
  • You want to upload public code to a hosted platform now. On a shared deployment, uploaded plugins come first to allow-listed teams (v0.6). They come to the public only after an external penetration test. On a deployment that you control, you can install and run your own plugins now.

docs.title: Where it stands
docs.text: v0.5 is complete, and we tested it on a laptop. The workflow, governance, mmm-framework, explorer and CLI journeys pass end to end against a live stack. All earlier journeys also pass. The numbers on the home page come from those runs. Two items are still open. We test the cloud controls against fakes until they meet a real Google Cloud project. Also, the study with five non-technical testers did not run yet. See M3.5 verification, M3 verification and the roadmap.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
modeling-api uses a small set of ideas that fit together. Each page in this section tells about one idea and gives code that you can run.

flowchart TB
    subgraph CP["Contracts — mapi-spec (pure JSON, no numpy)"]
        direction LR
        SCH["DataSchema<br/>dims · policies · roles"]
        SPEC["ModelSpec<br/>pipeline · model · split"]
        REQ["ScoreRequest<br/>mode · horizon · output"]
        CAT["Catalog<br/>settings schemas · schema effects · manifests"]
        VAL["Static validation<br/>stages · leakage · CoordPlan"]
    end
    subgraph RT["Runtime — mapi-sdk (xarray)"]
        direction LR
        PIPE["Pipeline<br/>fit → state · transform · inverse"]
        PLUG["Model plugin<br/>fit · score"]
        COORD["Coord canonicalisation"]
        SUM["Summariser<br/>representation-aware"]
        BUN[("Bundle")]
    end
    SPEC --> VAL
    SCH --> VAL
    CAT --> VAL
    REQ --> VAL
    VAL -->|"resolved spec"| PIPE
    PIPE --> PLUG --> BUN
    BUN --> COORD --> PLUG
    PLUG --> SUM

The split between the two halves is important. The contracts accept JSON and give JSON. The API of the platform uses only the contracts. Thus, it can validate all specs and score requests, and it does not import your code or decode your arrays. The runtime works on arrays and runs plugins in notebooks and in the sandboxed runner. The Architecture overview tells how the platform connects the two halves. The Security model tells how the platform keeps them safe.

docs.title: The ideas
docs.text:
• Labelled data

    Data is an xr.Dataset. A DataSchema gives each dim a policy (fixed, extend, new_levels). It gives each variable a role, units and rules for missing values. Bindings map your names to the canonical names of a model, and back.

  • Pipelines and stages

    Steps learn state on the train data and use it again when you score. The split occurs at a named stage. Look-back steps keep a context tail for each group. Inverse transforms stop at the last reshape and record the output space.

  • Representations and summaries

    Draws, quantiles, intervals, points and moments. The representation sets which summaries exist and which aggregations are correct.

  • Bundles

    The fitted artifact is one zarr zip and JSON sidecars. Each file has a hash. Bundles do not use pickle.

  • Coord plans and typed errors

    The platform compares score requests with the fitted coordinates before it calculates. It finds unseen levels, horizons, gaps, missing future covariates and impossible summaries.

  • Forecasts with actuals

    Send the actuals that came after the fit, and the dates to forecast. The model updates with fixed parameters and forecasts from the last actual. Or it refuses the request. It never ignores the actuals.

  • Capabilities and manifests

    The static data that a model declares about itself: representation, score modes, outputs, derived quantities and the preprocessing that it owns.

  • Tenancy and authentication v0.3

    Tenants, projects and roles. API tokens and their scopes. Sign-in from the browser. How the platform authorizes each request.

  • Quotas and cost v0.3

    Quotas in vCPU-seconds for each token, each tenant and the full platform. Priority for interactive and batch runs. The exact cost of each run, from a versioned price table.

  • Guided mode v0.4

    Templates, and questions in plain language that find the role of each column. Business priors and lift tests. The sanity scorecard. What-if sliders that show results immediately, from a response grid for each draw.

  • Integrations v0.4

    Endpoints and aliases, with gates on promotion. Code snippets, signed webhooks, and rendered and embedded plots. The trust lifecycle from sign-up to deletion.

  • Workflows v0.5

    Versioned DAGs of statistical tests, transforms, branches, train/test plans, searches, fits, comparisons, governance and reports. Workflows have typed ports, a safe condition language, a cache, schedules and triggers.

  • Governance v0.5

    Policies of checks: null tests with shuffled targets and fake drivers, benchmarks, residuals and stability. A validation state machine and approval by a second person. Evidence packs, and a promotion that needs validation.

  • About cards and choosing v0.5

    A card in plain language on each model, step, node, check and template. The deterministic Help me choose ranking.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Canonical name The name that a step or a model uses (geo, time, y). data.bind maps it to the name in your dataset (market, date, revenue). Stage The dataset after a named step. raw is the bound input. Splits, context and the entry points of scenarios (inputs_stage) all refer to stages. Step state The data that a step learned at fit time: JSON and labelled arrays (for example scale(geo, channel)). Look-back steps also keep a context tail. The platform never writes the step state into the spec. Score The general term for "predict with the same preprocessing as the fit". Modes: predict, forecast, counterfactual, simulate, filter, evaluate. Representation How a model shows uncertainty: draws, quantiles, interval, point or moments. Output space The space of the output values after the inverse transforms, for example raw or weekly. Bundle The verified result of a fit: states, model groups, native artifacts, manifest and hashes. Run A unit of work (fit, score, …) that the platform sends to an executor as JSON. Workflow A versioned graph of nodes (tests, transforms, splits, searches, fits, checks, reports). A workflow run is a parent run. Its nodes run in the orchestrator, as sandboxed workflow_node runs or as child fits. Policy The governance checks that a model must pass, with thresholds and severities, for each model family. A policy applies to a full tenant or to one project. Each policy has versions. Validation The measurement of one model version against the current policies. It has results, evidence, approvals and a status (draft … validated). About card The description in plain language that each catalog item has, if you can select the item.

docs.title: About cards and choosing v0.5
docs.text:
Just want to pick a model?

Choosing a model shows Help me choose in the web app, the terminal (mapi choose) and Python (api.catalog.recommend). It also compares the model families.

Many persons who are not statisticians must select a model, a preprocessing step or a workflow. Thus each item that they can select from a catalog has an About card in plain language. The Help me choose chooser asks some questions about their goal and their data. Then it gives a ranked list with the reasons.

docs.title: The About card
docs.text:
{
  "title": "Weekly totals",
  "summary_plain": "Adds up daily numbers into one number per week (or month), so that every row covers the same length of time.",
  "use_when": ["Your data is daily but you want to plan or report by week"],
  "avoid_when": ["Your data already has one row per week"],
  "data_needs": ["A date column"],
  "assumptions": ["Numbers can be added up (spend, sales); averages are averaged"],
  "outputs": ["The same columns, one row per week"],
  "difficulty": "beginner",
  "typical_runtime": "instant",
  "example": "Daily TV spend of 100 each day becomes 700 for the week.",
  "related": ["core.calendar"],
  "fits": {"goal": ["check_data"]}
}
Field What it holds title A name for persons summary_plain One or two sentences without jargon. They tell what the item does for you. use_when / avoid_when When the item fits, and when to select a different item data_needs The data that the item needs assumptions What the item accepts as true outputs What you get from the item difficulty beginner, intermediate or expert typical_runtime instant, seconds, minutes or long example A small example of how the item works related Ids of related catalog items expert_notes, references The maths and the sources, in a separate place fits Chooser tags: the answers that agree with this item

These items have cards:

  • model manifests and catalog entries (ModelManifest.about, StepCatalogEntry.about)
  • guided templates (GuidedTemplate.about)
  • workflow templates, node kinds and node implementations
  • governance checks.

Your own specs, pipelines and workflows can also have a card, in metadata.about. Then colleagues know when to use them again. GET /v1/catalog/abouts lists the cards of all items that a user can select (filter with kind). These items are the installed models and preprocessing steps, the splits, guided templates, workflow templates, workflow node kinds and nodes, and the governance checks.

Datasets have a DatasetAbout. It contains the description from the owner and a summary. The platform makes the summary from the schema and the coordinate summary. For example: "Weekly data from 2023-01-01 to 2024-12-29 (104 weeks) for 10 geos and 3 channels, with 3 measures: revenue (the result you want to explain), spend (marketing spend), price."

docs.title: Complete cards are enforced
docs.text:
mapi_spec.about.about_issues is the editorial rule. A card must agree with these conditions:

  • All necessary fields have a value.
  • The summary is one or two sentences without jargon words (for example "posterior", "stationarity" or "autoregressive").
  • The chooser tags name real questions and answers.
  • The related ids exist.

The catalog rule (Catalog.about_issues, problem code ABOUT_INCOMPLETE with a JSON pointer) and the contract kit (mapi_sdk.testing.check_about) apply this rule. Thus a plugin without a complete card fails its checks. The built-in cards are in mapi_spec.abouts.

docs.title: Help me choose
docs.text:
GET /v1/catalog/chooser returns the questions (ChooserQuestionnaire):

Question Answers goal - What do you want to do? measure what marketing adds, plan a budget, forecast, understand drivers, predict per item, understand choices, find regimes, compare series, check data, validate a model data_shape - What does your data look like? one series, a few related series, a panel (markets, stores), choices, a table frequency daily, weekly, monthly, not over time history less than a year, one to three years, more drivers - Other columns that could explain the result? yes, no uncertainty - Do you need a range? essential, nice to have, no experience new to statistics, the basics, expert speed within seconds, within minutes, can wait

GET /v1/catalog/recommendations?goal=forecast&data_shape=one_series&experience=beginner&kind=model returns a ChooserResult. The result has the candidates ranked from the best. Each candidate has a score between 0 and 1, the reasons that it fits ("Suits: forecast the future") and cautions ("Needs expert-level statistics knowledge", "Usually takes long"). To give more than one answer to a question, put commas between the answers.

The ranking (mapi_spec.about.recommend) is deterministic. It uses these rules:

  • An answer that agrees adds the weight of the question. The goal has the most weight.
  • An answer that does not agree subtracts the weight.
  • If an item does not use a question, that question has no effect on the item.
  • An item loses points if it is more difficult than your experience, or slower than your answer for speed.
  • At the same score, an item for more of your answers comes first. An item that says nothing about a question ranks below an item that says it fits.
  • If some items agree with your goal, the chooser does not show the other items.

Without kind, the candidates are the start points for a user: models, guided templates and workflow templates. kind=step, kind=node or kind=check ranks one kind of building block. If the chooser does not know a question or an answer, it returns 422 CHOOSER_ANSWER_INVALID.

docs.title: In the web app
docs.text:
About cards everywhere. Each place where you select an item shows its card, with plain language first. The Browse tab of the catalog lists all items that a user can select. You can filter by kind, by difficulty or by text. The kinds are Guided analyses, models, workflow templates, preparation steps, splits, governance checks, workflow nodes and node kinds. A card shows the uses, limits, data needs, assumptions, outputs, an example and related items. The maths and the references are under For experts: how it works, which is collapsed.

The same cards show in these locations:

  • on the Guided template cards (About)
  • in the spec editor: an About tab for the model, and an About button on each pipeline step
  • in the Model Explorer (About this kind of model).

Datasets show their About (the description from the owner and the generated summary) on the dataset page and in the Data Explorer.

Help me choose is at /choose. It is also in the "Not sure where to start?" panel on Home and at the top of Guided mode. It asks the questions one at a time. Each question has a set of large choices that you can use with the keyboard. You can skip each question. The chooser ranks the matches while you answer. It shows the reasons ("Suits: forecast the future") and cautions ("Needs expert-level statistics knowledge").

Start with this opens the selected item:

  • For a guided template, it opens a new Guided analysis.
  • For a model, it opens a new spec in the editor with that model, and its About as comments.
  • For a workflow template, it opens a recipe run on your data (Guided mode), or the "use this template" wizard (Expert mode).
  • For a governance check, it opens the check in the governance check catalog.

In Guided mode, a model starts the guided template that uses the model. For example, Demand by store and week opens the store demand analysis. Marketing mix model opens the geo marketing mix analysis. If a model has no guided template, the app tells you. It shows Set up in Expert mode. The app changes to Expert mode only when you click it. In a project that is locked to Guided mode, the app shows Needs Expert mode and gives no action.

The answers are in the address, so you can share a suggestion. The switch at the top ranks models, preparation steps, governance checks or workflow nodes, not start points.

docs.title: Architecture overview v0.4
docs.text:
modeling-api has three layers. The project made them in this sequence:

  1. A typed runtime for models: the SDK, the steps and the model plugins.
  2. A job platform around it: the API, the queue, the executors and the runner.
  3. From v0.3, a hosted platform for many tenants.

The rules that keep the last layer safe also apply to the first layers. The control plane never imports plugin code and never decodes your arrays. Each run occurs in a sandbox. The platform compares each output with the values that the storage calculated.

flowchart TB
    subgraph clients["Clients"]
        web["Web app<br/>(app origin)"]
        sandbox["Plot sandbox<br/>(separate origin)"]
        cli["mapi CLI · Python client ·<br/>curl · other apps"]
    end
    subgraph control["Control plane: JSON only, never imports plugins"]
        api["API<br/>/v1 · OpenAPI · SSE"]
        orch["Orchestrator<br/>dispatcher · reconciler ·<br/>finalizer · event ingestion"]
        pg[("PostgreSQL<br/>runs · queue · events ·<br/>registry · catalog")]
    end
    subgraph exec["Run sandbox: one per run"]
        sup["Supervisor<br/>(trusted, holds the run's URLs)"]
        wrk["Worker<br/>(untrusted: SDK + plugin)"]
    end
    store[("Object store<br/>quarantine · bootstrap · runs ·<br/>bundles · data")]

    web -->|"/v1"| api
    cli -->|"/v1"| api
    web -. "postMessage<br/>(validated)" .-> sandbox
    web -->|"signed PUT / GET"| store
    api --> pg
    orch --> pg
    api -->|"metadata, signed URLs"| store
    orch -->|"bootstrap object,<br/>verify, server-side copy"| store
    orch -->|"submit(run id, nonce)"| sup
    sup <-->|"socketpair"| wrk
    sup -->|"signed URLs only"| store
    sup -->|"HMAC-signed events"| orch

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text: Component Package What it does What it never does API mapi-server (mapi-server api) The /v1 HTTP API: datasets, specs and their static validation, runs, models, scores and plots. Server-sent events. Signed URLs Import mapi_sdk, a plugin, numpy or xarray. An import-linter contract prevents this, also in the server image Orchestrator mapi-server (mapi-server worker) The dispatcher, the reconciler, event ingestion and the finalizer. They use a procrastinate queue in the same PostgreSQL Decode a dataset or a bundle. It reads only object metadata and JSON sidecars with a size limit Executor mapi_server.executors Starts a runner for a run: local-process (a subprocess), docker / docker-gvisor (a container), and Cloud Run Jobs in v0.3 Send data other than the run id and a nonce Runner mapi-runner A trusted supervisor. It gets the instructions of the run, starts an untrusted worker, uploads outputs and signs events Let the worker use credentials, the network of the store or its stdout SDK and plugins mapi-sdk, mapi-steps, mapi-pymc, mapi-sklearn, mapi-plugin-* The runtime for models: pipelines with fitted state, models, coord plans, summaries and bundles Run in a location other than the worker (on the platform) or your own process (as a library) Contracts mapi-spec All the shapes that the two sides agree on: specs, schemas, DTOs, the run protocol and error codes Import numpy, xarray or pandas Object store mapi-gcs-shim locally, Cloud Storage later Buckets with object generations, CRC32C and MD5 that the server calculates, signed URLs and POST policies, and permissions for each principal — Web app, plot sandbox apps/web, apps/plot-sandbox The Guided and Expert UI and the Integrations hub. The plot sandbox is the only location where Vega-Lite and Plotly specs render, also for shared embed pages Render a plot on the origin of the app

docs.title: The control plane
docs.text:
The API and the orchestrator use the same PostgreSQL database. The API writes runs in state created. Then it sets queued or rejected from static checks. The orchestrator owns all the subsequent states.

flowchart LR
    subgraph api["API process"]
        routes["/v1 routes"]
        validate["Static validation<br/>(SchemaEffect JSON,<br/>CoordPlan, sanitizers)"]
        sse["SSE fan-out<br/>(one LISTEN per process)"]
    end
    subgraph worker["Worker process"]
        disp["Dispatcher<br/>token bucket · intent row"]
        rec["Reconciler<br/>every 10 s"]
        ev["Event ingestion<br/>HMAC verify · dedupe"]
        fin["Finalizer<br/>(procrastinate job)"]
    end
    pg[("PostgreSQL")]
    routes --> validate
    routes -->|"runs, specs,<br/>datasets"| pg
    disp -->|"lease queued runs"| pg
    rec -->|"executor status →<br/>state transitions"| pg
    ev -->|"run_progress upsert,<br/>run_events + NOTIFY"| pg
    fin -->|"model versions,<br/>signed manifests"| pg
    pg -->|"NOTIFY"| sse
  • Static validation runs in the API, synchronously, and uses only JSON. It uses the exported schema effect of each step, and the settings schema and schema template of each model, from the catalog. A sandboxed describe run of the real runner makes the catalog. The platform keeps the catalog in a cache for each image digest. Thus, the API validates against exactly the code that the runner will run.
  • The dispatcher leases queued runs through a token bucket. It writes an intent row (run, attempt, nonce) and then calls the executor. Thus, the platform can recover from a crash between the two operations.
