docs.title: Sharing plots: saved plots, images and embed links
docs.text:
The plots of a model are in the web app. The isolated plot sandbox renders them. You can use a plot in a different place, for example a slide, a report, a BI dashboard, a Notion page or a Slack thread. To do this, you can:

  1. save the plot with a title (POST /v1/plots),
  2. render the plot to PNG, SVG or PDF in the sandbox (POST /v1/plots:render), or
  3. embed the plot with a link that has a token, is read-only and expires (POST /v1/plots/{plot_id}/embeds).

The three actions need a signed-in caller or an API token of the project. The embed link is public. All persons who have the link can see that one plot. They can see it until the link expires or until you revoke it.

Use the correct method for each tool:

  • BI tools and Notion put an embed link in a frame and show the live chart.
  • Chat tools, for example Slack and Teams, never put a page in a frame. They change a link into a card from the tags of its page. The tags of the embed page are the same for all links: a "Shared chart" card with no plot name and no image. Thus, post a rendered PNG to a Slack thread. If people must open the live view, also add the link.

docs.title: Save a plot
docs.text:
To save a plot of a model version, name its source. The API first does a check of the signed bundle manifest of the model version. Then it sends the plot through the sanitizer again:

curl -s -X POST "$MAPI_URL/v1/plots" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MAPI_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "title": "EU response curves (v3)",
        "source": {"model_id": "mdl_01jaf3c1d2e3f4g5h6j7k8m9n0", "version": 3,
                   "plot_id": "mmm.response_curves"}
      }'

The answer is a SavedPlot. Its embeddable field tells if you can share the plot with a link (see what can be embedded).

You can also save a plot that you wrote ("spec": {...}, a PlotSpec). The plot must pass the same sanitizer. If it does not pass, the answer is 422 PLOT_UNSAFE. The plot must also contain its data inline. data_ref datasets belong to a model version. Thus, to save that type of plot, use source. The platform always records a hand-written plot with author provenance. The value in its provenance field has no effect.

  • GET /v1/plots lists the saved plots of the project (newest first).
  • GET /v1/plots/{plot_id} returns one plot with its spec.
  • DELETE /v1/plots/{plot_id} deletes the plot and its embed links.

docs.title: Render an image
docs.text:
POST /v1/plots:render changes one plot into a file. You can identify the plot by saved_plot_id, by source (a plot of a model version) or inline (plot):

curl -s -X POST "$MAPI_URL/v1/plots:render" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MAPI_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Prefer: wait=30" \
  -d '{"saved_plot_id": "plt_01jaf3n1p2q3r4s5t6v7w8x9y0", "format": "pdf", "width": 1200, "height": 600}'
Field Default Meaning format png png, svg or pdf scale 2 The pixel density of PNG and PDF (0 < scale ≤ 8). SVG ignores it. width, height The size of the plot The size in CSS pixels before scale (16–4096). For a composite plot (facets, concatenations), it is the size of each panel.

A PNG or a PDF contains a maximum of 50 megapixels. This is the width x height x scale² of the plot after layout, with all panels. If a request is larger, the answer is 413 PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE at the start. Sometimes only the layout shows the size. Then the render run fails with that code before it draws the plot. If you get this error, make the scale or the size smaller.

A render is a render run in the sandbox. Thus it counts against your quotas, as all small runs do. You can send Prefer: wait=N (a maximum of 60 seconds). If the run finishes in that time, the answer is 200 with signed links to renders/<plot>.<format>. If not, the answer is 202 with the run. Then poll GET /v1/plots/renders/{run_id} until done is true. The links expire after a short time. Download the file. Do not keep the URL.

Vega-Lite only, for now

vl-convert renders Vega-Lite plots. Plotly plots need kaleido and a Chrome or Chromium in the runner image. The images of the platform do not include them. Thus Plotly renders answer 422 MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED, unless the operator enables them (MAPI_RENDER_PLOTLY_ENABLED). You can export a Plotly plot from the plot viewer.

docs.title: Rendering never fetches anything
docs.text:
The renderer gets the sanitized plot and its data as pinned inputs of the run:

  • The API writes the plot as the plots.json of the run. It pins each bundle dataset of the plot (data_ref) to the verified object generation, as run inputs with the names plotdata.<n>.
  • The sanitizer refused URL data, href encodings, image marks, and Plotly layout images or tile maps before. The runner refuses them again before it draws.
  • vl-convert runs with no network access (allowed_base_urls=[]). Also, the sandbox has no egress.

An image has a limit of 32 MiB. The run has a time limit of MAPI_RENDER_TIMEOUT_S (5 minutes by default).

docs.title: Embed links
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST "$MAPI_URL/v1/plots/plt_01jaf3n1p2q3r4s5t6v7w8x9y0/embeds" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MAPI_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"label": "Q4 board deck", "expires_in_days": 90,
       "allowed_origins": ["https://acme.notion.site"]}'

The answer (PlotEmbedCreated) is the only time that you see the link:

{
  "embed": {"id": "emb_01jaf3p1q2r3s4t5v6w7x8y9z0", "display": "mpe_7k2m9q…", "status": "active", "...": "..."},
  "url": "https://plots.mapi.example/embed/mpe_7k2m9q4x0123456789abcdefghjkmnpqrstvwxyz",
  "token": "mpe_7k2m9q4x0123456789abcdefghjkmnpqrstvwxyz"
}

The platform keeps only a keyed hash of the token, as it does for API tokens. Paste the url into the tool that shows the plot, or put it in a frame:

<iframe src="https://plots.mapi.example/embed/mpe_7k2m…" width="900" height="520"
        style="border:0" loading="lazy" title="EU response curves"></iframe>
Option Default Meaning expires_in_days 30 1 to 365 days label none Your note. The list of links shows it. allowed_origins all sites The https sites (https://host[:port], a maximum of 10) whose pages can show the plot in a frame. If you open the link directly, it always works.
  • GET /v1/plots/{plot_id}/embeds lists the links of a plot. It shows their status (active, expired or revoked), the view count and the last view. It never shows their tokens.
  • DELETE /v1/plots/{plot_id}/embeds/{embed_id} revokes one link. If you revoke a link two times, no problem occurs.

The audit log records each new link and each revoked link (plot.embed_create, plot.embed_revoke).

docs.title: What can be embedded
docs.text:
You can embed only the plots that a model version drew with one of the platform's own recipes (core.*, mmm.*, ml.*, ts.*, choice.*). The platform refuses plots from a model plugin and plots that a person wrote. The answer is 422 EMBED_NOT_ALLOWED. This rule exists because a shared link runs the spec of the plot in the browser of a stranger. Also in the sandbox, a spec can navigate its own frame. Thus shared views run only specs that the platform wrote. Share other plots in the project, or render them to an image.

A model version that you fit with uploaded plugin code (a dev overlay or a vetted overlay) can embed none of its plots. The recipe that a plot names has no effect. The reason: the worker that writes the plot documents also runs that code. Thus the server decides from the lineage of the version, not from what a plot tells about itself. Existing links to these plots stop and do not show them.

An embed also contains its data inline. Thus you cannot embed a dataset that is larger than 1.5 MB.

docs.title: The embed page
docs.text:
The link opens a page of the plot sandbox (/embed/<token>). The page reads the plot from the public GET /v1/embeds/{token} of the API. It draws the plot with the same safeguards as the plot frames of the app:

  • The request sends no cookie or credential. If the API gets one, the API ignores it.
  • The Content-Security-Policy of the page lets it fetch only the /v1/embeds/ path of the API. The API answers cross-origin reads only from the origin of the plot sandbox.
  • The browser validates the answer again (inline data only, and the same checks for unsafe constructs as the plot frames of the app). The page writes all text as text.
  • If a site that is not in allowed_origins puts the page in a frame, the page shows a notice and not the plot.

If you can start render runs (the runner role), the platform renders a PNG of the plot when you create the link. The page then shows an Open as PNG link, for tools that cannot show interactive content. Editors can also create links, but without that image.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Status Code When 404 NOT_FOUND The token does not exist, or a person deleted its plot. 410 LINK_EXPIRED The link expired, or a person revoked it, or its tenant is suspended. 429 RATE_LIMITED This link has too many views (MAPI_EMBED_RATE_PER_MINUTE), or one address sent too many requests (MAPI_EMBED_IP_RATE_PER_MINUTE). Wait for the time in Retry-After.

docs.title: Hosting the embed page
docs.text:
The build of the plot sandbox has two pages: index.html (the plot frames of the app) and embed.html. The server sends embed.html for each /embed/<token> path. The embed page needs the origin of the API:

  • In development, the build includes VITE_API_URL (default http://127.0.0.1:8000).
  • The mapi/web image builds the page with a placeholder. When nginx serves the page, it puts MAPI_API_URL in the placeholder. It also adds the headers of the page (CSP with connect-src … $MAPI_API_URL/v1/embeds/, frame-ancestors 'self' https:).

The API allows cross-origin reads of /v1/embeds/ only from MAPI_PLOTS_ORIGIN. Thus that setting must be the origin from which the server sends the embed page.

docs.title: Tabular models with scikit-learn and xgboost
docs.text:
mapi-sklearn changes each scikit-learn or xgboost estimator on the allow-list into a full modeling-api plugin. You tell which dims are samples and which variables are features. The platform does the rest:

  • It stacks your labelled xr.Dataset into a design matrix.
  • It fits the estimator and keeps it safely.
  • At score time, it builds exactly the same columns again.
  • It accepts new stores and forecast horizons.
  • It unstacks the predictions back into labelled arrays, with correct uncertainty.

docs.title: The plugins
docs.text:
The kind of uncertainty sets the representation of the output. The representation then sets which summaries and aggregations are valid. Each kind is a different plugin:

Plugin Representation What y_hat contains Aggregate over cells? sklearn.tabular_regressor point A point prediction (+ contributions) Linear only, with a flag sklearn.tabular_quantiles quantiles Conditional quantiles (quantile, ...) No sklearn.tabular_bootstrap draws One joint draw for each bootstrap replicate (chain, draw, ...) Yes, all sklearn.tabular_conformal interval (bound=[lower, upper, point], ...), attr alpha No sklearn.tabular_classifier point The probability of the positive class Linear only, with a flag

Why conformal is an interval, not draws

A split-conformal interval guarantees the coverage for each cell (P(y in interval) >= 1 - alpha). It is not a distribution. A sum of intervals across stores or weeks claims a coverage that nobody measured. Thus the platform rejects these aggregations with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED. For totals, use sklearn.tabular_bootstrap, because its draws are joint.

docs.title: A store-demand forecast
docs.text:
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: store-demand-xgb, project: retail}
data:
  dataset: dataset://retail/store_sku_weekly@latest
  bind:
    dims: {store: store_id, sku: sku, time: week}
    vars: {y: units_sold, price: price, promo: promo_flag}
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: time, last: 12}
pipeline:
  - {id: imp,   use: core.impute@^1,   with: {vars: [price], method: ffill, along: time, within: [store, sku]}}
  - {id: plags, use: core.lag@^1,      with: {vars: [promo], along: time, within: [store, sku], lags: [1, 2]}}
  - {id: cal,   use: core.calendar@^1, with: {along: time, features: [week_of_year, month]}}
  - {id: logy,  use: core.log1p@^1,    with: {vars: [y]}}
model:
  use: sklearn.tabular_quantiles@^1
  settings:
    estimator: {kind: xgboost.XGBRegressor, params: {n_estimators: 600, max_depth: 6, learning_rate: 0.05}}
    rows: [store, sku, time]                  # dims stacked into samples
    columns: {roles: [covariate]}             # which variables become features
    coord_features: {store: category, sku: category}
    uncertainty: {kind: quantile, quantiles: [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]}
    forecast_strategy: direct
  fit: {seed: 7, mode: evaluate_then_refit}
evaluate: {metrics: [rmse, mape, coverage_80]}
execution: {resource_class: S, timeout: 10m}

What occurs:

  1. The platform scores the holdout (the last 12 weeks) through the score path. It uses context tails from the training weeks. It calculates rmse, mape and coverage_80 in units sold. The platform inverts the log1p. Quantiles map exactly through monotone transforms.
  2. The platform fits the model again on all weeks. The bundle keeps the xgboost model as JSON.
  3. A forecast request gives the future prices and promotions. The platform builds the lags again from the stored tail. It also does a check that the weeks continue the fitted range without gaps.
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://retail/store-demand-xgb
mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 4}
data: dataset://retail/plan_next_4_weeks
output: {summary: [median, q10, q90]}

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning estimator — {kind, params} from the allow-list below (necessary for the built-in plugins) target y The canonical name of the target variable rows — The dims that the platform stacks into samples. Each row dim of the target. time_dim / time_kind time / time The row dim that extends at forecast time, and its kind (time, integer, index). Use none if no row dim extends. columns {roles: [covariate, media, spend, control, exposure]} The feature variables by role, or an explicit vars list. exclude removes names. coord_features {} Encode the labels of row dims as features: category, onehot, ordinal, numeric new_levels pooled What an unseen level of a row dim becomes: pooled, zero or error pooled_max_levels 256 Pool over a maximum of this number of fitted levels (the most frequent) weight, mask — A variable for the sample weight. A boolean mask of the cells that you can use. forecast_strategy direct In v1, the platform rejects recursive with RECURSIVE_UNSUPPORTED. retransform median Point predictions through a non-linear inverse (log1p): median or Duan smearing contributions auto For the point and bootstrap plugins: auto, exact, zeroing, none n_jobs 1 The threads of the estimator. The default is 1, so that fits are the same bit for bit.

A variable with dims that are not in rows becomes one column for each label. For example, spend(store, channel, time) with the rows [store, time] gives spend[tv], spend[search]. The platform broadcasts a variable that does not have a row dim (calendar features over time only). The platform does not use some rows for the training:

  • Rows with a missing target
  • Rows with a weight that is zero or less
  • Rows where mask is false
  • Rows with a missing feature, for estimators that cannot accept missing values natively

A ROWS_DROPPED diagnostic reports these rows.

docs.title: Coordinate features
docs.text:
• category: integer codes. The platform declares them natively to xgboost and to HistGradientBoostingRegressor (a maximum of 254 levels). For all other estimators, it uses one-hot columns.
  • onehot: one 0/1 column for each fitted level.
  • ordinal: the position of the level as a number (for ordered dims).
  • numeric: the label. Numbers stay as they are. Datetimes become the days since the first fitted label.

docs.title: Estimators
docs.text:
Kind Task Quantiles Missing values Categories Stored as sklearn.LinearRegression regression — — one-hot skops sklearn.Ridge, sklearn.Lasso, sklearn.ElasticNet regression — — one-hot skops sklearn.QuantileRegressor regression one model for each level — one-hot skops sklearn.RandomForestRegressor regression — — one-hot skops sklearn.GradientBoostingRegressor regression one model for each level — one-hot skops sklearn.HistGradientBoostingRegressor regression one model for each level native native skops xgboost.XGBRegressor regression one native multi-quantile model native native xgboost JSON sklearn.LogisticRegression, sklearn.RandomForestClassifier, xgboost.XGBClassifier binary classification — xgboost only xgboost only skops / JSON

Each kind has a bounded Pydantic params model (extra="forbid"). You cannot set the parameters that the platform owns: seeds, threads, categorical declarations, and the loss or objective that a kind of uncertainty needs. For example, sklearn.tabular_quantiles sets the xgboost objective: reg:quantileerror. It rejects an objective that does not agree. The params models are a discriminated union. Thus the control plane validates them statically. For example, it rejects max_depth: -1 with a JSON pointer before a run starts.

docs.title: Uncertainty
docs.text:
Quantiles. xgboost fits all levels at the same time. The sklearn estimators that can do quantiles fit one model for each level. The platform sorts quantiles that cross (monotone rearrangement, which never increases the pinball loss). It reports the fraction of rows that cross as QUANTILE_CROSSING. If you do not set output.summary, the default (median, q5, q95) changes to agree with your grid. For example, with [0.1, 0.5, 0.9] you get median, q10, q90. If you request a level outside the grid, you get an error. The platform interpolates quantiles. It never extrapolates them.

Bootstrap. n replicates fit the estimator again on resampled rows. With by: store, they fit it on resampled whole stores. This is a cluster bootstrap that keeps the dependence in each store. expected outputs are the predictions of the replicates. predictive outputs add an out-of-bag residual for each cell. The draws are joint. Thus totals over stores, counterfactual deltas and all summaries are valid.

Split conformal. The platform keeps a calibration fraction out of the fit. By default, this fraction is the most recent weeks (calibration_by: last), as in a forecast. random selects rows at random. The radius is the ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))-th smallest absolute calibration residual. The calibration set can be too small for the requested alpha. Then you get a SETTINGS_INVALID error, not an infinite interval. refit: true fits the point model again on all rows after the calibration. The interval is then narrower, but the finite-sample guarantee is only approximate (not exact).

docs.title: New stores, skus and markets
docs.text:
Score data can contain a label of a row dim that the fit did not see. Then the effective policy of the dim decides. This policy is the stricter of the policy of the data and the new_levels of the plugin:

  • pooled: the prediction is an average of the predictions that the row gets under each fitted level. The training frequency of each level is the weight. For a linear model with one-hot features, this is equal to a prediction with the average encoding. The platform calculates the average of quantiles and interval bounds (Vincentisation). It calculates the average of bootstrap draws for each draw, so that they stay joint.
  • zero: the level adds nothing. All one-hot columns are 0. The category codes are missing (for estimators that accept missing values natively).
  • error (or a fixed dim): UNSEEN_LEVELS before the run starts.

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text:
The point plugins and the bootstrap plugins can return contributions(component, ...) next to y_hat:

  • exact (linear estimators. This is the default with contributions: auto): intercept plus coef × x for each column. The platform adds the one-hot columns of a coordinate feature into one component. The sum of the components is exactly equal to the prediction.
  • zeroing (all estimators): counterfactual zeroing. baseline is the prediction with all features at zero. The contribution of each feature is the decrease when only that feature is zero. interaction contains the remainder, so that the sum of the components stays correct. These contributions have the label counterfactual_zeroing. They are not Shapley values. SHAP is not in the scope of v1.

Contributions are additive in model space (output: {units: model}). Through a non-linear inverse, for example log1p, the inverse of each component is not a decomposition. If you want a sum of the parts that is correct, request model units.

docs.title: Persistence and safety
docs.text:
The bundle keeps the fitted estimators in its /native group. It never uses pickle:

  • scikit-learn estimators with skops. Before the platform loads the file, it lists the types in the file. It refuses all types that are not on the allow-list of that estimator. For example, a random forest can contain sklearn.tree._tree.Tree. A ridge regression can contain no extra types. The loaded object must be exactly the expected class.
  • xgboost models as the JSON document of the booster.

The bundle manifest records the size, CRC32C, MD5 and SHA-256 of each file. The contract kit does a check that the bundle contains no entry that looks like pickle.

docs.title: Write your own sklearn plugin
docs.text:
Implement estimator(). Then select a base class for the representation that you want:

from typing import ClassVar

from mapi_sklearn import PointSettings, SklearnModel, capabilities_for
from mapi_spec import Capabilities
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge


class LinearDemand(SklearnModel[PointSettings]):
    id = "t.acme.linear_demand"
    version = "1.0.0"
    capabilities: ClassVar[Capabilities] = capabilities_for("none").model_copy(
        update={"contribution_scale": "additive"}  # a linear model decomposes exactly
    )

    def estimator(self, s: PointSettings) -> Ridge:
        return Ridge(alpha=0.5)  # must be exactly an allow-listed class

estimator() can return an instance from the allow-list, a {kind, params} mapping or a choice model. The platform rejects subclasses of estimators and parameters that are not in the params model. The base classes are SklearnModel (point), SklearnQuantileModel, SklearnBootstrapModel, SklearnConformalModel and SklearnClassifier.

Before you publish, run the contract kit on synthetic data:

from mapi_sdk.testing import ModelFixture, check_model
from mapi_sklearn.testing import demand_dataset, demand_registry, demand_schema, demand_spec

data = demand_dataset()  # a store x sku x week demand panel
report = check_model(
    LinearDemand,
    ModelFixture(
        spec=demand_spec("t.acme.linear_demand@^1", {"estimator": None}),
        data=data,
        raw_schema=demand_schema(data),
        registry=demand_registry(),
    ),
)
print(report.summary())
# ... [PASS] additive_contributions: contributions sum to 'y_hat' ...

docs.title: Limits in v1
docs.text:
• Forecasts are direct only. You must give the future features, or the pipeline must calculate them.
  • Classification is binary.
  • The platform declares all row dims other than time_dim as categorical. Thus groups with integer labels (numeric store ids) need string labels.
  • Contributions are not available for the quantile plugins or the conformal plugins.

docs.title: Forecasting and sequential models
docs.text:
Time causes many problems that most modelling platforms do not show. A forecast can silently go past the range that the model can represent. A state-space model can start again from zero at each score. A platform can score a holdout without the history that the holdout needs. modeling-api makes each of these items explicit. It does a check of them before it uses compute.

Classical models

ARIMA/ARIMAX, exponential smoothing, theta, ARDL and error correction, VAR, VECM, VARMAX, dynamic factors and Markov switching come from statsmodels. See statsmodels time-series models.

docs.title: Horizons are part of the contract
docs.text:
A time dim declares its policy extend and, optionally, a max_extension. The max_extension is the distance after the fitted range that a forecast can go without a new fit. The control plane does a check of each score request against it. It uses only the metadata:

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://climate/mauna-loa-co2
mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: t, periods: 30}

{"code": "HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT", "status": 409,
 "detail": "horizon of 30 exceeds the 24 periods this fit supports along 't'; a refit is required"}

Models that need a bounded domain get it from the same place. ts.hsgp_trend sets the size of its Hilbert-space GP from ctx.anticipated_coords (the fitted labels and max_extension future labels). Thus the basis that it calculates at a forecast month is exactly the basis of the fit:

dom = HSGPDomain.from_positions(positions_of(ctx.anticipated_coords["t"]), s.c)
phi = hsgp_basis(dom.scale(ctx.position("t")), s.m, dom.L)   # same at fit and at score

Score payloads must also continue the fitted range without gaps (NON_CONTIGUOUS_EXTENSION). They cannot start before the fitted range (COORD_NOT_ALLOWED).

docs.title: Evaluate the way you will forecast
docs.text:
fit.mode: evaluate_then_refit is the default for models that you can promote. In this mode, the platform does these steps:

  1. It fits on the training window.
  2. It scores the holdout through the score path, with the context and the state from the training only.
  3. It records the metrics.
  4. It fits again on all the data, so that forecasts start from the latest data.

The production bundle links the evaluation bundle and its metrics.

docs.title: Sequential models keep a terminal state
docs.text:
Hidden Markov models, Kalman filters and particle filters keep a summary of the past in a state. They keep the state in a terminal_state group that the plugin owns. At score time, they read this group. They do not process the history again. ts.gaussian_hmm keeps the filtered state distribution at the last fitted step, alpha_T(chain, draw, animal, state):

  • forecast propagates it: P(z_{T+h}) = alpha_T · A^h, for each posterior draw.
  • filter continues the forward filter over new observations. It returns an updated terminal_state group. Thus, if you filter six new steps at the same time or in two batches of three, you get the same state.
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://ecology/animal-tracks-hmm
mode: filter
data: dataset://ecology/tracks_live@v1

The result has predictions (the one-step-ahead y_hat and the filtered state_prob). It also has a terminal_state group. Its attrs.step is the last filtered step.

docs.title: Missing values and sentinels
docs.text:
Raw series often use numbers for gaps (-99.99). Declare the code in the schema (missing_sentinel). Then change it into NaN with core.replace_sentinel. Some models can accept gaps (for example ts.hsgp_trend). These models do not use those periods in the likelihood, but they predict them.

For all settings, see Built-in models. For the fixtures (c08, e24) that keep this behavior tested, see the Conformance corpus.

docs.title: The Expert web app v0.3
docs.text:
The web app is the Expert-mode front end of the platform. In the app, data scientists upload data, write and validate specs, fit them, inspect the fitted models and score them. The app uses the same /v1 HTTP API as the CLI and the Python client. The app has no special permissions. Each button is one or two API calls.

This page shows each page in the sequence of the navigation. The screenshots come from the quickstart stack. make dev serves the app at http://127.0.0.1:5173.

Guided mode

The Guided / Expert switch in the header changes all of the app to the task flow for analysts. Your first analysis in Guided mode describes this flow. The two modes edit the same ModelSpec.

docs.title: The shell
docs.text:
Element What it does Project switcher Shows the tenant and the project for all the actions on the page, and your role there. You can switch to a different project, make a project (tenant admins) or open its members. See Authentication. Sidebar Home, Guided, Datasets, Build, Runs, Models, Score, Workflows, Governance, Integrations, Catalog and Help me choose. In Guided mode, Guided, Help me choose and Recipes (the workflow gallery as ready-made recipes) come first, and Home does not show. A project that is locked to Guided mode shows those three items and Integrations. Under Project: Usage, Members and Tokens. Under Platform: Admin (operators only). Settings is at the bottom. Collapse (Cmd+B) makes the sidebar narrow, with only icons. Jump to… (Cmd+K or /) A command palette. Go to a page, start a new spec, change the theme, or paste an id (run_…, mdl_…, ds_…, spc_…) to open it. API connected Polls GET /readyz. It is green when PostgreSQL, the object store and the catalog are ready. Otherwise, it is amber (API degraded) or red (API unreachable). It links to Settings, which shows each check. Guided / Expert The persona switch. This browser remembers it for each user. Until you make a selection, a self-service (public tier) workspace starts in Guided mode. All other workspaces (and platform operators) start in Expert mode. In Guided mode, / opens the Guided start page. If a project is locked to Guided mode, members below admin do not see the switch. Display icon Light, dark or system theme. ? The keyboard shortcuts. Single keys work when no text field has focus: G then H Home, G Guided, D Datasets, B Build, R Runs, M Models, S Score, W Workflows, V Governance, I Integrations, C Catalog, O Help me choose, , Settings.

The app always shows text from a run or a plugin as plain text. This text includes log lines, tracebacks, warning messages and plot captions. The app removes ANSI escapes, control characters and bidi characters from it. The label untrusted output shows next to this text.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
The landing page tells you if work is in progress and if something needs your attention:

  • Running (the heading shows Nothing running when no run is active): the active runs with their live progress bars.
  • Needs attention: the failed, stalled or partial runs in the latest 50. Each one links to its run page.
  • Recently finished: the latest runs of all types, with their state and input.
  • Models: the registered models with their latest version.
  • Start something: write a spec from the geo MMM template, upload a dataset or look at the catalog. Upload data and New spec in the header do the same.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
A dataset is a named collection of immutable versions.

  1. Click New dataset.
  2. Type a name (lowercase letters, digits, _ and -).
  3. If necessary, type a description.

The app then opens the upload panel.

Upload a file. Select a file:

  • A zarr zip (.zarr.zip) or netCDF (.nc) file describes itself. The app uses its dims and coordinates without changes. If the file has a mapi_schema attribute (roles, policies, units), the app also uses it without changes.

  • Your browser shows a preview of a CSV file. The server never parses the file. Map each column:

    • A dim: give its kind (time, categorical, …), its score-time policy (fixed, extend, new_levels) and its frequency.
    • A variable: give its role (target, spend, covariate, …), its units and its missing-value rule.

    You map Parquet files in the same way, but without the local preview.

Upload and ingest sends the file directly to object storage through a signed PUT URL. The API never sees the bytes. Then the app starts an ingest run in the sandbox. The page refreshes until the version is ready. If the ingest finds issues, the page shows them in plain language ("3 markets are missing 2 weeks in March").

A version page has five tabs:

Tab Shows Schema Dims with kind, score-time policy, frequency and new-level strategy. Variables with dims, dtype, role, units and missing-value rule. Coordinates The coordinate range and values of each dim. You can search them when there are many. Missingness A heatmap of missing values for each variable along the time dim. The plot sandbox renders it. Preview The first rows, as the ingest run wrote them (preview.json) About The content hash, the size, the ingest run, the date of creation and the version message

dataset://default/eu_media_daily@v1 (the copy button next to the title) is the reference that specs and score requests use. When you submit a run, @latest resolves to the newest ready version. The run records the version that it got.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Build shows a list of the specs with their latest revision. It also shows if each revision is valid. New spec opens the editor on the geo MMM template.

The editor is Monaco with YAML support. It uses the modelspec.json schema of the server. Thus, it completes keys and shows the documentation of a field when you hover over it. When you type (and when you push Cmd+Enter), the app sends the spec to POST /v1/specs:validate. The server then does these steps:

  1. It resolves each dataset:// reference, step and model plugin.
  2. It checks the settings against the sanitized JSON Schema of the plugin.
  3. It propagates the data schema through the pipeline. For this, it uses the exported schema effect of each step.

Problems show as squiggles at the exact YAML path and in the Issues tab. Each problem has its error code (LEAKAGE_RISK, SCHEMA_INVALID, …). The badge below the title shows valid or the number of errors.

The right-hand panel:

Tab Shows Pipeline The raw data after binding, then one card for each step. Each card shows the plugin and version, and the kind of step (reshape, value, feature). It also shows if the step learns state and is invertible, and the dims that it adds or changes. It also shows the context tail that it keeps for scoring, and Schema after this step. The Train / holdout split marker is at the position that data.split.after_step sets. Issues Each validation issue with its code, JSON pointer and message Revisions Each saved revision, with its message. Select two revisions to see a diff.

The buttons:

  • Save revision (Cmd+S) stores the text as a new immutable revision (r1, r2, …) with the optional message. You can also save revisions that are not valid. Thus, you never lose work in progress. You cannot fit a revision that is not valid.
  • Dry-run starts a validate run of the saved revision in the sandbox. It checks the real data against the spec, one array at a time. It fits the pipeline on the data (not the model). It records the schema at each stage. Use it when the effect of a step is dynamic. Also use it when the static check passes and you want to know if the data really fits.
  • Fit submits a fit run of the saved revision and opens its run page.

docs.title: Runs
docs.text: Each ingest, describe, dry-run, fit and score is a run. You can filter the list by state and by type. The list updates live.

docs.title: Run detail
docs.text:
The run page subscribes to the server-sent event stream of the run (Live next to the state). After a disconnect, it continues from the point where it stopped.

  • Progress: the current phase (Starting the sandbox, Loading inputs, Fitting, Rendering plots, Uploading outputs, …), the latest message from the runner and a progress bar. For a PyMC fit, the message shows the chain, draw and divergence counts. No progress reported recently shows when a run is quiet for longer than expected. The app then marks the run as stalled. This is a warning, not a failure. The status from the executor tells if the run is alive.
  • Logs: the stdout and stderr that the supervisor captured from the worker. The logs have a size limit, and the app removes unsafe characters. Use the All / stdout / stderr / system filters, a text filter and Follow.
  • Details: the timestamps, and the spec revision, model version or dataset of the run. It also shows the spec hash, the run that it retried and its cost (Not metered locally).
  • Events: each persisted event, with diagnostics and metrics. On a laptop, this includes the DEV_MODE_ISOLATION warning.

Actions:

  • Cancel: stops an active run. Fits with checkpoints stop as partial.
  • Resume: a partial run continues from its checkpoints as a new attempt.
  • Retry: makes a new run from a failed run. After RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, the dialog recommends the next resource class.

A fit that succeeded links to its model version: Inspect model://default/eu-geo-mmm@v1.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: Models shows a list of all the models (one for each spec name). The model page shows a list of its versions. After each fit that succeeds, the platform verifies the outputs of the run and signs the bundle manifest. Then it registers a new version. The version page has six tabs and a Score button.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Scorecard collects the diagnostics into pass, warn and fail items. Each item has a plain-language message, the metric and its threshold, and a suggested action. Metrics are the holdout metrics that the spec asked for (evaluate.metrics). The platform calculates them before the refit. It scores the holdout through the normal score path. Capabilities come from the plugin. They are the score modes, the representation (draws, quantiles, interval, point, moments) and how contributions combine. They also tell which preprocessing the model owns, and if results are deterministic for a seed.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text: The table has one row for each check and variable. You can sort and filter the rows. The checks are R-hat, bulk and tail ESS, divergences and Pareto k. A row can also show "LOO invalid" with the reason from the plugin.

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
This tab shows the plot recipes that the spec lists in outputs.plots. The app renders them from the precomputed plot data in the bundle. Each card tells the recipe that made it (core.ppc_fan@1.0.0) and the library (vega-lite or plotly). Each card also has a plain-language caption.

All plots, also the first-party plots, render in an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts">. This iframe comes from the own origin of the plot sandbox (port 5174 locally). The sanitizer of the server checked the specs when the run finished. It checks them again on each read. Before a chart library runs, the sandbox refuses URL data, links, external images and tile maps. The two windows communicate only through a small, validated postMessage protocol. See Web app and plot sandbox.

docs.title: Data tree
docs.text: This tab is a browser for the ui/tree_index.json file of the bundle. It shows each group of the fitted bundle with its variables, dims, shapes, units and attributes. The groups are binding, fit_coords for each stage, model/posterior, sample_stats, log_likelihood, preprocess/<step>/{arrays,context} and derived/…. The tab reads only the index. The arrays stay in the bundle. You can download the bundle from Provenance or with the client.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text: This tab shows a heatmap of the learned state of each step (for example scale(geo, channel)). The data comes from the ui/preprocess.json view of the bundle. The tab shows each step in sequence with its resolved plugin, and if it is stateful. It also shows its learned JSON and its numeric state arrays. For larger arrays, the list tells that they are omitted. You can also see the full state under preprocess/ in Data tree.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Signature: the signature of the bundle manifest (EC P-256 locally, in place of Cloud KMS), its status, and the spec, data and catalog hashes that it binds. Before the server gives a download link, it checks the signature, the tenant and each object generation.
  • Lineage: the fit run and attempt, the plugin and version, and the engine and seed. It also shows the executor and resource class, and the dataset and side-table versions. It also shows the evaluation bundle that the model was fitted again from, and the library versions in the runner.
  • Bundle objects: each stored object with its size, CRC32C and generation. You can open or download each object through a short-lived signed URL. The app compares the download with that CRC32C.

docs.title: Score
docs.text:
Select a model and a version, or come to this page from a model page. The app makes the page from the inputs of the version (GET /v1/models/{id}/versions/{v}/inputs). Thus, the page shows only the options that the model can do. The server checks the request statically before a run starts.

What this model needs shows these items:

  • The variable that the model predicts.
  • The inputs that the model reads. A label shows the inputs that the model needs on future periods, for example planned spend.
  • The data that the model was fitted on: the fitted date range and each level of the other dims.

The names are the canonical names of the spec (its data.bind).

Then do the steps of the form:

Step Meaning What do you want to do? Select a mode. The page shows only the modes that the plugin declares: Forecast, Predict, What if (counterfactual), Simulate, Evaluate and, for state-space models, Update with new data (filter). How far ahead? For a forecast: type the number of periods after the fitted end. The model uses its own time dim. Values to score Select one: Type values, Use a dataset or No new data. The grid of Type values starts with the periods to score and each fitted level. You can paste rows from a spreadsheet. You can also use Fill blanks to put one value in all the empty cells of a column. The app sends typed values inline (ScoreCall.inline, a maximum of 5 MB). The server checks them against the inputs of the model. You do not upload a file. For Use a dataset, Upload makes a dataset. Evaluate and filter need a dataset. Future values … not given For a forecast: select the value that empty future inputs get. The options are the last value, the value of the same period one year before, zero, or none. If you select none, you must give each value. Changes Change a variable on some levels before the model scores, for example multiply spend by 1.2 where channel=tv. What if compares the result with the changes and without them.

Advanced contains the other fields:

Field Meaning Inputs enter at stage The position where the data of a dataset goes into the pipeline. This can be raw (the units of the dataset), or a later stage, for example weekly, to send weekly EUR spend directly. The pipeline skips the steps before the stage and their side tables. Typed values go into the pipeline at raw. Scenario dataset A changed copy of the input data. What if compares it with the input. Side tables Tables with score_policy: supplied (here fx) use the version from the fit by default. They must cover the scored dates. The platform uses pinned tables again from the fit. Quantity Expected (the mean response) or Predictive (with observation noise) Units, Names Original units (inverted back through the pipeline) or model space. The names of your dataset or the canonical names of the plugin. Summaries, Draws The summaries to return (mean, median, sd, hdi_50, hdi_90, quantiles), and the number of joint draws. 0 returns only summaries. Counterfactual deltas need draws to show their uncertainty. Variables, Seed Limit the outputs. Set the seed to get draws that you can reproduce.

A checklist above the button shows the data that the app will send. It also shows the data that is missing. The button shows the name of the mode, for example Forecast or Predict.

The button sends POST /v1/models/{id}/versions/{v}:score with Prefer: wait=30 and an idempotency key. Then the page follows the run.

You can send actuals with a forecast if the model can use them. The grid then has a column for the target. The run also returns predictions on the periods of the actuals. These predictions are one-step-ahead: each one is the value that the model expected before it saw the actual. Predictions against your actuals shows these items:

  • The number of actuals that the app compared.
  • The typical error and the percentage error.
  • The percentage of actuals that are in the band.
  • A chart for each series. The actuals show as diamonds. After the last actual, the forecast shows as a dashed line.
  • A table with the error for each period.

The run returns the actuals that it used in ScoreSummary.actuals.

Results shows these items:

  • The plots of the run: a forecast fan for each market, or the scenario against the baseline for a counterfactual.
  • The outputs with their sizes and signed links. score.zarr.zip is the full xr.DataTree. ui/summary.arrow is the summary table.
  • The summary as a table, with one row for each coordinate and one column for each statistic.
  • A quick chart. You can plot it again by a different column.

If the model did not see a market before (for example FR above), the platform draws it from the fitted hierarchy. Thus, its band is wider. The issues of the result tell this.

docs.title: Workflows and governance v0.5
docs.text:
Workflows builds, runs, schedules and monitors workflows. It has a template gallery, a visual editor and a live run monitor. The editor has a node palette, typed ports and a YAML view. See In the web app. Governance edits policies, follows validations and holds the queue of the reviewers. See In the web app.

The screens link to each other:

  • A finished workflow run links each model that it fitted to the Model Explorer. It also links each model to the validations of the version. These links are in the run summary, in the runs of the fit step and in its outputs. The run page of a workflow run opens its monitor. The lineage of a model links back to the workflow run that fitted it.
  • The header of the Model Explorer shows the validation status of the version. This is a link to the validations of the version. Under Governance evidence, the Model Explorer links to the latest validation and the policies. A validation links back to the Model Explorer and to the run that calculated its checks.
  • The Data Explorer for data over time offers the readiness workflow, with that data already bound. In Guided mode, this is the Run this recipe page. In Expert mode, this is the template wizard.
  • Start with this on an About card or on a Help me choose result opens a workflow template. In Guided mode, it opens as a recipe. In Expert mode, it opens in the template wizard. For a governance check, it opens the check in the check catalog. In Guided mode, a model opens the guided template that uses it. If a model has no guided template, the app shows Set up in Expert mode (a deliberate switch). The app does not open the spec editor.

docs.title: Catalog
docs.text:
The catalog shows the contents of the runner image. Its sandboxed describe run exports these contents, and its digest identifies them:

  • Models: inference, representation, score modes and base image.
  • Steps: kind, if it learns state, invertibility and summary.
  • Plots: recipe, title, audience and the bundle groups that it needs.

Click a row to see its full entry. Specs can use only the items in this list. The generated catalogs have the same data.

Since v0.5, the catalog opens on Browse. It shows each item that a user can select, with its plain-language About card. Help me choose is one click away (see About cards and choosing).

docs.title: Explorers and budget plans v0.5
docs.text:
• Explore this version on a dataset version opens the Data Explorer.
  • Explore on a model version opens the Model Explorer. It shows parameters, diagnostics, fit, residuals, contributions, response curves, IRF/FEVD, forecasts, backtests, governance evidence and lineage.
  • Compare shows some versions side by side with Diebold-Mariano tests.
  • Optimise budget makes a plan for a marketing budget.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
This browser stores Appearance and Mode. Project admins also see Lock … to Guided mode under Mode v0.4. This is the persona lock of the project. The server stores and audits it (see Guided mode). Connection shows the API and the plot sandbox that the app was built for (VITE_API_BASE, VITE_PLOTS_ORIGIN). It also shows the server and contract versions, and the latency of each readiness check.

Organisation admins also see Data v0.4. Here, they can do a GDPR export of all the data that the organisation stored. They can also delete the organisation. The deletion has a 7-day grace period, and they can cancel it in that period. See Settings > Data.

docs.title: Integrations v0.4
docs.text:
This is where a model goes out of the platform. It has Guided cards for Google Sheets, a BI dashboard and a webhook. It also has these Expert pages:

  • Endpoints and aliases that you promote through the scorecard gate. These pages have the history, rollback, the input contract, Try it and snippets in six languages.
  • Webhooks with their delivery logs and replays.
  • Saved plots with PNG/SVG/PDF downloads and embed links that expire.

The Share button of a plot gallery also starts here. The Integrations hub describes each page.

If the server permits self-service sign-up, the sign-in screen links to the public sign-up page. See Sign-up and e-mail verification.

docs.title: Guided
docs.text:
This is the task flow for analysts:

  1. Select a template.
  2. Answer questions about the data.
  3. Tell what you believe.
  4. Fit the model.
  5. Read the report and the sanity scorecard.
  6. Try what-if scenarios.
  7. Share the result.

Each step has its own URL and View as YAML. For a full example, see Your first analysis in Guided mode.

docs.title: Usage, Members, Tokens and Admin v0.3
docs.text:
These pages help you operate the platform for many persons and organisations. The Administration guide describes them, with screenshots:

Page Who sees it What it is for Usage All members of the project. Organisation needs a tenant-wide admin. Cost and quota use for a UTC day or month Members All members. Changes need an admin. Who has which role, invitations Tokens All members (their own tokens). Admins see the tokens of all members. API tokens: create, list, revoke. ?preset=score:<alias> opens a token for one endpoint. Admin Platform operators Tenants, quotas, kill switches, executors and the audit log. v0.4 adds the sign-up review queue and tenant trust.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Your first model in the web app: the E33 demo, step by step in the app, from upload to counterfactual.
  • Web app and plot sandbox: build variables, the API client and the security headers.
  • Security model: the risks that the sandbox and the plot iframe prevent, locally and in production.

docs.title: Receive webhooks v0.4
docs.text: A webhook sends a small JSON envelope to your URL with POST. It does this when a run finishes, a model version is ready, an endpoint is promoted or a score is complete. In this tutorial, you create a webhook. You write a receiver that makes sure that each delivery came from the platform. Then you see how it reacts to a new model, first on your laptop. All persons can send a request to your URL. Thus the check is necessary. mapi_client.webhooks.verify does the check in one call.

docs.title: 1. Create the webhook
docs.text:
You must have the project admin role (or a token with the webhooks:manage scope).

Web appCLIPython
  1. Go to Integrations → Overview → Webhook → Set up a webhook (or the Webhooks tab → New webhook).
  2. Type an https URL and a description.
  3. Select the events.
  4. Copy the signing secret. The app shows the signing secret only one time.

Done stays disabled until you copy the secret or select the box that tells that you stored it.

mapi webhooks create https://hooks.acme.example/mapi \
  -e model.version.ready -e run.failed --description "Planning pipeline"

created = api.webhooks.create(
    "https://hooks.example.com/mapi", ["model.version.ready", "endpoint.promoted"]
)
signing_secret = created.secret  # the only copy: store it with the receiver
print(created.webhook.id, created.webhook.secret_hint)

Keep the secret in a place where your receiver can read it. For example, keep it as MAPI_WEBHOOK_SECRET in your secret manager. The platform refuses URLs on private, loopback or link-local addresses (WEBHOOK_URL_BLOCKED). It also refuses ports other than 443 and 8443. Step 4 shows how a development stack can send to a receiver on your computer.

docs.title: 2. What a delivery looks like
docs.text:
POST /mapi/webhook HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
Mapi-Signature: t=1792000000,v1=5257a869e7ecebeda32affa62cdca3fa51cad7e77a0e56ff536d0ce8e108d8bd
Mapi-Event-Id: evt_01jaf3k1m2n3p4q5r6s7t8v9w0
Mapi-Event-Type: endpoint.promoted
Mapi-Webhook-Id: whk_01jaf3h1j2k3m4n5p6q7r8s9t0
Mapi-Delivery-Id: whd_01jaf3m1n2p3q4r5s6t7v8w9x0

{"api_version": "v1", "created": "2026-10-15T09:30:00Z", "data": {"alias": "geo-mmm-prod", ...},
 "id": "evt_01jaf3k1m2n3p4q5r6s7t8v9w0", "project": "growth", "tenant": "acme",
 "type": "endpoint.promoted"}

v1 is the hex HMAC-SHA256 of the timestamp t, a dot and the raw body. The signing secret of the webhook is the key. During the rotation of a secret, the header contains one v1 for each active secret. Thus receivers that know one of the two secrets continue to work during the 24 hours of the rotation.

Event data run.succeeded, run.failed run_id, kind, state. If the run failed, also failure_class and code. model_version_id for a fit. model.version.ready model_id, model_version_id, ref, scorecard_overall (pass, warn or fail) endpoint.promoted alias, ref, revision, model_version_id, overridden score.completed run_id, endpoint (if it was an endpoint call), model_version_id, the names of the outputs tenant.deletion.completed deletion_id, requested_at, completed_at

The envelope contains only ids and states. It never contains data values, signed URLs or secrets. To get other information, use the API.

docs.title: 3. Write the receiver
docs.text:
verify(headers, body, secret) does these steps:

  1. It finds Mapi-Signature in all types of headers object. The names are not case-sensitive.
  2. It calculates the HMAC over the raw body again. It compares the HMAC with each v1 in constant time. secret can be a list: the old secret and the new secret during a rotation.
  3. It refuses a timestamp that is more than 300 seconds from your clock. This limits replays of a captured delivery. To change the limit, use tolerance=.
  4. It parses the body as a WebhookEnvelope. It does a check that Mapi-Event-Id names the same event.

If a step fails, verify raises MapiError with the code WEBHOOK_SIGNATURE_INVALID. Answer it with 401. is_valid(...) does the same check and returns a boolean. The function refuses bodies that are larger than 256 KiB before it parses them.

Use the raw body

Verify the bytes exactly as they came in. Your framework can parse a body and serialise it again (json.dumps(await request.json())). The spaces or the sequence of keys then change, and the body never agrees with its signature.

FastAPIFlask 
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Request
from mapi_client.webhooks import verify
from mapi_spec.errors import MapiError

app = FastAPI()
SECRET = os.environ["MAPI_WEBHOOK_SECRET"]  # the secret shown once by `mapi webhooks create`
seen: set[str] = set()  # use your database: deliveries are at least once


@app.post("/mapi/webhook")
async def mapi_webhook(request: Request) -> dict[str, str]:
    body = await request.body()  # the raw bytes: a re-serialised body fails the signature
    try:
        event = verify(request.headers, body, SECRET)
    except MapiError:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="invalid signature") from None
    if event.id in seen:
        return {"status": "duplicate"}
    seen.add(event.id)
    if event.type == "endpoint.promoted":
        print("now serving", event.data["ref"], "revision", event.data["revision"])
    elif event.type == "run.failed":
        print("run failed:", event.data["run_id"], event.data.get("code"))
    return {"status": "ok"}

from flask import Flask, abort, request
from mapi_client.webhooks import verify
from mapi_spec.errors import MapiError

app = Flask(__name__)
SECRET = os.environ["MAPI_WEBHOOK_SECRET"]  # the secret shown once by `mapi webhooks create`
handled: set[str] = set()  # use your database: deliveries are at least once


@app.post("/mapi/webhook")
def mapi_webhook() -> dict[str, str]:
    try:  # request.get_data(): the raw body, before anything reads request.json
        event = verify(request.headers, request.get_data(), SECRET)
    except MapiError:
        abort(401)
    if event.id in handled:
        return {"status": "duplicate"}
    handled.add(event.id)
    if event.type == "model.version.ready":
        print("model ready:", event.data["ref"], "scorecard:", event.data["scorecard_overall"])
    return {"status": "ok"}

The test suite runs the two receivers (docs/snippets/webhook_receiver.py and webhook_receiver_flask.py). It sends deliveries with exactly the same signature as the platform. Then it sends a replay, a body that was changed and an old timestamp.

docs.title: 4. Try it on your laptop
docs.text:
A make dev stack trusts a receiver on your own computer. The dev profile writes a temporary CA and a certificate for 127.0.0.1 and localhost to .local/dev/webhook-tls/. It trusts that CA and puts the two hosts on the allow-list (configuration). The workspace of the repository has FastAPI and uvicorn.

  1. Save the FastAPI receiver as receiver.py.
  2. Create a webhook for it from the repository.
  3. Export the secret that the command shows.
  4. Serve the receiver with that certificate:
uv run mapi webhooks create https://localhost:8443/mapi/webhook \
  -e endpoint.promoted -e run.failed               # prints the secret once
export MAPI_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_…                 # that secret
uv run uvicorn receiver:app --port 8443 \
  --ssl-certfile .local/dev/webhook-tls/cert.pem --ssl-keyfile .local/dev/webhook-tls/key.pem

Promote a fitted model to an endpoint. The Quickstart fits a model. Promote it in the Integrations hub. The receiver then prints now serving endpoint://<project>/<alias> revision 1.

In the web app, the Delivery log of the webhook shows the try, with the response code and the time of your receiver. Send test sends the newest delivery again. Thus you can do a check of a receiver that you changed. mapi webhooks replay <webhook_id> <delivery_id> does the same. The M3 end-to-end suite gets each event type in this way.

You can also send a delivery with a correct signature to your receiver yourself, without a stack. mapi_spec.webhooks.signature_header(body, [secret]) makes the header exactly as the platform does.

docs.title: Good receivers
docs.text:
• Answer fast with a 2xx. Then do the work in the background. After 5 seconds, the platform stops the delivery and tries it again (after 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h).
  • Expect duplicates. Retries and replays send the same event again. Keep the event.ids that you processed.
  • Answer 410 Gone to stop deliveries permanently. The platform disables the webhook immediately. After 20 failed events in a sequence, the platform also disables it. mapi webhooks ls shows the reason. To enable it again, use api.webhooks.update(id, active=True).
  • Keep the secret secret. The app shows it one time. Keep it in your secret manager. To rotate it, use mapi webhooks rotate <id>. Give the two secrets to the receiver until the old secret expires.
  • Serve HTTPS on port 443 or 8443 under a public host name in production. The platform does not send deliveries to private, loopback or link-local addresses (see SSRF protection).

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• When you get endpoint.promoted, refresh a Google Sheet or a cache.
  • Connect a pipeline. When you get model.version.ready with scorecard_overall: pass, promote the model version with a token that has the scope endpoints:promote (Endpoints and webhooks).

docs.title: Workflow cookbook v0.5
docs.text:
This page gives three complete analyses. Each analysis is one YAML document. You can save, run and schedule it, and give it to a colleague. The tests of the documentation validate each document on this page against the node catalog and run it from start to end. Thus the documents that you copy operate correctly. For the format, see Workflows. For all nodes, see the node reference. For short parts with one pattern each, see the workflows guide.

Recipe The question it answers Is my weekly KPI ready to forecast? Does the series need differencing? Which ARIMA orders are correct? Is ARIMAX better than a naive forecast on honest backtests? Can we use it? Do these series move together? Do some series have a long-run relation (VECM), or a relation only in their changes (VAR)? Does one series help to predict a different series? Which forecasting model? Which of SARIMAX, ARIMA, ETS and Theta forecasts best on the same folds? Is the advantage of the winner more than chance?

docs.title: Readiness to ARIMAX
docs.text:
In plain words. Before you trust a forecast, you must know four things:

  • If the series "wanders". If it does, you must model its changes, not its levels.
  • How much of the past is important.
  • If the model forecasts better than the obvious rule "next week is like this week".
  • If the model found a real effect, not noise.

This workflow answers each question with the standard statistical tool. It records each decision with the numbers that caused it. It keeps the model only if the model is better than the benchmarks. It also records the governance evidence.

For the statistician. ADF, KPSS, Phillips-Perron and Zivot-Andrews (one endogenous break) decide d with a conservative rule: difference the series unless the evidence for stationarity is clear on the two sides. Seasonal strength (STL) decides D. The ARMA orders come from a grid of information criteria over p ≤ max_p, q ≤ max_q. The workflow fits each point as ARIMA(p, d, q) on the levels. Thus the model estimates d, and does not apply it to data that is already differenced. The report shows ACF/PACF for the reader.

The backtest is a rolling origin with a fixed training window, a gap and some horizons. The workflow scores ARIMAX and the naive and seasonal-naive benchmarks on the same folds. A Diebold-Mariano test with the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction tells if the difference in squared errors at horizon 1 is significant. select.best keeps the model only if its MAE is better than each benchmark in must_beat.

flowchart LR
  T["adf · kpss · pp · za<br/>seasonal strength"] --> B{"wanders?<br/>seasonal?"}
  B -- then --> D["difference /<br/>seasonal difference"]
  T --> O["AR/MA order<br/>search (AIC)"]
  B --> O
  O --> BT["rolling-origin backtest<br/>ARIMAX"]
  F["folds: window 104,<br/>gap 1, h = 1, 4, 8"] --> BT
  F --> N["naive and<br/>seasonal naive"]
  BT --> C["compare +<br/>Diebold-Mariano"]
  N --> C
  C --> S{"select:<br/>beats naive?"}
  FIT["fit on all data<br/>(13-week holdout first)"] --> S
  S --> G["governance policy<br/>(null tests, benchmarks...)"]
  G --> P["evidence pack<br/>when it passed"]
  S --> R["report"]

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
# Workflow cookbook: is the weekly KPI ready to forecast, which ARIMAX, does it beat naive,
# and may we use it? (validated by conformance/tests/test_docs_v05.py and run end to end
# against a real server by packages/server/tests/test_docs_client_v05.py)
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata:
  name: weekly-readiness
  project: growth
  description: Unit roots -> differencing -> AR/MA orders -> rolling-origin backtest -> ARIMAX vs naive -> select -> governance
params:
  alpha: {type: number, default: 0.05, minimum: 0.001, maximum: 0.2, description: "Significance level of every test"}
  season: {type: integer, default: 52, minimum: 2, maximum: 400, description: "Season length (52 for weekly data)"}
  drivers: {type: array, default: [], description: "Drivers known for the future (planned price, promotions)"}
  window: {type: integer, default: 104, minimum: 20, description: "Training weeks per backtest fold"}
  horizons: {type: array, default: [1, 4, 8], description: "Forecast horizons scored separately"}
  gap: {type: integer, default: 1, minimum: 0, maximum: 52, description: "Weeks between training and test (data arrives late)"}
  max_p: {type: integer, default: 3, minimum: 0, maximum: 8}
  max_q: {type: integer, default: 3, minimum: 0, maximum: 8}
inputs:
  data: {type: dataset, description: "The weekly KPI with its drivers"}
nodes:
# 1. Unit-root tests. ADF and Phillips-Perron: "the series wanders" is the null hypothesis;
#    KPSS: "the series is stable" is the null; Zivot-Andrews allows one structural break.
- {id: adf, use: test.adf, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, with: {alpha: {$param: alpha}}}
- {id: kpss, use: test.kpss, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, with: {alpha: {$param: alpha}}}
- {id: pp, use: test.pp, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, with: {alpha: {$param: alpha}}}
- {id: za, use: test.zivot_andrews, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, with: {alpha: {$param: alpha}}}
- {id: seas, use: test.seasonal_strength, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, with: {period: {$param: season}}}
# 2. Decide the differencing (a branch reads the test results; never eval).
- id: wanders
  use: branch.if
  label: Difference?
  with: {condition: "(not nodes.adf.reject or nodes.kpss.reject) and not (nodes.pp.reject and nodes.za.reject)"}
- id: seasonal
  use: branch.if
  label: Seasonal difference?
  with: {condition: nodes.seas.seasonal}
- {id: sdiff, use: transform.seasonal_difference, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, when: seasonal.then,
   with: {period: {$param: season}}}
- {id: diff, use: transform.difference, inputs: {data: [sdiff.data, inputs.data]}, when: wanders.then}
# 3. AR and MA orders: autocorrelations to read, an information-criterion grid to decide.
- {id: acf, use: test.acf_pacf, inputs: {data: [diff.data, sdiff.data, inputs.data]},
   with: {max_order: {$param: max_p}}}
- id: order
  use: search.arma_order
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    d: {$expr: "if(nodes.wanders.value, 1, 0)"}
    max_p: {$param: max_p}
    max_q: {$param: max_q}
    exog: {$param: drivers}
    criterion: aic
# 4. An honest backtest: a rolling origin with a fixed training window, a gap and several
#    horizons; ARIMAX and the naive benchmarks on the very same folds.
- id: folds
  use: split.rolling_origin
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    window: {$param: window}
    horizons: {$param: horizons}
    gap: {$param: gap}
    n_folds: 6
    step: 4
- id: backtest
  use: model.backtest
  inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan}
  with:
    model: ts.sarimax@^1
    settings:
      order: {$expr: "[nodes.order.best_p, if(nodes.wanders.value, 1, 0), nodes.order.best_q]"}
      seasonal_order: {$expr: "[0, if(nodes.seasonal.value, 1, 0), 0, params.season]"}
      exog: {$param: drivers}
    metrics: [mae, rmse, mape, mase]
- id: naive
  use: evaluate.baseline
  inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan}
  with: {methods: [naive, seasonal_naive], season: {$param: season}}
# 5. ARIMAX vs naive: rank them, and test whether the difference is more than luck.
- {id: compare, use: compare.models, inputs: {candidates: [backtest.metrics, naive.metrics]},
   with: {metric: mae}}
- {id: dm, use: compare.diebold_mariano, inputs: {a: backtest.metrics, b: naive.metrics},
   with: {loss: squared, horizon: 1, alpha: {$param: alpha}}}
# 6. Fit (scored on the last 13 weeks first, then refitted on everything, so governance has
#    a test period) and keep it only if it beats naive.
- id: holdout
  use: split.holdout
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with: {split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: time, last: 13}}
- id: fit
  use: model.fit
  inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: holdout.plan}
  with:
    model: ts.sarimax@^1
    settings:
      order: {$expr: "[nodes.order.best_p, if(nodes.wanders.value, 1, 0), nodes.order.best_q]"}
      seasonal_order: {$expr: "[0, if(nodes.seasonal.value, 1, 0), 0, params.season]"}
      exog: {$param: drivers}
    fit: {mode: evaluate_then_refit}
    evaluate: {metrics: [mape, mase, coverage_90]}
- id: select
  use: select.best
  inputs: {table: compare.table, models: [fit.model]}
  with: {metric: mae, must_beat: [naive], margin: 0.0}
# 7. Governance: the policy in force (null tests, benchmarks, residuals...), recorded as a
#    validation of the model version when it passes; the evidence pack only if it did.
- {id: governance, use: governance.policy, inputs: {model: select.model, data: inputs.data},
   with: {submit: true}}
- {id: trusted, use: branch.if, with: {condition: nodes.governance.passed}}
- {id: pack, use: report.evidence_pack, inputs: {model: select.model, evidence: governance.evidence},
   when: trusted.then, with: {format: json}}
- id: report
  use: report.summary
  inputs:
    tests: [adf.result, kpss.result, pp.result, za.result, seas.result, acf.result, dm.result]
    metrics: [backtest.metrics, naive.metrics]
    items: [order.table, compare.table]
    model: select.model
  with: {title: Weekly readiness and ARIMAX}
outputs: {model: select.model, report: report.report, evidence: governance.evidence}

Copy these three details into your own workflows:

  • Alternatives keep the graph honest. diff reads [sdiff.data, inputs.data]. This is the seasonally differenced series if that node ran. If not, it is the raw series. acf uses the series with the most processing that exists. The workflow calculates nothing two times. If the workflow does not take a branch, nothing breaks: skipped nodes are skipped, not failed.
  • Decisions move as values. $expr: "[nodes.order.best_p, if(nodes.wanders.value, 1, 0), nodes.order.best_q]" changes the search result and the branch decision into the order of the model. The server parses the expression language and never uses eval on it. The run records each value that it read.
  • The fit has its own holdout. split.holdout keeps the last 13 weeks out of the first fit (mode: evaluate_then_refit). Thus the governance checks that need unseen data have it. These checks are the null tests, the naive benchmark and the holdout accuracy. Then the workflow fits the model again on all the data.

docs.title: Run it with the CLI
docs.text:
mapi workflows templates                      # the gallery, in plain words
mapi workflows init ts_readiness_arimax --name weekly-readiness   # writes weekly-readiness.yaml
mapi workflows validate weekly-readiness.yaml # checked by the server: pointers to every problem
mapi workflows apply weekly-readiness.yaml -m "first version"     # create, or save a revision
mapi workflows run weekly-readiness \
  --input data=dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest \
  --param 'drivers=["price"]' --param window=104 \
  --watch                                     # live node status; exit 1 if the run fails

mapi workflows init writes the ts_readiness_arimax template of the gallery with your name and project. This template is the same analysis with an expanding-window backtest. To get the rolling origin and the evidence pack, save the document above as weekly-readiness.yaml instead. --watch shows the status of each node during the run. On a terminal, it draws the status again in the same place. In a log, it writes one line for each change. At the end, it shows the summary.

docs.title: Run it with the Python client
docs.text:
Do these steps:

  1. Validate the file on the server. The server saves nothing.
  2. Make the workflow, or save a new revision.
  3. Run the workflow.
  4. Follow the live events.
from pathlib import Path

check = api.workflows.validate(Path("weekly-readiness.yaml"))  # on the server; saves nothing
for issue in check.issues:  # every problem with a JSON pointer into the document
    print(issue.severity.value, issue.pointer, issue.message)
print(" -> ".join(check.order))  # the order the nodes will run in

from mapi_client import WorkflowEnd, WorkflowEventFrame, WorkflowSnapshot

# create the workflow, or save the file as its next revision when it changed
workflow, revision = api.workflows.upsert(Path("weekly-readiness.yaml"))
run = api.workflows.run(
    workflow.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest"},  # pinned to a version at start
    params={"drivers": ["price"], "window": 80, "max_p": 2, "max_q": 2},
)
for item in api.workflows.stream_events(run.run_id):  # server-sent events, resumable
    match item:
        case WorkflowSnapshot(run=now):
            print(f"{len(now.nodes)} nodes, {now.status.value}")
        case WorkflowEventFrame(event=e) if e.type.value == "workflow.branch.decided":
            print(f"  {e.node_id}: took the {e.data['arm']} arm")
        case WorkflowEventFrame(event=e) if e.node_id is not None:
            print(f"  {e.node_id}: {e.type.value.rsplit('.', 1)[-1]}")
        case WorkflowEnd(status=status):
            print("run", status.value if status else "ended")

Read the results. They include the verdict of each test, each branch with the values that it read, the selected orders and the Diebold-Mariano verdict. They also tell why the workflow selected the model or did not select it:

run = api.workflows.wait(run.run_id)  # raises the run's error if it failed
nodes = {n.node_id: n for n in run.nodes}
print(nodes["adf"].result["verdict_plain"])  # e.g. "The series wanders: consider differencing it."
for d in run.decisions:
    print(d.node_id, d.arm, d.inputs)  # every branch with the values its condition read
order, d = nodes["order"].result, 1 if nodes["wanders"].result["value"] else 0
print(f"ARIMA({order['best_p']}, {d}, {order['best_q']})")  # chosen by information criterion
print(nodes["dm"].result["verdict_plain"])  # is ARIMAX's edge over naive more than luck?
print(nodes["select"].result["reason_plain"])  # kept only if it beats the benchmarks
model_ref = run.outputs["model"].ref  # model://growth/wf-weekly-readiness-fit@v1
report = run.outputs["report"].inline  # mapi.report/v1: every test, decision and table

The governance node measured the selected model against the policy that applies. Because submit: true is set, it recorded a validation of that model version:

gov = nodes["governance"].result  # the policy in force, measured on the selected model
print("passed" if gov["passed"] else f"failed: {gov['failed_checks']}")
validation = api.validations.get(gov["validation_id"])  # recorded because submit: true
print(validation.status.value)  # validated, or awaiting_approval when a reviewer must sign
for r in validation.results:
    print(f"{r.check:28} {r.status.value:7} {r.message_plain}")
api.validations.download_evidence_pack(validation.id, "evidence.html")  # for the auditor
