data.quality                 pass    No data problems found (156 periods of history).
convergence                  pass    The fit reported no convergence problems.
baseline.beats_naive         pass    On the 13 held-out periods the model's error is 25% lower than 'same as last period' (the strongest simple benchmark).
holdout.accuracy             pass    On data it was not fitted on, the model's average percentage error is 1.8% (limit 15%).
residuals.whiteness          pass    No pattern is left in the errors (Ljung-Box p = 0.39 at 10 lags).
null.permutation_target      pass    The model did better on held-out data (skill 0.236) than all 20 fits with the drivers price shuffled in blocks of 7 (the result untouched) (p = 0.048).
stability.rolling_params     fail    ar.L1 changes a lot across windows of history (variation 1205%): the relationship may not be stable over time.

Read the output as a reviewer does. On unseen weeks, the model is 25% better than naive. Its errors have no pattern. It forecasts better than each fit with the price driver shuffled in time. But the AR coefficient is not stable across windows.

That check failed, but the version is still validated. The status of a check and its severity are different things. The default forecast policy sets stability to information, so the check does not block. The reviewer can see it in the record and in the evidence pack. A stricter policy (see governance) makes the check block. Then this model needs more history or a simpler specification. This is the purpose: the evidence is written, and the decision is explicit.

What the shuffle test measures on a random walk

The model has a driver. Thus the test shuffles the driver in blocks and does not change the result. It scores each fit by its skill against the null forecast on the held-out weeks. Persistence ("next week is like this week") helps the shuffled fits exactly as much as it helps the real fit. Thus the test measures what the driver adds to persistence. For a model without drivers, the test uses shuffled changes of the series (null tests explained).

Then keep the workflow up to date:

weekly = api.workflows.schedule(
    workflow.id,
    "0 6 * * 1",  # Mondays at 06:00
    timezone="Europe/Berlin",
    inputs={"data": "dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest"},
    params={"drivers": ["price"]},
)
on_upload = api.workflows.trigger(
    workflow.id, "dataset://growth/weekly_sales", "data", debounce_seconds=600
)
print(weekly.next_run_at, on_upload.id)

docs.title: VAR/VECM cointegration
docs.text:
In plain words. Some series wander but stay together. Examples are the prices of close substitutes, sales and distribution, and income and consumption. If they have a relation, a model that knows the relation (an error-correction model) forecasts better. It also tells you how fast a gap closes. If they do not have a relation, model their changes. In the two cases, find out if one series helps to predict a different series.

For the statistician. The Johansen trace test (at 5%) on the levels decides the branch. If the series have a relation, search.coint_rank selects the rank. Then the workflow fits a VECM with k_ar_diff: 1 on the levels. If the series do not have a relation, the workflow differences them. Then AIC selects the VAR lag order up to maxlags, and the workflow fits a VAR on the changes. If the workflow took the changes (the first alternative), it tests Granger causality on them. If not, it tests on the levels. The forecast node uses the model that exists, with the related data.

# Workflow cookbook: do these series move together for good? VECM if they are tied in the
# long run, a VAR on the levels if they are already stable, else a VAR on the changes;
# Granger tests either way; a forecast of the winner.
# (validated by conformance/tests/test_docs_v05.py)
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {name: macro-system, project: growth}
params:
  target: {type: string, required: true, description: "The main result (one of the series)"}
  driver: {type: string, required: true, description: "A series that may help predict it"}
  maxlags: {type: integer, default: 8, minimum: 1, maximum: 52}
  horizon: {type: integer, default: 8, minimum: 1, maximum: 104}
inputs:
  # one value per series and period: value(series, quarter), the layout of ts.var/ts.vecm
  data: {type: dataset, description: "The series along one dimension"}
nodes:
# 1. Is there a long-run relationship? (Johansen trace test, every series of the dimension)
- {id: johansen, use: test.johansen, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, with: {alpha: "0.05"}}
# rank 0: no tie; rank = number of series: every series is stable (no unit root)
- id: tied
  use: branch.if
  with: {condition: "nodes.johansen.rank > 0 and nodes.johansen.rank < len(nodes.johansen.trace_stats)"}
# 2a. Tied: choose the cointegration rank and fit an error-correction model on the levels.
- {id: rank, use: search.coint_rank, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, when: tied.then}
- id: vecm
  use: model.fit
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  when: tied.then
  with:
    model: ts.vecm@^1
    settings:
      coint_rank: {$expr: "min(max(nodes.rank.rank, 1), len(nodes.johansen.trace_stats) - 1)"}
      k_ar_diff: 1
# 2b. Not tied: a VAR on the levels when every series is stable, else on the changes.
- id: stationary
  use: branch.if
  when: tied.else
  with: {condition: "nodes.johansen.rank >= len(nodes.johansen.trace_stats)"}
- {id: diff, use: transform.difference, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, when: stationary.else}
- {id: lags, use: search.var_lag_order, inputs: {data: [diff.data, inputs.data]},
   when: tied.else, with: {maxlags: {$param: maxlags}, criterion: aic}}
- id: var
  use: model.fit
  inputs: {data: [diff.data, inputs.data]}
  when: tied.else
  with:
    model: ts.var@^1
    settings: {lags: {$expr: nodes.lags.best_lag}}
# 3. Does the driver help predict the target? (on the changes when they were taken)
- id: granger
  use: test.granger
  inputs: {data: [diff.data, inputs.data]}
  with: {y: {$param: target}, x: {$param: driver}, maxlag: {$param: maxlags}}
# 4. Forecast with whichever system was fitted (the first alternative that ran).
- id: forecast
  use: model.forecast
  inputs: {model: [vecm.model, var.model], data: [diff.data, inputs.data]}
  with: {horizon: {$param: horizon}}
- id: report
  use: report.summary
  inputs:
    tests: [johansen.result, granger.result]
    items: [rank.table, lags.table]
    model: [vecm.model, var.model]
  with: {title: Series that move together}
outputs: {report: report.report, forecast: forecast.forecast}

The data keeps the series along one dimension, with one value for each series and period (value(series, quarter)). This is the layout of ts.var and ts.vecm. To ingest a wide sheet, use the wide mapping. Run the workflow as the first recipe, with the two parameters that it needs:

mapi workflows apply macro-system.yaml
mapi workflows run macro-system -i data=dataset://growth/us_macro@latest \
  -p target=realcons -p driver=realgdp --watch

run = api.workflows.run(
    wf.id,
    inputs={"data": "dataset://growth/us_macro@latest"},
    params={"target": "realcons", "driver": "realgdp", "maxlags": 4},
    wait=True,
)
nodes = {n.node_id: n for n in run.nodes}
print(nodes["johansen"].result["verdict_plain"])  # "The series share at least one long-run relationship."
print(nodes["granger"].result["verdict_plain"])   # "Past values of the driver help predict the result."
print([n.node_id for n in run.nodes if n.status.value == "skipped"])  # the branch not taken

A run on a laptop used three simulated weekly series. Two of the series have the same stochastic trend (target=a, driver=b). The run printed the two verdicts above and ['diff', 'lags', 'var']. The Johansen trace statistic (69.1) set the rank to 1, and the VECM branch ran. Granger found that b helps to predict a (p = 0.0015). See Macro and VAR analysis.

The Model Explorer shows the impulse responses, the variance decomposition, the Granger table and the Johansen table of the fitted model (mapi explore model … -s irf -s fevd).

docs.title: Forecast bake-off
docs.text:
In plain words. If you do not know which forecast method is correct for your data, let the methods compete fairly. They use the same history, the same cut-off points, the same horizons and the same naive benchmarks. Keep the winner only if it is clearly better than a simple method.

For the statistician. The plan is an expanding window with n_folds origins, one each 4 periods. The workflow scores each horizon. SARIMAX(1,1,1)(0,1,0)₅₂, ARIMA(0,1,1), damped-trend ETS and Theta compete against naive, seasonal-naive and drift. MASE puts them in sequence. MASE has no scale, so you can compare series of different sizes. Two Diebold-Mariano tests (absolute loss, horizon 1) compare the leaders with the benchmark. select.best needs a 5% MASE improvement over each benchmark. Only then does the branch fit the winner again.

# Workflow cookbook: a forecast bake-off. Four models and the naive benchmarks compete on the
# same expanding-window folds; Diebold-Mariano tests say whether the winner's edge is more
# than luck; the winner is refitted on all the data only if it beats naive.
# (validated by conformance/tests/test_docs_v05.py)
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {name: forecast-bakeoff, project: growth}
params:
  horizons: {type: array, default: [1, 4, 8]}
  season: {type: integer, default: 52, minimum: 2, maximum: 400}
  n_folds: {type: integer, default: 6, minimum: 2, maximum: 50}
inputs:
  data: {type: dataset}
nodes:
- id: folds
  use: split.expanding_window
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with: {horizons: {$param: horizons}, n_folds: {$param: n_folds}, step: 4, gap: 0}
# the candidates, each backtested on the same plan
- {id: sarimax, use: model.backtest, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {model: ts.sarimax@^1, settings: {order: [1, 1, 1], seasonal_order: [0, 1, 0, 52]}}}
- {id: arima, use: model.backtest, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {model: ts.arima@^1, settings: {order: [0, 1, 1]}}}
- {id: ets, use: model.backtest, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {model: ts.ets@^1, settings: {trend: add, damped_trend: true}}}
- {id: theta, use: model.backtest, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {model: ts.theta@^1}}
- {id: naive, use: evaluate.baseline, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {methods: [naive, seasonal_naive, drift], season: {$param: season}}}
# the league table, then two head-to-head tests against the benchmark
- id: compare
  use: compare.models
  inputs: {candidates: [sarimax.metrics, arima.metrics, ets.metrics, theta.metrics, naive.metrics]}
  with: {metric: mase}
- {id: dm_ets, use: compare.diebold_mariano, inputs: {a: ets.metrics, b: naive.metrics},
   with: {loss: absolute, horizon: 1}}
- {id: dm_sarimax, use: compare.diebold_mariano, inputs: {a: sarimax.metrics, b: naive.metrics},
   with: {loss: absolute, horizon: 1}}
# the winner, if it beats naive by at least 5%, refitted on everything
- {id: best, use: select.best, inputs: {table: compare.table},
   with: {metric: mase, must_beat: [naive], margin: 0.05}}
- {id: winner, use: branch.if, with: {condition: nodes.best.beats_baselines}}
- id: refit
  use: model.fit
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  when: winner.then
  with: {model: {$expr: nodes.best.selected_model}}
- id: report
  use: report.summary
  inputs:
    tests: [dm_ets.result, dm_sarimax.result]
    items: [compare.table]
    model: [refit.model]
  with: {title: Forecast bake-off}
outputs: {model: refit.model, comparison: compare.table, report: report.report}

mapi workflows apply forecast-bakeoff.yaml
mapi workflows run forecast-bakeoff -i data=dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest \
  -p 'horizons=[1,4]' -p n_folds=6 --watch
mapi workflows node "$RUN" compare      # the league table
mapi workflows node "$RUN" best         # who won, and whether they beat naive by 5%

On a short series with much noise, the usual result is the honest result: "ets is the best model (0.0456) but does not beat naive.drift by the required 5%: no model is selected." The workflow skips the refit node, and the report tells why. Thus nobody ships a model that only looks clever.

docs.title: Make your own
docs.text:
1. Start from the recipe that is nearest to your analysis. Use mapi workflows init <template>, or copy a document above.
  2. Find nodes with mapi workflows nodes-catalog --kind test. To see the About card, ports and parameters of one node, use --about test.kpss.
  3. Validate the document after each change. Before anything runs, mapi workflows validate my.yaml shows each problem with a JSON pointer.
  4. Save the workflow (apply).
  5. Run the workflow with --watch.
  6. Read the summary.
  7. Add a schedule or a dataset trigger to run the workflow automatically.
  8. Add a governance gate to the workflow.

docs.title: Workflows v0.5
docs.text:
A workflow connects statistical tests, data processing, train/test plans, models, governance checks and reports into one graph. The graph runs the same way each time. This guide gives the practical information:

  • How to start from the gallery.
  • The canonical "readiness → ARIMAX" document, line by line.
  • A cookbook of patterns.
  • Where each node runs.
  • How to schedule runs and how to monitor them.

The Workflows concept page gives the full data about the document format, the condition language and the validation. The node reference lists all nodes with their About cards, ports, parameters and result fields.

You want to Go to Run an analysis that is ready to use Start from the gallery Build, run and monitor workflows in the browser In the web app Understand the canonical example The canonical workflow Build your own workflow Cookbook Know what runs where and what it costs Where nodes run Run it automatically Schedules and triggers Try it in a notebook without a server Run it locally Copy a complete analysis that has tests Workflow cookbook Control it from Python or a terminal api.workflows (client), mapi workflows (CLI)

docs.title: Start from the gallery
docs.text:
The gallery has four templates. Each template has an About card in plain language (GET /v1/workflow-templates):

Template Select it when ts_readiness_arimax You have one weekly or daily KPI and you want an ARIMAX forecast that you can defend. The tests decide the differencing. A search selects the AR and MA orders. A backtest shows that the model is better than naive forecasts. var_vecm_cointegration Some series move together (for example sales, price and distribution). You want to know if they have a long-run relation before you select a VECM or a VAR. mmm_governed You need a marketing mix model that must pass the governance policy before a person uses it. forecast_bakeoff You do not know which forecast model is correct for the data. SARIMAX, ETS, Theta and a smooth trend compete on the same folds.

When you make a workflow from a template, the server copies the template document into your project as revision 1. After that, the workflow is yours and you can edit it.

# create it (the name and project come from the request's project)
api POST /v1/workflows -d '{"template": "ts_readiness_arimax"}' | jq '{id, ref, latest_revision}'

# run it on the latest version of a dataset, overriding a few parameters
api POST "/v1/workflows/$WF/runs" -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" -d '{
  "inputs": {"data": "dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest"},
  "params": {"drivers": ["price"], "n_folds": 4, "gap": 1, "horizons": [1, 4, 8]}
}' | jq '{run_id, status}'

# follow it: each node, each branch decision, then the result
api GET "/v1/workflow-runs/$RUN" | jq '.nodes[] | {node_id, status, result}'

api is the helper of the HTTP API guide. It adds the token and the project header. To do the same from the command line, use mapi workflows create --template ts_readiness_arimax, then mapi workflows run ts-readiness-arimax -i data=dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest -p 'drivers=["price"]' --watch. From Python, use api.workflows.create(template="ts_readiness_arimax") and api.workflows.run(...). The server resolves @latest when the run starts and records it as an exact version. Thus you can make the run again with the same result: GET /v1/workflow-runs/{run_id} shows dataset://growth/weekly_sales@v7.

When you start a run, the server answers 202 with the view of the run. If you start a run with an Idempotency-Key that you used before, the server returns the first run (200). It does not start a different run.

docs.title: In the web app
docs.text: To open the workflows of the project and the gallery, click Workflows in the sidebar (G then W). All the functions below use the same endpoints as the remaining part of this guide.

docs.title: Recipes for Guided users
docs.text:
In Guided mode, the sidebar item shows Recipes, and the page opens on the recipes. The recipes are the gallery templates as About cards. Each card tells in plain words:

  • What the recipe does.
  • When to use it and when not to use it.
  • What it needs and what it gives.
  • A very small example.

Run on my data asks for a dataset. It also asks for the settings that the recipe cannot guess, but only when the recipe needs them (for example, the drivers of the marketing-mix recipe). The other settings are under Fine-tune. The first run makes the workflow of the project from the template. Subsequent runs use that workflow again. The Data Explorer of data over time shows the readiness recipe with that data already selected (Check it is ready to forecast). Then the run page shows each step in plain words when the step is complete. It also shows the decisions and the summary of the report.

docs.title: Start from a template (Expert)
docs.text:
Use this template opens a wizard that has three steps:

  1. The About card of the template and the name of the workflow.
  2. The parameters. The app saves them as the defaults of the workflow. Each run can change them.
  3. The default data for the run. The app saves it as the default reference of the input. Schedules use it, and runs that start without data use it.

The app makes the workflow as revision 1.

docs.title: The editor
docs.text:
The Editor tab of a workflow has three panes. On wide screens the panes are side by side. On narrow screens they are one above the other.

Pane What it does Nodes (the palette) Shows all nodes of GET /v1/catalog/workflow-nodes in groups by kind. Each kind and each node has its About card. You can search by name, by id or by purpose. To add a node, drag it onto the canvas. Or, select it and push Add (this is the keyboard method). Canvas Shows the graph. The color of a data edge shows the port type. If a port has alternatives, the edges have numbers (alt 1, alt 2). Dashed edges go from the then/else arm of a branch to the top edge of the nodes that the arm controls. Dotted edges show results that a condition or $expr reads. To bind an output to an input, drag from the output to the input. The canvas refuses an edge between ports of different types, a node that feeds itself and a cycle. It shows the reason above the canvas. To remove a node or an edge, select it and push Del. Each node shows the number of problems that it has. Your browser keeps the node positions, and only your browser keeps them (Tidy layout removes them). The document never keeps them. Node editor Shows the selected node: its About card, its id and label, and each input port with its type and its sources in sequence. You can add a source, change the sequence of alternatives and disconnect a source. It also shows the branch arm that controls the node (When it runs). It shows the settings: a form that the app makes from the JSON Schema of the node. Each field can also use a workflow parameter or an expression. Then it shows how the node runs: retries, time limit, failure handling and caching. A model node selects its model from the catalog, with the About card of the model. governance.check selects a check. subworkflow.run selects a saved workflow and revision. The inputs and outputs of that workflow become the ports of the node. If you select no node, the pane edits the description, parameters, inputs, outputs and run limits of the workflow.

A branch node has a condition editor. Write the condition. Insert results of upstream nodes (nodes.adf.reject) or parameters from the list. The server does a check of the condition while you type (POST /v1/workflows:validate, with the issue at /nodes/<i>/with/condition). The browser never calculates a condition.

YAML and JSON show the same document in the code editor. Markers show the problems that the server found. When the text is a correct workflow, an edit there updates the canvas immediately. Until then, the canvas keeps the last version that it could read and tells why. The app does a check of each change immediately. The status shows Ready to run or N problems. The Problems list goes to the node of each problem.

Undo and redo operate across all three views. Save revision (Cmd+S) saves the next revision with a message. The app also saves a revision that has problems, but that revision cannot run. If a different person saved a newer revision in the meantime, the app refuses the save and keeps your draft. Revisions lists all revisions with their verdicts. You can open a revision in the editor or compare two revisions side by side.

docs.title: Running and watching
docs.text:
Run workflow binds the inputs. An input is a dataset from the project: the latest version at the time of the run, or an exact version. You can change the parameters for this run only. The app starts the run with an Idempotency-Key. The run page follows GET /v1/workflow-runs/{run_id}/events live. If the connection stops, the page continues with Last-Event-ID. The run page has these tabs:

  • Graph: the canvas with the status of each node (waiting, queued, running, done, reused, skipped, failed, cancelled).
  • Steps: each node in plain words. It shows the verdict and the meaning of a decision ("The tests found that the series wanders ..., so it was differenced"). It also shows why the run did not need a node, and how long the node took. A comparison or a selection identifies its candidates by their step labels ("ARIMAX").
  • Decisions: the plain explanation of each branch and the steps that it ran or skipped. It also shows the verdicts of the earlier steps that it read ("What decided it"). Under For experts: the condition, it shows the expression and the values that it read. This section is open in Expert mode and closed in a Guided recipe.
  • Outputs and Events: the outputs of the run (the app shows the report) and the event log.

To open the drawer of a step, select the step. The drawer shows:

  • If the step ran or used an earlier result again. If it used an earlier result, a link goes to the run that made that result.
  • The test verdict: the statistic, the p-value and the decision. For panels, it shows them for each series.
  • The outputs: tables, scores, train/test folds, reports, governance evidence, charts in the plot sandbox, and a download for file outputs (for example, derived datasets).
  • The settings of the step.
  • Its sandbox run, its fits or its child workflow runs, with their logs.
  • Its cost.

Cancel run stops a workflow that runs and its children. When the run stops, the app shows the cost of the run.

You can open a model that the run fitted in the Model Explorer. The link Explore name vN is in these locations:

  • Below the summary of the run, when the run is successful.
  • Next to the runs of the fit step.
  • On each model_version output.

The link has a Validation link to the validations of that version. The lineage in the Model Explorer has a link back to this run.

docs.title: Schedules and triggers in the app
docs.text: Schedules and triggers adds a schedule from presets or from a cron expression, in a time zone. It shows the next five run times exactly as the server calculates them. It skips daylight-saving gaps, and it fires repeated times only once. If an expression fires more frequently than each 15 minutes, the app refuses it before it sends it. You can pause and delete schedules. A trigger runs the workflow each time a selected dataset gets a new version. The trigger binds the dataset to one of the dataset inputs and runs after a debounce.

docs.title: The canonical workflow
docs.text:
This is the ts_readiness_arimax template exactly as the server keeps it. The docs build makes sure that the two are identical:

# The canonical workflow: time-series readiness -> ARIMAX (template ts_readiness_arimax).
# Kept identical to mapi_spec.workflow_templates.TS_READINESS_ARIMAX by a test.
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {name: ts-readiness-arimax, project: templates}
params:
  alpha: {type: number, default: 0.05, minimum: 0.001, maximum: 0.2, description: The significance level of the tests}
  season: {type: integer, default: 52, minimum: 2, maximum: 400, description: The length of a season in periods (52 for weekly data)}
  horizons:
    type: array
    default: [1, 4, 8]
    description: The forecast horizons that the backtest scores
  gap: {type: integer, default: 0, minimum: 0, maximum: 52, description: The periods between the training data and the test data (for late data)}
  n_folds: {type: integer, default: 6, minimum: 2, maximum: 50}
  max_p: {type: integer, default: 3, minimum: 0, maximum: 8}
  max_q: {type: integer, default: 3, minimum: 0, maximum: 8}
  drivers:
    type: array
    default: []
    description: The driver columns that you know for the future
inputs:
  data: {type: dataset, description: The weekly (or daily) series to model}
nodes:
# 1. the seasonal difference first (as nsdiffs before ndiffs) ...
- id: seas
  use: test.seasonal_strength
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    period: {$param: season}
- id: seasonal
  use: branch.if
  label: Seasonal difference?
  with:
    condition: nodes.seas.seasonal
    explain_then: The series has a strong seasonal pattern. The workflow compared each value with the same period one season earlier (a seasonal difference).
    explain_else: The series has no strong seasonal pattern, so the workflow did not apply a seasonal difference.
- id: sdiff
  use: transform.seasonal_difference
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  when: seasonal.then
  with:
    period: {$param: season}
# 2. ... then the unit-root tests on the seasonally differenced series
- id: adf
  use: test.adf
  inputs:
    data: [sdiff.data, inputs.data]
  with:
    alpha: {$param: alpha}
  label: Does it wander? (ADF)
- id: kpss
  use: test.kpss
  inputs:
    data: [sdiff.data, inputs.data]
  with:
    alpha: {$param: alpha}
  label: Is it stable? (KPSS)
- id: pp
  use: test.pp
  inputs:
    data: [sdiff.data, inputs.data]
  with:
    alpha: {$param: alpha}
- id: za
  use: test.zivot_andrews
  inputs:
    data: [sdiff.data, inputs.data]
  with:
    alpha: {$param: alpha}
# over-differencing guard: a first difference whose lag-1 autocorrelation is below -0.5
# removed a unit root that was not there
- id: cand
  use: transform.difference
  inputs:
    data: [sdiff.data, inputs.data]
  label: Trial difference
- id: overdiff
  use: test.acf_pacf
  inputs: {data: cand.data}
  with: {nlags: 4, max_order: 1}
  label: Too many differences?
- id: wanders
  use: branch.if
  label: Difference?
  with:
    condition: (not nodes.adf.reject or nodes.kpss.reject) and not (nodes.pp.reject and nodes.za.reject) and nodes.overdiff.acf[1] > -0.5
    # plain words for the run report and the run monitor
    explain_then: The tests found that the series wanders and does not return to a steady level. The workflow applied a difference, so the model uses the change from one period to the next.
    explain_else: The tests found that the series returns to a steady level, or that a difference would go too far. The workflow used the series as it is.
- id: diff
  use: transform.difference
  inputs:
    data: [sdiff.data, inputs.data]
  when: wanders.then
- id: acf
  use: test.acf_pacf
  inputs:
    data: [diff.data, sdiff.data, inputs.data]
  with:
    max_order: {$param: max_p}
# the orders of the model that is fitted (same d and D), searched before the backtest's
# first test window
- id: order
  use: search.arma_order
  inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan}
  with:
    d: {$expr: 'if(nodes.wanders.value, 1, 0)'}
    D: {$expr: 'if(nodes.seasonal.value, 1, 0)'}
    period: {$param: season}
    max_p: {$param: max_p}
    max_q: {$param: max_q}
    exog: {$param: drivers}
    criterion: aic
  label: AR and MA orders
- id: folds
  use: split.expanding_window
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    horizons: {$param: horizons}
    gap: {$param: gap}
    n_folds: {$param: n_folds}
    step: 4
- id: backtest
  use: model.backtest
  label: ARIMAX
  inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan}
  with:
    model: ts.sarimax@^1
    settings:
      order: {$expr: '[nodes.order.best_p, if(nodes.wanders.value, 1, 0), nodes.order.best_q]'}
      seasonal_order: {$expr: '[0, if(nodes.seasonal.value, 1, 0), 0, params.season]'}
      exog: {$param: drivers}
    metrics: [mae, rmse, mape, mase]
- id: naive
  use: evaluate.baseline
  label: Naive forecast
  inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan}
  with:
    methods: [naive, seasonal_naive]
    season: {$param: season}
- id: compare
  use: compare.models
  inputs:
    candidates: [backtest.metrics, naive.metrics]
  with: {metric: mae}
- id: fit
  use: model.fit
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: ts.sarimax@^1
    settings:
      order: {$expr: '[nodes.order.best_p, if(nodes.wanders.value, 1, 0), nodes.order.best_q]'}
      seasonal_order: {$expr: '[0, if(nodes.seasonal.value, 1, 0), 0, params.season]'}
      exog: {$param: drivers}
    evaluate:
      metrics: [mape, coverage_90]
- id: select
  use: select.best
  inputs:
    table: compare.table
    models: [fit.model]
  with:
    metric: mae
    must_beat: [naive]
    margin: 0.0
- id: governance
  use: governance.policy
  inputs: {model: select.model, data: inputs.data}
- id: report
  use: report.summary
  inputs:
    tests: [adf.result, kpss.result, pp.result, za.result, seas.result, acf.result]
    metrics: [backtest.metrics, naive.metrics]
    items: [order.table, compare.table]
    model: select.model
  with: {title: Time-series readiness and ARIMAX}
outputs: {model: select.model, report: report.report, evidence: governance.evidence}

This list explains the document from the top:

params All values that a user can change for each run. Each value has a type, a default and limits. If a run sends {"alpha": "x"}, the server refuses it with 422 and the pointer /params/alpha. The server also refuses a number that is more than 1e15 or less than -1e15, because conditions and $expr calculate with parameters. seas, seasonal and sdiff The seasonal decision is first (as nsdiffs is before ndiffs). The seasonal strength of the raw series decides if the workflow takes a seasonal difference. The seasonal difference runs only on the then arm of seasonal. If the workflow does not take the arm, the node is skipped. It is not failed. adf, kpss, pp, za Four unit-root tests on the seasonally differenced series. If there is no seasonal difference, the tests use the raw series. data: [sdiff.data, inputs.data] is a list of alternatives: the workflow uses the first node that ran. A test of the raw levels of a seasonal series finds the seasonal unit root. Thus it adds a first difference on top of the seasonal difference, and the series gets too much differencing. The null hypothesis of ADF and Phillips-Perron is "the series wanders". The null hypothesis of KPSS is "the series is stable", so its decision labels go in the opposite direction. Zivot-Andrews accepts one structural break. Each test returns a StatTestResult with a verdict_plain sentence. cand and overdiff A guard against too much differencing: a trial first difference and its autocorrelations. If the lag-1 autocorrelation is less than -0.5 after differencing, it shows a unit root that does not exist. wanders (branch.if) (not nodes.adf.reject or nodes.kpss.reject) and not (nodes.pp.reject and nodes.za.reject) and nodes.overdiff.acf[1] > -0.5 means this: difference the series unless the evidence for stationarity is clear. Never difference when differencing gives too much differencing. The safe expression language parses the condition (it never uses eval). The run records which values it read, so you can audit the decision later. diff The first difference of the same alternatives, on the then arm of wanders. acf uses three alternatives, so it always uses the series that has the most processing. order (search.arma_order) A grid of information criteria over AR orders 0..max_p and MA orders 0..max_q. d and D give the differencing decisions to the search. Thus the search scores exactly the model that the workflow fits: ARIMA(p, d, q)(0, D, 0) with the season length, on the raw series. The split port has the plan of the backtest. With this plan, the search uses only the periods before the first test window. Thus the backtest stays out of sample. folds (split.expanding_window) An expanding-window plan. It has n_folds origins, with step: 4 periods between them. It has a gap between the training and the test, for data that arrives late. It scores each horizon in horizons separately. The server calculates the folds from the number of periods only. backtest and naive The workflow fits the ARIMAX model again on each fold. It also makes naive and seasonal-naive forecasts on the same folds. $expr makes the settings from upstream results. compare, fit, select compare.models puts the candidates in sequence by MAE. select.best keeps the fitted ARIMAX only if it is better than each benchmark in must_beat (here naive) by at least margin. If not, the workflow stops with a plain explanation (reason_plain). governance Runs the governance policy that applies to the project and makes an evidence record. The policy includes null tests, residual checks, stability and other checks (see Governance). The result shows passed and lists failed_checks. The report shows the two. The gate recipe stops a workflow on a failure. report and outputs A mapi.report/v1 document with a section for each test, decision, table and metric. outputs gives the names of the values that the run returns. A parent workflow can read these values.

docs.title: Cookbook
docs.text: Each recipe is a part of nodes:. Paste it into a document that declares inputs: {data: {type: dataset}}. Before you save, validate the document with POST /v1/workflows:validate. The server returns each problem with a JSON pointer.

docs.title: Difference only when the tests say so
docs.text:
- {id: adf, use: test.adf, inputs: {data: inputs.data}}
- {id: kpss, use: test.kpss, inputs: {data: inputs.data}}
- id: wanders
  use: branch.if
  with:
    condition: "not nodes.adf.reject or nodes.kpss.reject"
    # optional: what each path means, for the run report and the run monitor
    explain_then: The tests found that the series wanders, so it was differenced.
    explain_else: The tests found that the series is steady, so it was used as it is.
- {id: diff, use: transform.difference, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, when: wanders.then}
# downstream nodes take the differenced series if it exists, else the original
- {id: lb, use: test.ljung_box, inputs: {data: [diff.data, inputs.data]}}

The run records explain_then and explain_else (each has a maximum of 300 characters) with the decision (BranchDecision.explain_plain). They are the first part of the summary of the report. Without them, the summary shows "Difference? yes". The gallery templates set the two values.

If a node needs diff.data without an alternative, the workflow skips that node together with diff. To run a node only when the workflow did not change the series, add when: wanders.else to the node.

docs.title: Pick AR and MA terms
docs.text:
- {id: acf, use: test.acf_pacf, inputs: {data: [diff.data, inputs.data]}, with: {max_order: 4}}
- id: order
  use: search.arma_order
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with: {d: {$expr: "if(nodes.wanders.value, 1, 0)"}, max_p: 4, max_q: 4, criterion: bic}
- id: fit
  use: model.fit
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    model: ts.sarimax@^1
    settings:
      order: {$expr: "[nodes.order.best_p, if(nodes.wanders.value, 1, 0), nodes.order.best_q]"}

acf gives possible orders from the significant autocorrelations (suggested_p, suggested_q). Its result is fast to read. search.arma_order fits each candidate, and the model must use its result. search.sarima_order adds seasonal orders. search.var_lag_order selects the lag length of a VAR. search.coint_rank selects the cointegration rank of a VECM.

docs.title: Honest train/test plans
docs.text:
# 6 expanding folds, 2 periods between training and test, horizons 1, 4 and 13
- id: folds
  use: split.expanding_window
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with: {n_folds: 6, step: 4, gap: 2, horizons: [1, 4, 13]}

# tune on the inner folds of each outer training window, score on the outer test windows
- id: nested
  use: split.nested
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with:
    outer: {kind: expanding_window, n_folds: 4, horizons: [4]}
    inner: {kind: rolling_origin, n_folds: 3, window: 52, horizons: [4]}

# hold out whole markets (MMM, geo experiments)
- {id: geo, use: split.geo_holdout, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, with: {n: 2, seed: 7}}

split.blocked_kfold and split.purged_kfold cut continuous blocks (with a purge gap) for models that do not forecast. A plan is a split_plan value. Give the same plan to each model.backtest, evaluate.baseline and search.grid node that you want to compare.

If search.grid gets a split.nested plan, it does nested cross-validation. Each outer fold selects its grid point on its own inner folds. The node fits that point again on the outer training window and scores it on the outer test window. best_score is the score of those outer forecasts (the honest error of the tuned model). outer_scores and selected_per_fold show each fold. best_settings is the point that the outer folds selected most frequently. model.backtest on a nested plan scores its outer folds.

docs.title: Beat the benchmarks, or stop
docs.text:
- {id: naive, use: evaluate.baseline, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {methods: [naive, seasonal_naive, drift], season: 52}}
- {id: bt, use: model.backtest, inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan},
   with: {model: ts.sarimax@^1, settings: {order: [1, 1, 1]}}}
- {id: compare, use: compare.models, inputs: {candidates: [bt.metrics, naive.metrics]},
   with: {metric: mase}}
- {id: dm, use: compare.diebold_mariano, inputs: {a: bt.metrics, b: naive.metrics},
   with: {loss: squared, horizon: 4}}
- {id: fit, use: model.fit, inputs: {data: inputs.data},
   with: {model: ts.sarimax@^1, settings: {order: [1, 1, 1]}}}
- {id: select, use: select.best, inputs: {table: compare.table, models: [fit.model]},
   with: {metric: mase, must_beat: [naive, seasonal_naive], margin: 0.05}}

compare.diebold_mariano tests if the difference in forecast errors is more than chance. It uses the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold small-sample correction. If there is no single winner, select.threshold keeps the rows of a comparison table that are in the limits (max, min).

docs.title: Long-run relationships: VECM or VAR
docs.text:
- {id: joh, use: test.johansen, inputs: {data: inputs.data}}
- {id: tied, use: branch.if,
   with: {condition: "nodes.joh.rank > 0 and nodes.joh.rank < len(nodes.joh.trace_stats)"}}
- {id: vecm, use: model.fit, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, when: tied.then,
   with: {model: ts.vecm@^1, settings: {coint_rank: {$expr: "nodes.joh.rank"}}}}
- {id: stable, use: branch.if, when: tied.else,
   with: {condition: "nodes.joh.rank >= len(nodes.joh.trace_stats)"}}
- {id: d, use: transform.difference, inputs: {data: inputs.data}, when: stable.else}
- {id: lags, use: search.var_lag_order, inputs: {data: [d.data, inputs.data]}, when: tied.else}
- {id: var, use: model.fit, inputs: {data: [d.data, inputs.data]}, when: tied.else,
   with: {model: ts.var@^1, settings: {lags: {$expr: "nodes.lags.best_lag"}}}}

If the Johansen rank is equal to the number of series, each series is already stable (for example, growth rates or changes). Then there is no error to correct, and ts.vecm refuses that rank. Thus the workflow fits the VAR on the levels. Rank 0 means separate random walks. Then the workflow fits the VAR on the changes. A VAR that is fitted on the output of transform.difference forecasts the changes, not the levels. It cannot update its forecast with actuals, because the endpoint does not difference the data that you send. The model has the label mapi.io/data-space: transformed, the server refuses actuals, and each answer shows a warning (Forecasts with actuals).

The data keeps the series along one dimension, with one value for each series and period (value(series, quarter)). This is the layout of the statsmodels multivariate models. To ingest a wide sheet, use the wide mapping. The tests and searches use all series of that dimension, or the series in vars (labels such as [sales, price]). The model nodes bind the variable dimension of the models to it. The var_vecm_cointegration template is the complete version, with Granger tests and a report.

docs.title: Search model settings on a plan
docs.text:
- id: grid
  use: search.grid
  inputs: {data: inputs.data, split: folds.plan}
  with:
    model: ts.sarimax@^1
    settings: {order: [1, 1, 1]}
    grid: {"/order/0": [0, 1, 2], "/order/2": [0, 1, 2]}   # JSON pointers into settings
    metric: rmse
    max_points: 9

The node does a backtest of each grid point on the plan. best is the winning settings, fitted again on all the data (best_settings, best_score in the result). If a grid has more points than max_points, the node fails (WORKFLOW_INVALID) before it fits a point.

docs.title: Gate on governance and keep the evidence
docs.text:
- {id: gov, use: governance.policy, inputs: {model: select.model, data: inputs.data},
   with: {submit: true}}
- {id: approved, use: branch.if, with: {condition: "nodes.gov.passed"}}
- {id: pack, use: report.evidence_pack, inputs: {model: select.model, evidence: gov.evidence},
   when: approved.then}

governance.policy records the result of each check of the policy that applies (or of the policy in policy) as evidence. It does not fail when a check fails, so it also keeps the evidence of a rejected model. Because of the branch, all nodes after it depend on the verdict. governance.check runs one check with its own thresholds. This is useful while you design a policy.

The checks are the implementations of the platform. They are the same as the checks of a validation request. The node measures them in its sandbox, on the model and its data. The policy that applies is the policy that the project or tenant set for the model family. The default policies of the platform apply until you add your own policies.

If submit: true is set and the model passes, the server records a validation of that model version. The status is validated, or awaiting_approval if the policy needs a reviewer (see governance). The policy of a node only adds to the policies that apply. The tenant floor and the policies of the project always apply. The server records the validation as submitted by the person who started the run, or by the person who made its schedule or trigger. Thus that person cannot approve it. The server never caches governance nodes: the checks run again on each run.

docs.title: Reuse a workflow as a node
docs.text:
# workflow "readiness" declares  outputs: {stationary: wanders.result, report: report.report}
- id: ready
  use: subworkflow.run
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  with: {workflow: "workflow://growth/readiness@r3", params: {alpha: 0.01}}
- {id: summary, use: report.summary, inputs: {items: [ready.report]}}

The child runs as a separate workflow run (trigger: parent). It has its own page, and it stops when the server cancels its parent. Its ports are the outputs of the child. Pin a revision (@r3). Then a subsequent edit of the child does not change the parent without notice. You can also use @latest. If a workflow runs itself, directly or through a different workflow, it fails with WORKFLOW_INVALID. Sub-workflows can go a maximum of 8 levels deep.

docs.title: Failures, retries and time limits
docs.text:
- id: za
  use: test.zivot_andrews
  inputs: {data: inputs.data}
  retries: 1            # retry once on a transient failure (0-3)
  timeout: 20m          # this node's limit (default: the server's workflow_node_timeout_s)
  on_failure: continue  # treat a failure like a skip: downstream alternatives still work
  cache: false          # always recompute
execution: {max_parallel: 4, timeout: 2h}

execution applies to the full run. It sets how many nodes run at the same time. It also sets a deadline. After the deadline, the run fails with TIMEOUT. If a node fails and it does not have on_failure: continue, the run fails. Then the server cancels the nodes that wait, stops the nodes that run, and gives the name of the node in the error of the run.

If a condition or $expr cannot calculate on the data that it reads, its node fails with EXPRESSION_ERROR. For example, a number is too large, or the values are nested too deeply. If the orchestrator cannot move a run forward, the run fails with INTERNAL_ERROR. Then the server stops the children of the run that run. This does not stop other runs.

docs.title: Where nodes run
docs.text:
The control plane never decodes your data. Each node implementation declares where it runs (runs_in in the node catalog):

Runs in Nodes How The orchestrator branch.if, compare.models, select.best, select.threshold, report.summary, report.evidence_pack Only on the JSON results of upstream nodes, in the API process. There is no child run and no cost. A sandboxed workflow_node run tests, transforms, splits, order searches, model.backtest, model.forecast, evaluate.*, compare.diebold_mariano, governance.* A child run on the same executor and isolation as fits. It reads its inputs through signed URLs that are pinned to a generation. It writes a result. The finalizer does a check of that result. A child fit run model.fit, and the winner of search.grid (after a workflow_node run scored the grid) A usual fit of a stored spec with the name wf-<workflow>-<node>. Thus the model version is a usual model version (scoring, endpoints, approvals). A child workflow run subworkflow.run The child workflow, with its own nodes.

Two important results of this:

  • Derived datasets are real datasets. The server registers the differenced series of node diff of workflow ts-readiness as dataset://<project>/wf-ts-readiness-diff@vN. You can open it in the Data explorer or start a different workflow from it. These datasets do not fire dataset triggers, so a workflow cannot trigger itself.
  • Fitted models keep their preprocessing. When model.fit reads the output of a transform.steps node, the server writes the steps into the stored spec before the model. Thus, when you score new data, the model uses the same preprocessing. Differencing nodes are the exception. For them, give d (or order) to the model, as the canonical template does.

The cost of the run is the sum of the costs of its child runs. Orchestrator nodes have no cost. Each node lists its child runs (child_runs, one for each attempt). They are usual runs with a parent_run_id and the labels workflow and workflow-node.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Each node has a cache key. The key contains the implementation and its version, the resolved parameters and the identity of the inputs (dataset content hashes, model versions, upstream keys). If a project already has a successful result with the same key, the server marks the node as cached. Then cached_from gives the name of the run that made the result, and no child run starts. If you change one parameter of the final report, only the report runs again. To calculate all nodes again, start a run with "use_cache": false. Or, set cache: false on a node.

docs.title: Watching a run
docs.text:
Endpoint What you get GET /v1/workflow-runs/{run_id} The status, each node (status, attempt, result, outputs, child runs, timing), the branch decisions with the values that they read, the outputs, the error and the cost GET /v1/workflow-runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id} The details of one node GET /v1/workflow-runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id}/outputs/{port} A signed download link for a file output (a derived dataset, or a table that is too large to show inline) GET /v1/workflow-runs/{run_id}/events The event log as JSON, or as server-sent events with Accept: text/event-stream. The stream sends a snapshot first. Use Last-Event-ID to continue. The stream sends end when the run is complete. POST /v1/workflow-runs/{run_id}:cancel Cancels the run and each child that runs. The status is cancelling until the children stop.

When a run is complete, the server sends the workflow.run.succeeded or workflow.run.failed webhook. The webhook contains the run id, the workflow revision, the status and the outputs.

docs.title: Schedules and triggers
docs.text:
# every Monday at 06:00 Berlin time, on the latest data
api POST "/v1/workflows/$WF/schedules" -d '{
  "cron": "0 6 * * 1", "timezone": "Europe/Berlin",
  "inputs": {"data": "dataset://growth/weekly_sales@latest"},
  "description": "Weekly refresh"
}' | jq '{id, next_run_at}'

# whenever weekly_sales gets a new version (wait 10 minutes for more uploads first)
api POST "/v1/workflows/$WF/triggers" -d '{
  "dataset": "dataset://growth/weekly_sales", "input": "data", "debounce_seconds": 600
}'
  • A schedule fires one time for each due time, in its time zone. This includes daylight-saving changes. The server refuses expressions that fire more frequently than each 15 minutes. It also refuses unknown time zones. To pause a schedule, send PATCH with {"active": false}. last_run_id and next_run_at show the status of the schedule.
  • A trigger binds a new dataset version to one of the inputs of the workflow. If some versions arrive in debounce_seconds of each other, they start one run, on the newest version.
  • Runs that schedules and triggers start have trigger: schedule or trigger: dataset.version.created, and the schedule id or trigger id. The audit log records them as the platform that acts for the person who made the schedule. They count against the quotas of the project, as all other runs do.
  • These runs run as the person who made the schedule. If an API token made the schedule, they run as the owner of the token. The creator possibly cannot run workflows in the project any more. For example, the creator is removed, or has a role below runner, or the token is revoked or expired. In this case, the schedule or trigger pauses itself (active: false, audited). It does not fire.

docs.title: Run it locally
docs.text:
The same engine runs in a Python process. This is the fastest method to develop a workflow on a dataset that you have in memory. LocalRunner runs each node in threads. It obeys branches, alternatives, retries, timeouts and cancellation. It keeps results in a memory cache:

from mapi_spec.workflow_templates import TS_READINESS_ARIMAX, instantiate_template
from mapi_workflows.runtime.local import LocalRunner
from mapi_workflows.testing import test_registry, weekly_series

spec = instantiate_template(TS_READINESS_ARIMAX, name="weekly-readiness", project="growth")
data = weekly_series(156, random_walk=True, beta=3.0)  # 3 years of a wandering weekly KPI

runner = LocalRunner(registry=test_registry())
result = runner.run(
    spec,
    inputs={"data": data},
    params={"drivers": ["price"], "n_folds": 4, "gap": 1, "horizons": [1, 4, 8]},
)
print(result.status.value)  # succeeded

nodes = {n.node_id: n for n in result.nodes}
print(nodes["adf"].result["verdict_plain"])  # the plain-language verdict of the ADF test
print(nodes["wanders"].result)  # {'value': True, 'arm': 'then'}: the series was differenced
print(nodes["sdiff"].status.value)  # skipped: no strong yearly season
print(nodes["backtest"].params["settings"]["order"])  # [p, 1, q] chosen by the order search
print(nodes["select"].result["beats_baselines"])  # True: ARIMAX beat the naive forecasts
for d in result.decisions:
    print(d.node_id, d.arm, d.inputs)  # every branch with the values its condition read

again = runner.run(
    spec,
    inputs={"data": data},
    params={"drivers": ["price"], "n_folds": 4, "gap": 1, "horizons": [1, 4, 8]},
)
print({n.node_id: n.status.value for n in again.nodes}["backtest"])  # cached

The example uses mapi_workflows.testing.test_registry(). It contains the real statsmodels models (ts.sarimax, ts.var, ts.vecm, ...), the toy models of the SDK and the built-in steps (install mapi-workflows[testing]). mapi_sdk.default_registry() gives all installed plugins. LocalRunner(governance=GovernanceServices(...)) gives the policy resolver for governance nodes. The check runners are the installed check runners. mapi-runner exports all checks through the mapi.governance_checks entry point. Use runners= to add or replace some check runners.

docs.title: Limits and settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning MAPI_WORKFLOW_TICK_S 1.0 How frequently the orchestrator moves active runs forward MAPI_WORKFLOW_MAX_ACTIVE_RUNS 20 The number of runs that a project can have at the same time, sub-workflow runs included. More runs get 429. A subworkflow.run node above this limit fails with QUOTA_EXCEEDED. MAPI_WORKFLOW_MAX_SCHEDULES 20 Active schedules for each project MAPI_WORKFLOW_MAX_TRIGGERS 20 Active triggers for each project MAPI_WORKFLOW_NODE_TIMEOUT_S 1800 The timeout of a node that does not have its own timeout MAPI_WORKFLOW_MAX_JSON_OUTPUT_BYTES 1 MiB The largest JSON output that a node can return

A document has a maximum of 200 nodes. A condition has a maximum of 2000 characters. Workflows, revisions, runs, node runs, events, schedules and triggers are tenant data with row-level security, as all other data are.

docs.title: Known limitations in v0.5
docs.text:
• The nodes evaluate.residuals and model.forecast do not make plot outputs yet. They make their tables and results.
  • Detrending, STL adjustment and lag/lead features are not separate nodes. Use transform.steps with the preprocessing steps of the catalog.
  • In the web editor, each browser keeps the node positions as a view preference. The document has no place for them. The ports of a sub-workflow show when the app loads its revision.
  • The Python client and the CLI can do all workflow operations. The screens of the web app are in In the web app.

docs.title: Marketing-mix models on mmm-framework
docs.text:
From v0.5, all marketing-mix models (MMM) on the platform run on mmm-framework (PyPI mmm-framework==1.5.0, Apache-2.0). mmm-framework is a Bayesian MMM framework that uses PyMC. mapi-plugin-mmm puts it behind the platform contract as two built-in models:

Model In plain words Engine mmm.bayesian Measures how much each marketing channel adds to your sales, in total or per market. It also shows what will occur if you move budget between channels. mmm-framework BayesianMMM: NUTS (nutpie, PyMC or NumPyro), or fast approximations (MAP, ADVI, Pathfinder) mmm.frequentist Gives a first estimate in seconds. Its ranges come from samples of the data, not from the uncertainty of a full Bayesian model. mmm-framework's ridge estimator with bootstrap intervals

Each model has an About card in plain language. The card tells what the model is for, when not to use it, what data it needs and what you get from it. Help me choose in the web app recommends these models for the goals "explain my marketing" and "plan my budget" (mapi choose -a goal=plan_budget, see Choosing a model). mmm-framework is the only marketing-mix engine on the platform. The platform itself optimises budgets (below).

docs.title: What the data looks like
docs.text:
mmm-framework does the scaling, the carry-over and the conversion back to your units (owns: [scaling, carryover, inverse_units]). Thus, the pipeline only converts currencies, adds the data up to weeks and adds controls. The spec validation refuses a scaling step or a lag step on the KPI or on the spend (CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED). Thus, the platform does not scale a value two times.

The table gives the canonical names. Bind the names of your dataset to them in data.bind:

Name Dims Role time - the period dim (extend: forecasts continue after the data) channel - one label for each media channel (fixed) geo, product - the panel dims in the list hierarchy.pool_over (none for one national series) y (*panel, time) the KPI spend (*panel, channel, time) the spend for each channel (future_required: a forecast needs it) any other numeric variable over time (*panel?, time, ...) a control (or put them in the list controls). Each label of an extra dim, for example a Fourier mode, becomes one feature. 
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: eu-geo-mmm, project: growth}
data:
  dataset: dataset://growth/eu_media_daily@latest
  side_tables:
    fx:       {ref: dataset://growth/fx_daily@latest, score_policy: supplied}
    holidays: {ref: dataset://shared/holidays_eu@v3, score_policy: pinned}
  bind:
    dims: {geo: market, channel: channel, time: date}
    vars: {y: revenue_local, spend: spend_local}
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: time, last: 8, after_step: weekly}
pipeline:
  - {id: to_eur, use: core.fx_convert@^1,
     with: {vars: [y, spend], table: fx, table_along: date, currency_dim: geo,
            currencies: {UK: GBP}, default_currency: EUR}}
  - {id: weekly, use: core.resample@^1, with: {dim: time, freq: W-SUN, how: sum, full_periods_only: true}}
  - {id: hols,   use: core.holidays@^1, with: {table: holidays, table_along: date, along: time}}
model:
  use: mmm.bayesian@^1
  settings:
    hierarchy: {pool_over: [geo]}
    new_levels: hyperprior
    adstock: {kind: geometric, l_max: 6}
    saturation: {kind: hill}
    trend: {kind: linear}
    seasonality: {yearly_order: 3}
  fit: {mode: evaluate_then_refit, engine: nutpie, tune: 1000, draws: 1000, chains: 4, seed: 7}
outputs:
  derived: [contributions, response_curves, marginal_cost]
  plots: [core.ppc_fan, core.convergence, mmm.decomposition, mmm.response_curves]
evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo, coverage_90, mape]}

The plugin includes a smaller version of this spec that you can run: mapi_plugin_mmm.examples.E33_SPEC_YAML. It has a simulator (e33_dataset) that gives known true contributions. NATIONAL_SPEC_YAML with national_dataset() is the smallest national example.

docs.title: MFF data
docs.text:
The native format of mmm-framework is the Master Flat File (MFF). It has one row for each Period, Geography, Product, Campaign, Outlet, Creative and VariableName. The value is in VariableValue.

Upload the file with the mff ingest preset, or as a Guided upload. Each variable becomes its own data variable. The key columns have the same meaning as in the MFF of mmm-framework:

  • Geography and Product become dims when they have more than one level.
  • Some variables have only a total: a blank, National or Total label. An example is national TV next to regional sales. The platform divides such a variable across the levels in the same way as MFFLoader. Each geography gets an equal part. Each product gets a part that agrees with its share of the KPI. MffOptions.allocation changes this.
  • A variable cannot have both rows for each level and total rows.
  • The platform adds Campaign, Outlet and Creative up to the dims of the model, unless MffOptions.split keeps them.
  • The Guided geo template puts the media variables that you select into spend(channel).

The plugin gives the panel to mmm-framework in the same layout that its own MFFLoader makes. The observations are in period order first, then geography, then product. Tests compare an MFF file that the platform ingests with the same file that mmm_framework.load_mff loads. They make sure that the two give the same panel, with the national media rows and the campaign rows.

docs.title: How the spec maps onto mmm-framework
docs.text:
Spec mmm-framework y, spend, controls PanelDataset (y, X_media, X_controls) with MFFConfig (KPIConfig, MediaChannelConfig for each channel, ControlVariableConfig for each control feature) hierarchy.pool_over: [geo, product] the Geography/Product dimensions of the KPI; HierarchicalConfig.pool_across_geo/product (a baseline for each level, partially pooled) hierarchy.media_by_geo HierarchicalConfig.vary_media_by_geo (channel effects for each geo, partially pooled) adstock.kind, l_max, normalize AdstockConfig (geometric, delayed, weibull, none) on all channels saturation.kind SaturationConfig (logistic, hill, michaelis_menten, tanh, root, none) channels.<c>.adstock/saturation the configs of that channel trend.kind TrendConfig (none, linear, piecewise, spline, gp) seasonality.yearly_order ... SeasonalityConfig.yearly/monthly/weekly (Fourier pairs) media_prior: roi ModelConfig.media_prior_mode="roi": the return on spend sets the parameters of the channel effects priors.roi.<c>: {mu, sigma} MediaChannelConfig.roi_prior_mu/roi_prior_sigma priors.intercept: {mu, sigma} ModelConfig.intercept_prior_mu/sigma likelihood: student_t LikelihoodConfig(family=student_t) fit.engine nutpie/pymc/numpyro: NUTS with that backend. map, advi, fullrank_advi, pathfinder, laplace, smc: BayesianMMM.fit(method=...) fit.tune, draws, chains, target_accept, seed the same fit() arguments

The plugin reads frequency (W, D or M) from the time labels. If the labels are integers, set frequency. When you score, new_levels sets what occurs for new panel levels:

  • pooled: the overall level and the average channel effects.
  • hyperprior: for each draw, a level from the fitted spread. Thus, its range is correctly wider.
  • zero: no channel effects.
  • error.

docs.title: What is stored, and how scoring works
docs.text:
A fit keeps these items. It never keeps them as a pickle:

  • The parameters of mmm-framework (posterior).
  • The sampler statistics.
  • A thinned prior of the free parameters (for the prior/posterior overlap on the scorecard).
  • The observed KPI.
  • A fit_data group with the KPI, the spend and the control features at the model stage.

When you score, the plugin makes the BayesianMMM again from fit_data. The same data give the same scaling, Fourier features and trend basis. Then the plugin calculates the fitted model again in NumPy for each posterior draw. This calculation includes the intercept, trend, seasonality, panel levels, the adstock and saturation of each channel, each control and the observation noise. It is the same forward pass as the PosteriorForecaster of mmm-framework. Tests compare it with the forecaster and with the deterministics of the graph, to floating-point precision.

  • Carry-over. The plugin writes the scored periods over the fitted history. Thus, a TV burst of last month has an effect on the sales of next month. A four-week window gives the same scores as the same weeks of the full series. Periods after the fit window must follow it with no gap.
  • Trends after the data. The plugin extends a linear trend. Piecewise, spline and GP trends stay at their last fitted level (the forecast policy of mmm-framework). The forecast tells you this. Their intervals do not become wider with the horizon.
  • Outputs. y_hat(*panel, time) and contributions(component, *panel, time). There is one component for each channel, baseline (intercept and panel levels), trend, seasonality and one for each control. They add up to y_hat. A predictive request adds noise from a seeded generator. Thus, the scenario and the baseline of a counterfactual use the same noise.

docs.title: Priors in business terms
docs.text:
The return on spend sets the parameters of the channel effects. With media_prior: roi (the default), each channel samples roi ~ LogNormal(mu, sigma). This is the KPI that the channel returns for each unit of spend over the fit window. mmm-framework calculates the coefficient from it. Thus, you give a prior in the units that a business owner uses:

settings:
  priors:
    roi:
      tv:     {mu: 0.69, sigma: 0.4}    # median ROI e^0.69 = 2.0, 90% within about [1.0, 3.9]
      search: {mu: 1.1, sigma: 0.3}
    roi_default: {mu: 0.0, sigma: 1.0}  # channels not listed: median break-even
    intercept: {mu: 0.2, sigma: 0.3}    # the baseline, in KPI standard deviations

The platform changes business priors into these priors in closed form. Business priors come from Guided task 3, from calibration.business_priors or from a translate_priors run:

  • An ROI range [low, high] with credibility p becomes the log-normal that has this range as its central p interval.
  • A range for the contribution share is an ROI range, multiplied by the KPI total divided by the spend of the channel (share = roi x spend / KPI).
  • The platform reads a range that starts at 0 as [high / 20, high], and gives an info issue.
  • The baseline share (the result with no media) sets the intercept prior. The platform calculates it by bisection against the prior of mmm-framework for the trend, seasonality, levels and controls.

The preview samples the prior predictive of the translated model (the graph of mmm-framework). It shows the ROI, the share, the baseline share and a KPI fan in business units. It also shows the prior mass in each range that you gave (coverage). This value is near the credibility that you gave.

docs.title: Lift tests
docs.text:
calibration.lift_tests become experiment likelihoods in mmm-framework (BayesianMMM.add_experiment_calibration). Each is a likelihood term on the estimand that the model gives. It updates the effect of the channel, its saturation curve and its carry-over together.

Lift test mmm-framework measurement extra spend (spend_delta > 0) MROAS, spend_lift_pct = 100 x spend_delta / window spend, value kpi_delta / spend_delta a holdout that removes all (or almost all) of the spend of the channel (-spend_delta >= 95% of it) CONTRIBUTION of -kpi_delta a partial cut (less than 95% of the spend) skipped. The reason is in learned.calibration.lift_tests.skipped. This test measures the slope below the current spend, (f(S) - f((1-c)S)) / cS. MROAS is the slope above it (spend_lift_pct > 0 only). When returns decrease, the two slopes are different (by e^(c lam) for 1 - exp(-lam x)). Thus, the mapping would bias the curve.

geo limits the measurement to that geo. The plugin skips a test after the data. It also skips a test that the fit window cuts (a holdout fit that ends in the test). It puts the skipped tests in a list.

docs.title: Derived quantities
docs.text:
Ask for them in outputs.derived. The plugin calculates them at fit time over the first outputs.ui_draws draws. It keeps them in the bundle:

  • contributions: channel_contribution(sample, channel, *panel, time), baseline, trend, seasonality and one variable for each control.
  • response_curves: contribution(sample, channel, multiplier[, geo]). This is the total contribution over the fit window, with the spend of the channel multiplied by the multiplier (0 to 2.5 x by default). It also gives the spend on each grid point, the current spend, the largest spend in one period and the baseline. The what-if sliders of Guided mode interpolate these values for each draw. The plausibility checks of the scorecard read them.
  • marginal_cost: the extra spend for each extra unit of KPI at the current spend, and its inverse.

docs.title: Budget optimisation
docs.text:
POST /v1/models/{model_id}/versions/{version}:optimize asks how to divide a budget across channels (and, optionally, geos). An optimize run in the sandbox makes the response curves of the fitted model for each posterior draw. It gives them to the planning module of mmm-framework:

  • optimize_budget: greedy marginal allocation, or a constrained multi-start solver for risk objectives, groups and money bounds.
  • budget_frontier.
curl -s -X POST "$API/v1/models/$MODEL/versions/3:optimize" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MAPI_TOKEN" -H "X-Mapi-Project: growth" \
  -H "Prefer: wait=60" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
    "total_budget": 1000000,
    "channels": {"tv": {"min_multiplier": 0.5, "max_multiplier": 1.5},
                 "search": {"min_spend": 50000}},
    "groups": [{"name": "digital", "channels": ["search", "social"], "min_share": 0.4}],
    "objective": "p10",
    "frontier": {"n_points": 10}
  }'
Request mmm-framework total_budget / budget_change_pct the budget (default: the current total) mode: fixed / free spend the budget / give each channel money up to break-even (value_per_kpi converts KPI to money) channels.<c>.min_multiplier/max_multiplier bounds (multiples of the current spend) channels.<c>.min_spend/max_spend abs_bounds (money; they override multiples) channels.<c>.locked the multiplier stays at 1 groups portfolio constraints (shares and/or money) objective mean, p<q> (a cautious percentile) or cvar<a> (the mean of the worst draws) by_geo allocate for each (geo, channel) arm together horizon the periods of the plan (the curves are scaled again from the fit window at its average spend) max_draws, n_steps, seed sampling controls

The answer is 200 if the run finished in the Prefer: wait time. If not, the answer is 202. Then poll GET /v1/optimizations/{run_id}. The answer contains these items:

  • The allocation for each channel, with its expected contribution and marginal return. It also tells how stable the recommendation is across draws.
  • The expected KPI of the plan and of the current plan.
  • The uplift and the probability that it is positive.
  • The expected regret if you use one plan.
  • The shadow price of the next unit of money.
  • The efficient frontier.
  • Notes. For example, a note tells you when a recommendation is more than the spend that the model has seen.

The run also makes the mmm.budget_plans plot. If the data cannot meet the bounds, the run fails with OPTIMIZE_INFEASIBLE.

docs.title: End to end with the client
docs.text:
These steps go from a fitted version to a plan that you can defend, in Python. The equivalent CLI commands follow.

  1. Do a check of the model first. A plan is only as good as its response curves. Run the governance policy for marketing-mix models. It does null tests against shuffled sales and false noise channels. It also does a check of the effect signs and the holdout accuracy. Read why each check passed:

    validation = api.models.validate(model_id, version, note="Q4 refresh", wait=True)
print(validation.status.value)  # validated, awaiting_approval or checks_failed
for r in validation.results:
    print(r.check, r.status.value, r.message_plain, r.suggested_action or "")
if validation.status.value == "checks_failed":
    validation = api.validations.resubmit(validation.id, note="refitted on clean data")

  2. Look at the curves. The response_curves section of the Model Explorer shows the contribution of each channel when its spend changes, for each posterior draw. A mark shows the current spend. decomposition shows the part that the model gives to each channel over time:

    explored = api.models.explore(model_id, version, sections=["response_curves", "decomposition"])
curves = api.explorations.view(explored, "response_curves")

  3. Ask for the plan. api.models.optimize sends Prefer: wait. It sends the request again with the same Idempotency-Key until the run in the sandbox is done. Thus, a slow plan never starts two times:

    plan = api.models.optimize(  # mmm-framework's planner on the posterior; waits for the plan
    model_id,
    version,
    budget_change_pct=0,  # reallocate today's total
    channels={"tv": {"min_multiplier": 0.5, "max_multiplier": 1.5}},
    objective="p10",  # plan for a cautious outcome, not the average one
    frontier={"n_points": 8},
)
assert plan.result is not None
for a in plan.result.allocation:
    print(f"{a.channel:10} {a.current_spend:>12,.0f} -> {a.optimal_spend:>12,.0f}")
uplift = plan.result.uplift
print("uplift", uplift.mean if uplift else None, "P(better)", plan.result.prob_positive_uplift)

  4. Test the largest change. Score the weekly spend of the plan as a forecast. Then design a lift test for the channel that the plan changes most. Put its result into the calibration block of the model (see Lift tests). The next plan uses it.

You can do the same steps from a terminal:

mapi validate model model://growth/geo-mmm@v7
mapi explore model model://growth/geo-mmm@v7 -s response_curves -s decomposition --out views/
mapi optimize model://growth/geo-mmm@v7 --change-pct 0 \
  --channel 'tv={"min_multiplier": 0.5, "max_multiplier": 1.5}' \
  --objective p10 --frontier 8

This output shows the plan for the two-channel model of the demo (eu-geo-mmm). The model is the fit from the Python client guide, with very small sampler settings and half a year of data. The output is from a laptop:
