    In all other conditions (macOS, a non-root shell), the run continues in dev mode. The supervisor reports a DEV_MODE_ISOLATION warning event. Dev mode is not a security boundary. An executor that promises the split sets MAPI_REQUIRE_ISOLATION=1 (the docker executor does this). Then the supervisor does not go into dev mode. It fails the run with SANDBOX_VIOLATION. - The supervisor validates worker messages. Each message is a JSON frame with a length prefix and a maximum size of 256 KiB. It must agree with its Pydantic model. These are a SANDBOX_VIOLATION: a malformed frame, an unknown type, or a message after the final result. - Logs have caps. The supervisor removes ANSI escapes, control characters and bidi overrides. It cuts lines at limits.log_line_bytes (4 KB) and flags them truncated. More than limits.log_total_bytes (20 MB) of worker output is SANDBOX_VIOLATION (log_flood). - The supervisor cleans worker text. It removes the same characters from all other strings that the worker sends. These strings are state and progress messages, warnings, diagnostics, metric labels, and error and issue messages. Line breaks become spaces, except in untrusted_text. - The supervisor coalesces progress. It sends a maximum of one progress event in each limits.progress_interval_s (2 s). The newest value wins. - The supervisor uploads outputs only from regular files. It opens each file with O_NOFOLLOW, relative to directories that it opened before. A symlink, FIFO or device in the outputs tree is a violation. The reserved names manifest.json and checkpoints/ are also violations. The object caps and byte caps from limits apply. The supervisor selects the content type of each object from its extension. - The manifest tells exactly which bytes the supervisor sent. The supervisor calculates CRC32C and MD5 while it streams each file through the POST policy. It signs the OutputManifest with the key of the run and PUTs it last. The complete event comes after the manifest. - The supervisor enforces the scratch budget. It measures the scratch directory each 2 s. The worker refuses all inputs that are larger than the remaining space. If the run uses more than limits.scratch_bytes, the result is RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED.

docs.title: SIGTERM, the deadline and checkpoints
docs.text:
The supervisor does these steps on SIGTERM, or when the time gets to the deadline minus the reserve:

  1. It sends a RUN_TERMINATING warning event and sends SIGTERM to the session of the worker.
  2. It waits for the worker to stop. The worker cooperates when it cancels. Samplers do a check for cancellation after some draws. The segmented sampler of PyMC writes a final checkpoint before it stops. After --term-grace, the supervisor kills the worker.
  3. It waits for the checkpoint uploads that did not finish.
  4. If checkpoints exist, it uploads a manifest with status: partial that lists the checkpoint objects. Then it exits with 16 PARTIAL. If no checkpoints exist, it exits with 143 (SIGTERM) or 14 (deadline).

The worker writes checkpoints to {scratch}/checkpoints/ as two flat files for each fit key: ckpt-<key>.draws.zarr.zip and ckpt-<key>.meta.json. The supervisor uploads the two files with the checkpoints POST policy. It sends a checkpoint event for each file. A resumed attempt gets the same names in RunSpec.resume: the resume names are equal to the object names relative to the checkpoint prefix. The runner downloads them before the fit starts, and the engine continues from them.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Exit When 0 The supervisor uploaded the outputs and the manifest, and sent the complete event 2 The environment is bad, the bootstrap is missing or not valid, or the supervisor cannot use outputs. (There are no events if the supervisor could not read the RunSpec.) 10 The worker reported a user, spec or data error, crashed, or exited without a result 11 Out of memory (MemoryError, or SIGKILL killed the worker), or the run used more than the scratch budget 12 The uploads or downloads of the supervisor failed after retries 13 The size, CRC32C or MD5 of an input was not correct, or a bundle did not agree with its manifest 14 The run got to the deadline without a checkpoint 15 Sandbox violation: log flood, malformed messages, unsafe outputs, oversized events or output caps 16 Partial: the worker flushed a checkpoint after SIGTERM or at the deadline 143 SIGTERM with no checkpoint to flush

The supervisor always reports a failure in an error event. The supervisor writes the message of this event. Text from the worker or from a plugin goes in untrusted_text. The supervisor also sends typed issues from the worker as diagnostic events, for example MISSING_FUTURE_COVARIATE.

The supervisor accepts only three failure classes from the worker: resource_exhausted, integrity and sandbox. If the worker reports INFRA_ERROR, the run fails as user. An example is a failed input download. The reason is that the infra exit makes the platform retry the full run automatically. Thus only failures that the supervisor sees itself can use infra. All other failures that the worker reports become user.

docs.title: What RunSpec.spec holds, per kind
docs.text:
The dispatcher writes these documents, and the runner reads them. The two sides import the models and the names of the inputs and outputs from mapi_spec.jobs. Refer to the run protocol. The runner reads inputs with HTTP range requests. Each dataset is one object *.zarr.zip. The raw schema of a dataset comes from one of these sources, in this sequence:

  1. the schema input, if there is one
  2. the zarr root attribute mapi_schema (mapi_spec.jobs.DATASET_SCHEMA_ATTR). Ingest writes this attribute, and uploads can contain it.
  3. a schema that the runner infers.
Kind spec Inputs Outputs (relative to the attempt prefix) ingest IngestMapping, or IngestJob ({"mapping": …} or {"preset": "mff", "mff": {…}}, and also dataset and source, which are only for information) upload data.zarr.zip, schema.json, summary.json (DataSummary), profile.json (mapi.profile/v1, with the sha256 and size_bytes of the data), preview.json (mapi.preview/v1) describe DescribeJob ({"image_digest": …?}) none catalog.json (Catalog), describe.json (catalog_digest, versions) validate a ModelSpec dataset, optional schema, side.<name> validation.json (ValidateResponse with the stages that a dry run resolved) fit a ModelSpec dataset, optional schema, side.<name> bundle.zarr.zip, bundle.manifest.json, diagnostics.json, plots.json, metrics.json, coords.json ({stage: {dim: CoordSummary}}), scorecard.json (Scorecard, v0.4), evaluation/…, ui/thin.zarr.zip, ui/summaries.json, ui/tree_index.json (mapi.tree-index/v1), ui/preprocess.json (mapi.preprocess/v1), ui/grids/*.arrow, ui/grids/response_curves.json (mapi.response-grid/v1, v0.4), ui/plotdata/*.arrow score a ScoreRequest, or {"request": …, "plots": […], "max_draws": n} bundle, optional bundle.manifest, dataset (payload), scenario, side.<name>, history (v0.4) score.zarr.zip, result.json, ui/summary.arrow, plots.json. Forecasts add ui/guided/forecast.json (mapi.forecast/v1). Counterfactuals add ui/guided/counterfactual.json (mapi.counterfactual/v1) (v0.4). evaluate {"request": …?, "metrics": […]?} bundle, dataset, side.<name> the score outputs and also metrics.json derive {"names": […], "draws": n?, "data": "dataset://…"?} bundle, dataset, side.<name> derived.zarr.zip, ui/grids/<name>.arrow, result.json render {"plots": […]?, "format": "png" \| "svg", "scale": 2} plots (a plots.json) renders/<plot id>.<format> translate_priors PriorTranslationJob ({"spec": …, "business_priors": …, "lift_tests": […], "draws": n, "seed": s}, v0.4) dataset, optional schema, side.<name> priors.json (PriorTranslationResult), plots.json (mmm.prior_beliefs, core.prior_predictive)

At the top level of the attempt prefix, manifest.json is the OutputManifest of the runner. Thus the runner uploads the manifest of the SDK bundle as bundle.manifest.json. The evaluation sub-bundle keeps the SDK layout (evaluation/manifest.json).

In plots.json, the runner moves inline Arrow datasets that are larger than 64 KiB to ui/plotdata/<plot>.<dataset>.arrow. The plot refers to them as data_ref, with their size and CRC32C.

docs.title: MFF preset
docs.text: The preset reads a long table with the columns Period, VariableName and VariableValue. Period becomes the time dim (date, policy extend, inferred frequency). Each key column (Geography, Product, Campaign, Outlet, Creative) becomes a categorical dim only if it has more than one distinct value. Each VariableName becomes a variable. You can override roles, units and column names in mff.

docs.title: Not implemented yet
docs.text:
• optimize runs. They fail with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED. The runner reports this as exit 10.
  • render needs vl-convert-python (Vega-Lite) or kaleido (Plotly) in the image. If the image does not have them, the run fails with a clear message. The runner does not render plots with data_ref datasets.
  • netCDF-4 (HDF5) uploads need h5netcdf in the image. The runner reads netCDF-3 files with SciPy.

docs.title: Python SDK (mapi-sdk)
docs.text:
mapi-sdk is the runtime that operates on your arrays. It runs in runner images and in your notebook. It never runs in the API server. It does all the work between a spec and a fitted model that you can score:

  • binding
  • preprocessing with fitted state
  • the train and holdout split
  • the model plugin
  • the coordinates at score time
  • inverse transforms
  • summaries and bundles
uv add mapi-sdk          # or: pip install mapi-sdk

docs.title: Fit and score in a notebook
docs.text:
The first-model walkthrough shows these steps one by one. The short version is below. It uses spec, data and schema from that page:

from mapi_sdk import fit_spec

bundle = fit_spec(spec, data, registry=registry, raw_schema=schema)
print(bundle.metrics.values)  # holdout metrics, in units sold: {'rmse': ..., 'mape': ..., ...}
print(bundle.metrics.n_holdout)  # 48 cells: 3 stores x 2 skus x 8 weeks

from mapi_sdk import score_bundle

future_weeks = pd.date_range(weeks[-1] + pd.Timedelta(weeks=1), periods=4, freq="W-SUN")
plan = xr.Dataset(
    {
        "price": (dims, np.full((4, 2, 4), 2.9)),
        "promo": (dims, np.zeros((4, 2, 4))),
    },
    # "west" opens next month: the model has never seen it
    coords={"store": [*stores, "west"], "sku": skus, "week": future_weeks},
)

forecast = score_bundle(
    bundle,
    """
    apiVersion: mapi/v1
    kind: ScoreRequest
    model: endpoint://quickstart/fruit-demand
    mode: forecast
    horizon: {dim: time, periods: 4}
    output: {summary: [median, q10, q90]}
    """,
    plan,
    registry=registry,
)
summary = forecast["summary"].to_dataset()
print(summary["y_hat"].dims)  # ('stat', 'store', 'sku', 'week'), in your names
print(summary["y_hat"].sel(stat="median", store="west").values.round(1))
print(forecast.attrs["representation"])  # quantiles: what this model's uncertainty is
print(forecast.attrs["output_space"])  # {"y_hat": "raw"}: log1p undone, back in units sold
print(forecast.attrs["issues"])  # an info notice: 1 new level of 'store' uses 'pooled'

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from mapi_sdk import Bundle

out = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "fruit-demand-v1"
manifest = bundle.write(out)
print(sorted(p.name for p in out.iterdir()))
# ['bundle.zarr.zip', 'diagnostics.json', 'evaluation', 'manifest.json', 'metrics.json',
#  'plots.json']  - `evaluation/` is the train-only fit that produced the holdout metrics

again = Bundle.read(out, registry)  # every file's size and hashes are verified here
assert again.bundle_id == bundle.bundle_id

For a model with the draws representation, add draws: 50 to output. Then the tree also has a draws group. This group has 50 joint draws from the thinning index of the bundle.

score_bundle returns an xr.DataTree. Its root attributes record these items:

  • The representation.
  • The output kind (expected or predictive).
  • The output space of each variable, for example weekly. Inverse transforms stop at the last reshape step.
  • The retransformation labels for point models.
  • All warnings.

Counterfactual requests add baseline/ and delta/ groups.

docs.title: How the fit works
docs.text:
fit.mode: evaluate_then_refit (the default) does these steps:

  1. Bind the dataset names to canonical names. Do a check of the data against its schema.
  2. Run the stateless prefix of the pipeline on all the data, up to the split stage.
  3. Split the data. Fit the remaining steps and the model on train.
  4. Score the holdout through the usual score path (with context rows from train). Calculate evaluate.metrics.
  5. Fit each step and the model again on all the data. Thus, forecasts start from the latest context tails and the latest terminal state. The lineage of the production bundle has a link to the evaluation bundle.

train_only stops after step 4 and keeps the fit on train.

docs.title: How the score works
docs.text: Phase What occurs CoordPlan The SDK finds typed errors early from the metadata: UNSEEN_LEVELS, COORD_NOT_ALLOWED, HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT (409), MISSING_FUTURE_COVARIATE, NON_CONTIGUOUS_EXTENSION, MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED, ... Entry The data goes in at inputs_stage (default raw). The SDK skips the steps before this stage and their side tables. Replay The SDK applies the stored state of each step. Some steps look back (lags). For these steps, the SDK first does a contiguity check. Then it puts the stored context rows of each group before the data. Canonical coords The SDK puts the model-stage data in the fit order and pads it to the full fit set. It adds new levels at the end with a <dim>__is_new flag. Model plugin.score(...) returns the predictions group in the representation of the plugin. Back to you The SDK removes the context rows and selects the requested coords. It inverts the outputs to the output space. It aggregates them (only if this is statistically valid) and makes summaries. Then it binds the names back to your dataset names.

docs.title: Representations and summaries
docs.text:
Representation Shape Summaries Aggregation draws (chain, draw, …) mean, sd, median, hdi_<p>, eti_<p>, q<p> All (for each draw) quantiles (quantile, …) median, q<p>, eti_<p> (interpolated, never extrapolated) None interval (bound, …) interval, point None point (…) mean, point sum/mean, flagged moments (moment, …) mean, sd, eti_<p> None

If you ask for something that is not valid, the request fails with CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED. For example, you cannot add quantiles together, or get draws from a point model. The SDK does not return a number that can cause an incorrect decision.

docs.title: Data on the wire
docs.text:
mapi_sdk.wire reads and writes the formats of the platform. The readers think that each payload can be hostile.

  • XrJSON (to_xrjson / from_xrjson): The xr.Dataset.to_dict() shape with explicit dtypes and null for missing values. It has limits on elements, dims and string length. Use it for small payloads and for curl.
  • zarr zip (write_zarr_zip / read_zarr_zip, write_datatree_zip / read_datatree_zip): zarr v3 archives in one object. These rules apply:
    • Strings are vlen-utf8.
    • Datetimes are int64 nanoseconds with explicit units.
    • The reader accepts only zstd/blosc compression.
    • The writer resets MultiIndexes, and the reader restores them.
    • The bytes are deterministic.
  • Rows (stack_rows / unstack_rows): These functions stack dims into rows and remove empty rows. Later, they restore the rows from the recorded row mask.
  • Arrow IPC (to_arrow_table, write_arrow_ipc): Tidy tables for UI views.

The SDK never uses pickle.

docs.title: Data checks in plain language
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
from mapi_sdk import infer_schema, validate_dataset
from mapi_spec import DimPolicy

days = pd.date_range("2026-03-01", periods=28, freq="D")
markets = ["DE", "FR", "UK"]
channels = ["tv", "search"]
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
media = xr.Dataset(
    {
        "revenue": (("market", "date"), rng.gamma(50.0, 20.0, (3, 28))),
        "spend": (("market", "channel", "date"), rng.gamma(5.0, 100.0, (3, 2, 28))),
    },
    coords={"market": markets, "channel": channels, "date": days},
)

schema = infer_schema(
    media,
    targets=["revenue"],
    policies={"market": "new_levels"},
    units={"revenue": "EUR", "spend": "EUR"},
)
print(schema.dims["date"].policy, schema.dims["date"].freq)  # extend D
print(schema.dims["channel"].policy)  # fixed
print(schema.vars["revenue"].role)  # target

broken = media.copy(deep=True)
broken["revenue"].loc[{"market": ["FR", "UK"], "date": days[10:12]}] = np.nan

for issue in validate_dataset(schema, broken):
    print(issue.severity, issue.code, "-", issue.message)
# error SCHEMA_INVALID - 2 markets are missing 2 days of revenue in March 2026

docs.title: Bundles
docs.text:
A bundle directory contains bundle.zarr.zip and the files manifest.json, diagnostics.json, plots.json and metrics.json. bundle.zarr.zip contains these items:

  • the spec, the schemas and the binding
  • the state and the context of each step
  • the groups of the model, with ArviZ names
  • native artifacts
  • the fit coordinates of each stage
  • pinned side tables
  • the thinning index

The manifest records CRC32C and MD5 (in the form that GCS reports) and SHA-256 for each file. Bundle.read verifies them.

docs.title: Run work with an executor
docs.text:
InprocExecutor implements the Executor protocol of the platform in your own process. Use it for notebooks and tests. Never use it for untrusted code:

import asyncio

from mapi_plugin_tabular.datasets import (
    STORE_DEMAND_SCHEMA,
    STORE_DEMAND_SPEC_YAML,
    store_demand_dataset,
)
from mapi_sdk import InprocExecutor
from mapi_spec.executor import ExecState, RunEventType, RunKind, RunSubmit

history = store_demand_dataset(stores=4, skus=2, weeks=60, seed=1)
recent = history.isel(week=slice(-8, None))  # a window of fitted weeks to re-score

executor = InprocExecutor(
    # dataset refs in specs and requests resolve to in-memory datasets
    resolver={
        "dataset://retail/store_sku_weekly@latest": history,
        "dataset://retail/last_8_weeks@v1": recent,
    },
)
print(executor.caps().isolation.name)  # NONE: your own code, in your own process

async def main() -> None:
    fit = await executor.submit(
        RunSubmit(
            run_id="fit-001",
            kind=RunKind.FIT,
            payload={
                "spec": STORE_DEMAND_SPEC_YAML,
                "raw_schema": STORE_DEMAND_SCHEMA.model_dump(mode="json"),
            },
        ),
        nonce="nonce-fit-0001",  # resubmitting the same nonce returns the same run
    )
    status = await executor.wait(fit, timeout=300)
    print(status.state)  # succeeded
    for event in executor.events(fit):  # the same event stream a cloud run will produce
        if event.type is RunEventType.PROGRESS:
            print(event.seq, event.payload.get("message"))  # 2 validated the spec and the data

    executor.put_bundle("store-demand@1", executor.result(fit))
    score = await executor.submit(
        RunSubmit(
            run_id="score-001",
            kind=RunKind.SCORE,
            payload={
                "bundle": "store-demand@1",
                "request": {
                    "apiVersion": "mapi/v1",
                    "kind": "ScoreRequest",
                    "model": "endpoint://retail/store-demand-xgb",
                    "mode": "predict",
                    "data": "dataset://retail/last_8_weeks@v1",
                },
            },
        ),
        nonce="nonce-score-0001",
    )
    assert (await executor.wait(score, timeout=300)).state is ExecState.SUCCEEDED
    tree = executor.result(score)  # an xr.DataTree, exactly what score_bundle returns
    print(dict(tree["summary"].to_dataset()["y_hat"].sizes))
    # {'stat': 3, 'store_id': 4, 'sku': 2, 'week': 8}


asyncio.run(main())  # in Jupyter: `await main()`

See Runs and executors.

docs.title: Error codes that you can see
docs.text:
Each error is a MapiError with a stable code. Where it is useful, the error also has a JSON pointer. Text from your data or from a plugin goes in untrusted_text, separate from the message. These are the error types:

  • StepError (USER_CODE_ERROR) contains failures in steps.
  • SchemaValidationError (SCHEMA_INVALID) reports problems in the data.
  • BundleError (INTEGRITY_FAILURE) reports bundles that are damaged or that someone changed.
  • RunCancelled (CANCELLED) reports a cooperative cancellation.

docs.title: Spec format reference
docs.text:
Each model on modeling-api starts as a ModelSpec. This is a small YAML (or JSON) file. It gives your dataset, the preprocessing pipeline and the model plugin. It also tells how to fit and evaluate the model. The Guided wizard, the Expert editor, the CLI and the API all use the same file.

apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ModelSpec
metadata: {name: eu-geo-mmm, project: growth}

data:
  dataset: dataset://growth/eu_media_daily@latest
  side_tables:
    fx: {ref: dataset://growth/fx_daily@latest, score_policy: supplied}
  bind:
    dims: {geo: market, channel: channel, time: date}   # canonical name: dataset name
    vars: {y: revenue_local, spend: spend_local}
  split: {kind: time_holdout, dim: time, last: 8, after_step: weekly}

pipeline:
  - {id: to_eur, use: core.fx_convert@^1, with: {vars: [y, spend], table: fx, to: EUR}}
  - {id: weekly, use: core.resample@^1,   with: {dim: time, freq: W-SUN, how: sum}}

model:
  use: mmm.bayesian@^1              # mmm-framework scales and carries spend over itself
  settings:
    hierarchy: {pool_over: [geo]}
    dim_policies: {geo: fixed}      # may only tighten the plugin's policy
  fit: {mode: evaluate_then_refit, draws: 1000, chains: 4, seed: 7}

evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo, coverage_90, mape]}
execution: {resource_class: M, timeout: 45m}

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: Section Purpose metadata name and project (lowercase slugs). Optional: labels and description data.dataset dataset://<project>/<name>@latest|vN|sha256:<hex> — The API pins it to an exact version when you submit data.side_tables Small constant datasets (FX, holidays). score_policy is pinned, latest or supplied data.bind Maps canonical names (the names that plugins and steps use) to dataset names. By default, the outputs get the dataset names again data.split time_holdout, last_per_group, as_of, leave_group_out or mask_block. The split occurs at after_step pipeline Steps in sequence: {id, use: <id>@<semver range>, with: {...}} model The plugin use, its settings and the fit block outputs Derived quantities, plot recipes and the number of draws that the UI keeps evaluate Holdout metrics (elpd_loo, coverage_90, mape, rmse, ...) execution The resource class (S, M, L, XL) and the timeout (45m, 1h30m). Each class has a limit for the input data that a run reads (dataset plus side tables): S 0.5 GB, M 2 GB, L 5 GB, XL 50 GB. If the data is larger, validation reports PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE at /execution/resource_class. The message gives the class that fits. Ingest runs select the smallest class that holds the upload.

docs.title: Versions in use:
docs.text: use: takes a semver range in the npm style: ^1 (all 1.x), ~1.2 (1.2.x), >=1.2 <2, 1.x, an exact 1.2.3, or *. When you submit, the API selects the highest version that matches and is not yanked. The run records this version. Thus, you can run a revision again and get the same result.

docs.title: Where the split happens
docs.text: Some dims exist only after preprocessing. For example, a resample step can change daily data to weeks. Thus, the split occurs at a named stage (after_step). If you do not give a stage, the split occurs immediately after the first steps that learn nothing from the data. Examples are unit conversion and resample steps. A step that learns from the data (scale, encode, seasonality fit) can run before the split. Then validation reports LEAKAGE_RISK, because the step learns its state from the holdout.

docs.title: Validation messages
docs.text:
mapi spec check and POST /v1/specs:validate return all the problems at the same time. Each problem has a stable code and a JSON pointer to the incorrect field:

{"code": "SPLIT_INVALID", "pointer": "/data/split/dim",
 "message": "split dim 'week' does not exist at stage 'raw'",
 "suggested_action": "Set data.split.after_step to the stage where the dim exists (e.g. after a resample step)."}
Code Meaning SCHEMA_INVALID A field has the wrong shape, or a step or model needs data that the pipeline does not make SPEC_PARSE_ERROR The text is not valid YAML/JSON, or it uses anchors, aliases or tags (not permitted) PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE More than 256 KB, more than 32 levels of nesting, or more than 10 000 values REF_UNRESOLVED The step, model, plot, side table or derived quantity is unknown, or no version matches SETTINGS_INVALID The settings do not agree with the settings schema of the step or model BINDING_INVALID data.bind gives a name that the dataset does not have SPLIT_INVALID The split dim does not exist at the split stage LEAKAGE_RISK A stateful step runs before the split DIM_POLICY_LOOSENED dim_policies tries to make the dim policy of a plugin less strict RECURSIVE_UNSUPPORTED A lag of the target is shorter than the holdout/horizon

docs.title: Score requests
docs.text:
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://growth/eu-geo-mmm-prod
mode: forecast                    # predict | forecast | counterfactual | simulate | filter | evaluate
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 26}
inputs_stage: scale_spend         # supply weekly EUR spend directly; earlier steps are skipped
scenario: dataset://growth/plan_2027h1
interventions: [{var: spend, sel: {channel: meta}, multiply: 1.2}]
output: {kind: expected, summary: [mean, hdi_90], draws: 200}

Before something runs, the API does a check of each score request against the fitted model. It finds these problems:

  • Unseen levels on fixed dims (UNSEEN_LEVELS).
  • Horizons that are longer than the fit can support (HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT, HTTP 409). You must fit the model again.
  • Missing future values of covariates (MISSING_FUTURE_COVARIATE).
  • Gaps after the fitted range (NON_CONTIGUOUS_EXTENSION).
  • Summaries that the uncertainty representation of the model cannot support (CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED). An example is the sum of quantiles.

docs.title: JSON Schemas
docs.text: Editors can use the published JSON Schemas to validate specs while you type (GET /v1/schemas/modelspec.json, or python -m mapi_spec export-schemas ./schemas).

docs.title: Built-in steps (core.*)
docs.text:
The mapi-steps package contains the preprocessing steps. Each spec can use these steps, and you do not write code. Each step is a small, typed transform that has a version. Each step has these parts:

  • A settings model. The settings get two validations. The API validates them against the exported JSON Schema. The runner validates them with Pydantic.
  • A fitted state, for steps that learn something (scales, levels, a Fourier origin). A step learns its state from the training data only. At score time, the step uses the same state again. It does not fit the state again.
  • A static schema effect. With this effect, the API can do a check of a full pipeline in milliseconds (names, dims, units, the split stage). It does not run step code.
  • A context need, for steps that look back in time (lags, carry-over). Thus, when you score a forecast, the step sees the same history that the model used for the fit.

To refer to a step in a spec, give its id and a semver range, for example use: core.mean_scale@^1.

Where the data is after each step

The API shows the schema at each stage (POST /specs:validate). Use it before you fit a model. It shows the variables, dims and units that each step makes.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
Step Kind Learns state Invertible Looks back What it does core.resample reshape – – – Aggregates a time dim to a coarser frequency (W-SUN, MS, …). Removes partial periods core.count_events reshape – – – Counts the rows of an event table for each period (and each group) on a dense grid core.filter_coords reshape – – – Keeps or removes labels of a dim, or keeps an inclusive date range core.to_long reshape – – – Changes padded ragged data → one row for each observation, plus *_idx index variables core.to_padded reshape – – – Changes long ragged rows → a padded (group, position) grid with a mask core.stack / core.unstack reshape – – – Combines dims into one dim, and changes them back core.fx_convert value – ✓ – Converts currency with rates for each period from a side table core.mean_scale value ✓ ✓ – Divides by the mean absolute value over the named dims core.max_abs_scale value ✓ ✓ – Divides by the maximum absolute value over the named dims core.standardize value ✓ ✓ – (x - mean) / sd over the named dims core.log1p value – ✓ (non-linear) – log(1 + x) core.logit value – ✓ (non-linear) – log(p / (1 - p)) for shares core.impute value ✓ – – Fills gaps: mean, median, constant or forward fill (ffill) core.replace_sentinel value – – – Changes codes such as -99 (or values below or above a bound) to missing values core.clip value – – – Limits values to [lower, upper] core.fourier feature ✓ (origin) – – Seasonal sin/cos features core.trend feature ✓ (origin, span) – – A polynomial time trend, scaled to the fitted range core.calendar feature – – – Day of week, ISO week, month, quarter, and flags for weekend and month end core.holidays feature – – – Holiday days for each period, from a side table core.lag feature – – ✓ Lagged copies {v}_lagged(…, lag) in groups core.lag_tensor feature – – ✓ Replaces v with its lags 0 … l_max-1 (for carry-over in the model) core.one_hot feature ✓ (levels) – – Indicator columns for the categories that the fit saw core.encode_levels feature ✓ (levels) – – Integer codes for categories or dim labels core.missing_indicator feature – – – {v}_missing flags core.formula feature – – – A new variable from an arithmetic expression core.adstock value – – ✓ Carry-over with fixed parameters (point models) core.saturation value – – – Diminishing returns with fixed parameters (point models)

Reshape steps change the structure. The runner never inverts them. Predictions go back through the value steps until the last reshape. For example, an E33 model that has a fit on weekly EUR data gives weekly EUR predictions. The runner inverts value steps that are invertible when the predictions go out. For non-linear inverses (log1p, logit), point predictions have the label median, or they use retransform: smearing.

docs.title: The E33 pipeline, step by step
docs.text:
pipeline:
  - {id: to_eur,      use: core.fx_convert@^1, with: {vars: [y, spend], table: fx, to: EUR,
                                                     currency_dim: geo, currencies: {UK: GBP},
                                                     default_currency: EUR}}
  - {id: weekly,      use: core.resample@^1,   with: {dim: time, freq: W-SUN, how: sum}}
  - {id: scale_spend, use: core.mean_scale@^1, with: {vars: [spend], over: [time], unseen_levels: pooled}}
  - {id: scale_y,     use: core.mean_scale@^1, with: {vars: [y], over: [time], unseen_levels: pooled}}
  - {id: lags,        use: core.lag_tensor@^1, with: {vars: [spend], along: time, within: [geo], l_max: 6, pad: first}}
  - {id: season,      use: core.fourier@^1,    with: {along: time, period: 52.18, order: 3}}
  - {id: hols,        use: core.holidays@^1,   with: {table: holidays, along: time}}
  1. to_eur multiplies the daily revenue and spend in local currency by the rate of the day. The currencies setting gives the currency of each market. Markets that are not in the list use default_currency. Thus, you can score a new market. Markets that are already in EUR use a rate of 1. The rates must cover each necessary day. If they do not, the step raises SIDE_TABLE_COVERAGE.
  2. weekly adds the days into weeks that end on Sunday. It removes the partial first and last weeks. This is the default split stage, and the holdout is the last weeks.
  3. The scale_* steps learn scale(geo, channel) and scale(geo) on the training weeks. A market that the fit did not see gets the average scale (unseen_levels: pooled).
  4. lags changes spend(geo, channel, time) to spend(geo, channel, time, lag). At fit time, it keeps the last 6 weekly, scaled rows for each market. When you forecast, the step puts those rows before the new rows. Thus, the first forecast week sees real history. A new market has no stored history. Thus, the step pads its first lags with its first value (pad: first).
  5. season learns the origin week one time. Forecasts continue the same seasonal phase.
  6. hols counts the holiday days in each week from the daily holidays table.

docs.title: Unseen levels
docs.text:
Some steps learn a state for each level (mean_scale, max_abs_scale, standardize, impute, one_hot, encode_levels). These steps take unseen_levels. This setting tells the step what to do when a score request has a level that was not in the training data:

Policy Scale and impute steps one_hot encode_levels error (default) UNSEEN_LEVELS (422) UNSEEN_LEVELS UNSEEN_LEVELS pooled The average of the learned values The training frequencies of each level One shared "new" code fill fill_value (neutral by default) All zeros fill_code

docs.title: Looking back: lag, lag_tensor, adstock
docs.text:
along is the time dim. within gives the group dims. On long data, it gives row variables, for example a household id. Each step keeps the last n rows for each group at its own input stage. A forecast can start immediately after the fitted range. Then the step puts the stored rows before the new rows. The result is the same as a transform of the full series. If the request skips periods, the step raises NON_CONTIGUOUS_EXTENSION.

core.lag of a target is a recursive feature. The API rejects a forecast horizon that is longer than the smallest lag with RECURSIVE_UNSUPPORTED. This rule does not apply if the model does the recursion itself.

docs.title: Forward fill
docs.text: core.impute with method: ffill moves the last observation forward along along in each group. At fit time, the step also keeps the last observed value of each series. Some data starts immediately after the fitted range (a holdout or a forecast). This data continues the fitted series exactly, for all gap lengths. limit gives the maximum number of consecutive missing values that the step fills. This number includes the missing rows at the end of the training data.

docs.title: Full periods
docs.text: core.resample with full_periods_only: true (the default) keeps a period only if the source data covers each day of the period. The step compares with the source frequency (for example D). Thus, a short February is also a full month.

docs.title: core.formula
docs.text:
- {id: margin, use: core.formula@^1,
   with: {out: margin, expr: "(price - cost) / price", dims: [store, sku, time], units: "1"}}

The expression language has numbers, variable names and 'strings' (for dim names). It has these operators:

  • + - * / **
  • comparisons < <= > >= == !=
  • & | ~
  • parentheses
Functions element-wise log log1p exp expm1 sqrt abs sign floor ceil sin cos tanh expit logit two arguments minimum maximum fillna three arguments clip(x, lo, hi), where(cond, a, b) missing values isnull notnull reductions sum mean max min — sum(spend, 'channel') names that are not identifiers var('unit-price')

The result is float64 and must have the declared dims. If the result has fewer dims, the step broadcasts it. The language has no attribute lookups, indexing, imports or other calls. The length and the nesting of expressions have limits.

Note

The formula language makes specs easier to write. It is not a security boundary. Like all step code, it runs only in the runner sandbox.

docs.title: Precompute for point models: adstock and saturation
docs.text:
Bayesian models learn carry-over and saturation in the model. Point models (sklearn, ridge) get them as preprocessing with fixed parameters. Each parameter is a number, or a mapping for each level of by. For example, you can give a different decay to each channel:

- {id: carry, use: core.adstock@^1,
   with: {vars: [spend], along: time, within: [geo], kind: geometric, l_max: 8,
          alpha: {tv: 0.7, search: 0.2, social: 0.4}, by: channel, normalize: true}}
- {id: sat, use: core.saturation@^1, with: {vars: [spend], kind: hill, slope: 1.2, half: 80}}
adstock kind Weights over lags l = 0 … l_max-1 Parameters geometric alpha ** l alpha in [0, 1) delayed alpha ** ((l - theta) ** 2) alpha, theta ≥ 0 weibull_pdf The Weibull density at l + 1, scaled to [0, 1] lam, k > 0 weibull_cdf The cumulative survival, which starts at 1 lam, k > 0 saturation kind Curve Parameters logistic (1 - exp(-lam x)) / (1 + exp(-lam x)) lam hill x^slope / (half^slope + x^slope) slope, half michaelis_menten alpha x / (lam + x) alpha, lam tanh alpha tanh(x / (alpha c)) alpha, c

docs.title: Splits
docs.text:
A spec sets its train and holdout split in data.split. The runner applies the split at the split stage, after the stateless prefix. In E33, the split stage is after the weekly resample, because the week dim starts to exist only there. The built-in kinds also have catalog identities. Thus, the UI and the docs can describe them:

Split Use it for core.time_holdout The last last periods, a fraction, or all periods after a label core.as_of Backtests: train up to as_of, skip gap periods, and evaluate the remaining periods core.leave_group_out New markets or stores: hold out full groups core.last_per_group Panels and choice data: the last rows of each group that has a minimum of min_len rows core.mask_block Random blocks of cells over many dims (the model must accept missing targets)

docs.title: The catalog the API uses
docs.text:
python -m mapi_steps.catalog            # Catalog JSON: steps, settings schemas, effects
python -m mapi_steps.catalog --splits   # … plus the split catalog

When the build of a runner image occurs, the build makes this JSON. The API validates specs against the JSON, and it does not import step code. The package also contains the same file as mapi_steps/catalog.json.

In a notebook, mapi_steps.registry() returns a registry with all the steps. The mapi.steps entry point also gives the steps to mapi_sdk.default_registry().

docs.title: Web app and plot sandbox v0.2
docs.text:
The front end in the browser has two apps in the pnpm workspace. Each app has its own server:

App Package Local origin What it is Web app @mapi/web (apps/web) http://127.0.0.1:5173 The SPA (React 19, TanStack Router/Query/Table, Monaco, Arrow). It has Expert mode and the Guided task flow Plot sandbox @mapi/plot-sandbox (apps/plot-sandbox) http://127.0.0.1:5174 The only place where Vega-Lite and Plotly specs render. It is on a separate origin

make dev starts the two apps with the local API (Local development). In production, the apps are static files. The server sends them with the headers that this page describes. The mapi/web image uses nginx for this.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Area What you can do Home See the runs that are in progress, the runs that need attention, and the recent runs and models Datasets Create a dataset. Preview a CSV file locally. Map columns to dims and variables. Upload through a signed PUT. Monitor the ingest run. See the schema tables, the coordinate browser, the missingness heatmap and the preview (preview.json, profile.json) Build Use the Monaco YAML editor. It uses /v1/schemas/modelspec.json and shows live :validate diagnostics at their JSON pointers. See the pipeline as step cards with the schema at each stage, and markers for the split and the context. Save a revision, do a dry run, fit, and compare revisions Runs Filter by state and kind. See live progress over SSE (it continues with Last-Event-ID), a lane for each chain, the STALLED banner, the event timeline and the logs. Cancel a run. Resume a partial run. After RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, retry with the next larger resource class Inspect See the scorecard, the diagnostics for each variable, the DataTree browser (ui/tree_index.json), the viewer for the preprocessing state (ui/preprocess.json), the lineage, the signature, the bundle objects and the plot gallery Score Set the mode (only the modes that the model can do), the horizon, inputs_stage, the input and scenario datasets, the side tables of the spec, the interventions and the output selector. Supplied side tables use the version from the fit by default. Pinned side tables use the same version again. The app sends Prefer: wait=30, then follows the run over SSE. It shows the plots of the run (GET /v1/runs/{id}/plots, sanitized) in the sandbox. It shows Arrow outputs as a table (summaries pivoted by statistic) and a quick chart Guided Use the task flow for analysts (/guided, /guided/new/<template>, /guided/<spec>/<step>). It has templates and questions. The browser makes a profile of the upload for the questions. Set business priors and lift tests, with a preview in a sandbox. Fit the model, with progress in plain language. See the report and the sanity scorecard. Use what-if sliders. The browser interpolates the response grid of each draw (src/features/guided/whatif.ts, tested against packages/spec/tests/snapshots/whatif_golden.json). Use "Run exact", forecasts, scenario presets, promotion and embed links. See Your first analysis in Guided mode Catalog, Settings See the steps, models and plots of the image. Set the theme and the persona (the app keeps it for each user). See the health of the connection

docs.title: API client
docs.text:
apps/web/openapi.json is the OpenAPI 3.1 document of the control plane. uv run python apps/web/scripts/gen_openapi.py writes it from mapi_server.app.openapi_document(). This does not need a database. pnpm --filter @mapi/web openapi:types makes src/api/schema.d.ts from the document. openapi-fetch gives typed calls. If one of the two files is different from the server, CI fails (gen_openapi.py --check, openapi:check). make api-types runs the two generators. The document also publishes the run-event payloads (StatePayload, ProgressPayload, …) as components. Thus, the SSE frames also have types.

Variable Default Meaning VITE_API_BASE http://127.0.0.1:8000 The API. It must permit this origin (MAPI_WEB_ORIGIN, CORS). VITE_PLOTS_ORIGIN http://127.0.0.1:5174 The plot sandbox. It must be different from the app origin. VITE_STORAGE_ORIGINS http://127.0.0.1:4443 The origins of signed URLs that the CSP connect-src permits. The GCS shim answers CORS for MAPI_WEB_ORIGIN. VITE_APP_ORIGINS (sandbox) http://127.0.0.1:5173,http://localhost:5173 The origins that can embed the sandbox and send messages to it.

scripts/dev.py sets these variables from the MAPI_* URLs. Thus, make dev also works on other ports.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• App origin. The app has a strict CSP with these parts:

    • script-src 'self'.
    • connect-src, which permits only the API and storage origins.
    • frame-src, which permits only the plot sandbox.
    • require-trusted-types-for 'script', with a default policy that permits only script URLs from the same origin.

    Untrusted text (logs, tracebacks, untrusted_text, plugin messages) renders as text. The app removes ANSI, control and bidi characters from it. The app does a check of each artifact download against the size and the CRC32C in the ArtifactLink. - Plots. Each plot renders in a sandbox="allow-scripts" iframe on the sandbox origin (no allow-same-origin). This rule also applies to first-party plots. Before a library loads, the sandbox refuses URL data, href encodings, image marks, Plotly layout images and tile maps. Vega runs with ast: true and the interpreter. It also has a loader that rejects all URLs, and a tooltip that shows only text. Plotly uses the strict bundle. The CSP of the sandbox is default-src 'none', with frame-ancestors set to the app origins. - Messages. The app and the sandbox do a strict validation of the mapi.plot/v1 postMessage protocol in the two directions. The document in the frame has an opaque origin. Thus, the app accepts a message only when event.source is the window of the iframe and event.origin is "null". If the frame goes to a different page after its first load, the app stops sending messages.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
pnpm -r test            # Vitest (both apps) + the Playwright smoke suite (mock API, production build)
pnpm --filter @mapi/web e2e   # @e2e specs against a running stack (MAPI_E2E=1)

The smoke suite runs the production build in mock mode. It fails on each CSP or Trusted Types violation. e2e/guided.spec.ts runs the full Guided flow against the mock API (src/mocks/guided.ts). The @e2e specs use a make dev stack that is running. If the stack runs on other ports, set VITE_API_BASE, MAPI_WEB_ORIGIN and MAPI_PLOTS_ORIGIN.

docs.title: Workflow node reference
docs.text: Every node a workflow can use, grouped by kind. Each entry starts with the plain description the web app shows on the node's About card. See the workflows guide for how to wire nodes together.

docs.title: Statistical test (test)
docs.text: Tests a property of the data or of the errors of a model. It gives a yes/no verdict with its evidence.

docs.title: test.acf_pacf — How far back does the past matter? (ACF/PACF)
docs.text:
Measures how strongly each past period is related to the present. It also suggests the number of past values for a forecast model.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: seconds.

Use it when: You must select the orders of an ARIMA model; You want a quick look at the seasonality.

Avoid it when: The series still wanders (apply a difference first).

Example: The partial correlations stop after lag 2 and the plain correlations decrease slowly. Try an AR(2).

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level var string The variable to test (default: the dataset's target) nlags integer 24 The number of lags to calculate max_order integer 5 The largest order to suggest

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number), significant_acf_lags (array), significant_pacf_lags (array), suggested_p (integer), suggested_q (integer), acf (array), pacf (array).

Expert detail

Sample ACF/PACF (statsmodels acf, pacf with Yule-Walker-MLE) with Bartlett / 1.96/sqrt(n) bands; suggested p = last significant PACF lag before the cut-off, q from the ACF.

docs.title: test.adf — Does the series wander? (ADF)
docs.text:
Tests whether a series returns to a stable level or wanders away. The result tells you whether to apply a difference before you forecast.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: seconds.

Use it when: Before you fit a forecast model that needs a stable series; With the KPSS test, which examines the same question from the opposite side.

Avoid it when: The series is very short (less than about 30 periods); The series has one clear break (use Zivot-Andrews).

Example: Weekly sales give p = 0.57. The series wanders, so apply one difference.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level var string The variable to test (default: the dataset's target) regression c \ ct \ ctt \ autolag AIC \ BIC \ t-stat \ maxlag integer The largest lag to try (default: Schwert's rule) per_series boolean true For panels, test every series (geo, product) separately

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number).

Expert detail

Augmented Dickey-Fuller (statsmodels adfuller); H0: unit root. Lag length by AIC/BIC/t-stat; regression 'c', 'ct', 'ctt' or 'n'; MacKinnon p-values.

docs.title: test.arch_lm — Do volatile periods cluster? (ARCH-LM)
docs.text:
Tests whether calm periods and turbulent periods occur in groups. If they do, the ranges must become wider after a shock.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: expert. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: Financial or demand series with bursts of volatility.

Avoid it when: Series without visible bursts.

Example: The errors after promotions are larger for several weeks (p = 0.02).

Inputs: data (dataset, optional), model (model_version, optional).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level var string The series to test (default: the residuals of the model input) nlags integer 4 Lags

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number).

Expert detail

Engle's ARCH LM test (statsmodels het_arch); H0: no ARCH effects.

docs.title: test.breusch_pagan — Even-sized errors? (Breusch-Pagan)
docs.text:
Tests whether the errors of a model are larger at some times or for some inputs. Then the ranges of the model are too narrow in some places.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: expert. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: You want to test the errors of a regression model.

Avoid it when: Models without inputs.

Example: The errors increase with spend (p = 0.003). The ranges are too narrow for weeks with a large spend.

Inputs: model (model_version).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level robust boolean true Use the studentised version of Koenker

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number).

Expert detail

Breusch-Pagan LM test (statsmodels het_breuschpagan); H0: homoskedasticity.

docs.title: test.chow — Did it change on this date? (Chow)
docs.text:
Tests whether the relationship between a result and its drivers is different before and after a date that you select.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: You know a date when something changed (a relaunch, a new competitor).

Avoid it when: You do not know the date (use CUSUM).

Example: The price effect is different after the 2023 relaunch (p = 0.01).

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level y string required The result x array required The drivers break_at string or integer required The date or position of the break

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number).

Expert detail

Chow F test comparing pooled and split OLS fits at the break point.

docs.title: test.cusum — Did the relationship change? (CUSUM)
docs.text:
Tests whether the relationship between the result and the drivers of a model stayed the same over time. You do not have to guess when it changed.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: expert. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: You think that something changed, but you do not know when.

Avoid it when: You know the date (use the Chow test).

Example: The cumulative errors go across the bound in 2022. The relationship changed.

Inputs: model (model_version).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number), break_detected (boolean), break_at (string).

Expert detail

OLS-residual CUSUM test (statsmodels breaks_cusumolsresid); H0: parameter stability.

docs.title: test.engle_granger — Are two series tied together? (Engle-Granger)
docs.text:
Tests whether two wandering series stay tied together in the long run, so that the gap between them closes again.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: expert. Typical runtime: seconds.

Use it when: Before you make an error-correction model of one result and one driver.

Avoid it when: More than two series (use Johansen).

Example: Your price and the price of a competitor are tied (p = 0.02).

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level y string required The first series x string required The second series trend c \ ct \ ctt \

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number).

Expert detail

Engle-Granger two-step test (statsmodels coint); H0: no cointegration.

docs.title: test.granger — Does one series help predict another? (Granger)
docs.text:
Tests whether the past values of a driver help to predict a result better than the past values of the result alone.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: seconds.

Use it when: You must decide which series to include in a VAR; You want to make sure that a leading indicator really leads.

Avoid it when: You want to prove cause and effect (the test shows only help with the prediction).

Example: Search interest helps to predict sales two weeks later (p = 0.004).

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level y string required The result x string required The candidate driver maxlag integer 4 The largest lag to test lag integer Test only this lag (no correction is necessary)

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number), min_p_value (number), best_lag (integer), p_values (object), correction (string).

Expert detail

Granger causality F-tests for lags 1..maxlag (statsmodels grangercausalitytests, ssr F test); H0: the driver's lags have zero coefficients. The verdict uses the smallest p-value Holm-corrected for the maxlag lags tried (an uncorrected minimum about doubles the false-positive rate), or the F test at one prespecified lag; the per-lag p-values are descriptive.

docs.title: test.jarque_bera — Bell-shaped errors? (Jarque-Bera)
docs.text:
Tests whether values, usually the errors of a model, follow a bell curve. If not, the ranges that use this assumption can be wrong.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: You want to test the errors of a model before you trust its ranges.

Avoid it when: Small samples (the test is not reliable with less than about 50 values).

Example: The errors are skewed (p < 0.001). A small number of misses are very large.

Inputs: data (dataset, optional), model (model_version, optional).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level var string The series to test (default: the residuals of the model input)

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number), skew (number), kurtosis (number).

Expert detail

Jarque-Bera on skewness and kurtosis (statsmodels jarque_bera); H0: normality.

docs.title: test.johansen — Are the series tied together? (Johansen)
docs.text:
Tests whether several wandering series stay tied together in the long run. It also finds the number of these ties.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: expert. Typical runtime: seconds.

Use it when: Before you make one model of several series that have a trend.

Avoid it when: The series do not wander (they need no difference); Only one series.

Example: The prices of two close competitors share one long-run tie (rank 1).

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha 0.1 \ 0.05 \ 0.01 vars array The series: variable names, or labels along the series dimension of the data (if empty, all the series of the target) det_order integer 0 Deterministic terms: -1 none, 0 constant, 1 trend k_ar_diff integer 1 Lagged differences method trace \ maxeig "trace"

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number), rank (integer), trace_stats (array), max_eig_stats (array).

Expert detail

Johansen trace and maximum-eigenvalue tests (statsmodels coint_johansen); rank from sequential tests at the critical values for the chosen level.

docs.title: test.kpss — Is the series stable? (KPSS)
docs.text:
Tests whether a series stays near a stable level or trend. It is the opposite of the ADF test, so the two tests together give a better answer.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: seconds.

Use it when: With ADF, to confirm whether the series needs a difference.

Avoid it when: The series is very short.

Example: KPSS rejects stability (p = 0.01) and ADF cannot reject a wandering series. Apply a difference.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level var string The variable to test (default: the dataset's target) regression c \ ct "c" nlags auto \ legacy "auto" per_series boolean true For panels, test every series (geo, product) separately

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number).

Expert detail

KPSS (statsmodels kpss); H0: level (or trend) stationarity; p-values are interpolated within [0.01, 0.1] and clipped outside.

docs.title: test.ljung_box — Is there a pattern left? (Ljung-Box)
docs.text:
Tests whether the errors of a model are still related to their own past. If they are, the model does not find all of the structure.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: seconds.

Use it when: On the errors of a forecast model, after you fit it.

Avoid it when: On the raw series (use ACF/PACF to look for structure).

Example: The errors of an ARIMA model show no pattern up to lag 10 (p = 0.42). This is good.

Inputs: data (dataset, optional), model (model_version, optional).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level var string The series to test (default: the residuals of the model input) lags integer 10 The number of lags to test model_df integer The number of fitted ARMA terms to subtract (default: from the model)

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number).

Expert detail

Ljung-Box Q (statsmodels acorr_ljungbox); H0: no autocorrelation up to the lag; model_df adjusts the degrees of freedom for fitted ARMA terms.

docs.title: test.pp — Does the series wander? (Phillips-Perron)
docs.text:
Tests whether a series wanders, as ADF does. It gives better results when the errors are uneven or related over time.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: expert. Typical runtime: seconds.

Use it when: You want a second test after ADF on a noisy series.

Avoid it when: The series is very short.

Example: PP and ADF agree that monthly demand wanders.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level var string The variable to test (default: the dataset's target) trend n \ c \ ct lags integer Newey-West lags (default: automatic) per_series boolean true For panels, test every series (geo, product) separately

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number).

Expert detail

Phillips-Perron Z-tau test (arch.unitroot.PhillipsPerron or an equivalent Newey-West corrected regression); H0: unit root.

docs.title: test.seasonal_strength — How strong is the season?
docs.text:
Measures how much of the changes in a series come from a seasonal pattern that repeats. The scale is from 0 (none) to 1 (all).

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: beginner. Typical runtime: seconds.

Use it when: You must decide whether to model the seasonality or to apply a seasonal difference.

Avoid it when: Less than two full seasons of data.

Example: Weekly ice-cream sales have a seasonal strength of 0.85. Model the season.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level var string The variable to test (default: the dataset's target) period integer The season length in periods (default: from the frequency) threshold number 0.64 The strength that the test counts as seasonal

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number), strength (number), trend_strength (number), period (integer), seasonal (boolean).

Expert detail

STL decomposition; F_s = max(0, 1 - Var(R) / Var(S + R)) (Wang, Smith & Hyndman); 'seasonal' when F_s >= threshold.

docs.title: test.vif — Are drivers too alike? (VIF)
docs.text:
Tests whether some drivers change almost together. Then it is difficult to find their separate effects.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: Before a regression or marketing mix model with many drivers.

Avoid it when: You only predict and the separate effects are not important.

Example: TV spend and radio spend have a VIF of 14. You cannot reliably separate their effects.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level vars array required The drivers limit number 10 The VIF limit for a driver

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number), max_vif (number), table (object), high_vif_vars (array).

Expert detail

Variance inflation factor 1/(1 - R_j^2) per regressor (statsmodels variance_inflation_factor) with a constant added.

docs.title: test.white — Even-sized errors? (White)
docs.text:
Tests whether the errors of a model are larger in some places. It is a more general test than Breusch-Pagan.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: expert. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: You think that the size of the errors has a curved relation to the inputs.

Avoid it when: Models with many inputs and little data (the test uses all the combinations of the inputs).

Example: The White test also finds uneven errors (p = 0.01).

Inputs: model (model_version).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number).

Expert detail

White's test (statsmodels het_white); H0: homoskedasticity.

docs.title: test.zivot_andrews — Wandering or one break? (Zivot-Andrews)
docs.text:
Tests whether a series that seems to wander is stable with one sudden jump. For example, a price change or a new product can cause a jump.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: expert. Typical runtime: seconds.

Use it when: The series has one clear shift.

Avoid it when: There are several breaks; The series is short.

Example: Sales jump after a relaunch in March 2023. If the test permits that break, the series is stable.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: result (test_result).

Parameter Type Default Meaning alpha number 0.05 The significance level var string The variable to test (default: the dataset's target) regression c \ t \ ct trim number 0.15 The share at each end that cannot be a break date per_series boolean true For panels, test every series (geo, product) separately

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): statistic (number), p_value (number), alpha (number), reject (boolean), decision (string), verdict_plain (string), critical_values (object), n_obs (integer), lags (integer), details (object), per_series (array), reject_share (number), break_index (integer), break_at (string).

Expert detail

Zivot-Andrews (statsmodels zivot_andrews); H0: unit root without a break; break in intercept, trend or both.

docs.title: Data processing (transform)
docs.text: Changes the data before later steps use it. For example, it calculates differences or logs.

docs.title: transform.box_cox — Stabilise the spread
docs.text:
Bends a positive series so that its changes have about the same size at high and low levels. It finds the best bend from the data.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: The spread increases with the level and a log is too strong or too weak.

Avoid it when: The values can be zero or negative.

Example: Lambda 0.3 makes the spread of monthly sales approximately constant.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: data (dataset).

Parameter Type Default Meaning vars array The variables (default: the target) lmbda number A fixed lambda (default: an estimate from the data)

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): vars (array), lmbda (number).

Expert detail

Box-Cox with lambda by maximum likelihood (scipy.stats.boxcox) or fixed.

docs.title: transform.difference — Change from the previous period
docs.text:
Replaces each value with its change from the previous period. This changes a wandering series into a stable series.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: A unit-root test shows that the series wanders.

Avoid it when: The series is already stable (a difference adds noise).

Example: Sales of 100, 104, 103 become changes of +4 and -1.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: data (dataset).

Parameter Type Default Meaning vars array The variables for the difference (default: the target) order integer 1 The number of differences dim string "time"

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): vars (array).

Expert detail

First differences of order d along the time dim, per series; the last d levels are kept as state to integrate forecasts.

docs.title: transform.log — Logarithm
docs.text:
Calculates the logarithm of positive values. This changes growth into steady steps, and you can compare large series with small series.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: beginner. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: The values increase by percentages; The spread increases with the level.

Avoid it when: The values can be zero or negative.

Example: Sales of 10, 100 and 1000 become 2.3, 4.6 and 6.9.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: data (dataset).

Parameter Type Default Meaning vars array The variables (default: the target)

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): vars (array).

docs.title: transform.seasonal_difference — Change from the same period last season
docs.text:
Replaces each value with its change from the same period one season earlier. This removes a strong pattern that repeats.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: Strong seasonality that you do not want a seasonal model to learn.

Avoid it when: Less than two seasons of history.

Example: The sales of week 53 minus the sales of week 1 one year earlier.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: data (dataset).

Parameter Type Default Meaning vars array The variables for the difference (default: the target) period integer required The season length in periods order integer 1 The number of differences dim string "time"

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): vars (array).

docs.title: transform.select — Keep some variables or dates
docs.text:
Keeps only the variables, markets or dates that you select. For example, you can test one series or a recent period.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: beginner. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: Later nodes must see only part of the data.

Avoid it when: The workflow needs all of the data.

Example: Keep only y and price for the market DE.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: data (dataset).

Parameter Type Default Meaning vars array The variables to keep sel object dim -> labels to keep start string or integer The first time label to keep end string or integer The last time label to keep

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): vars (array).

docs.title: transform.steps — Preprocessing steps
docs.text:
Runs catalog preprocessing steps on the data. For example, the steps can make weekly totals, scale values or add calendar features.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: seconds.

Use it when: The data needs the same preparation as a model spec gives.

Avoid it when: A model node runs the same steps (put them in its pipeline).

Example: Weekly totals, then a log of spend, before the tests.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: data (dataset).

Parameter Type Default Meaning steps array required Pipeline steps, as in a ModelSpec ({id, use, with})

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): vars (array).

docs.title: Decision (branch)
docs.text: Uses earlier results to select the path of the workflow.

docs.title: branch.if — Choose a path
docs.text:
Uses earlier results to decide the path of the workflow. For example: 'apply a difference only if the tests show that the series wanders'.

Runs in the orchestrator (no data; computed from earlier results). Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: A step must run only under a condition.

Avoid it when: All steps must always run.

Example: nodes.adf.p_value >= params.alpha or nodes.kpss.reject decides whether to apply a difference.

Parameter Type Default Meaning condition string required The condition in the workflow expression language explain_then string What it means when the condition is true, in plain words for the run report (for example, 'The tests found that the series wanders, so the workflow applied a difference.') explain_else string What it means when the condition is false, in plain words

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): value (boolean), arm (string).

Expert detail

Conditions use the safe expression language (mapi_spec.expr): comparisons, and/or/not, arithmetic, a few functions; no code is executed.

docs.title: Train/test plan (split)
docs.text: Decides which periods or groups the model learns from, and which periods or groups test the model. It can do this many times.

docs.title: split.blocked_kfold — Blocked cross-validation
docs.text:
Cuts the time line into some blocks and uses each block one time as the test. A buffer around each block stops data leaks from adjacent periods.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: expert. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: Models that explain, where the future is not the only important thing; Short series, where rolling backtests leave too little data.

Avoid it when: Forecasts only (a model that trains on the future is not realistic).

Example: Five blocks with a 4-week buffer on each side.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: plan (split_plan).

Parameter Type Default Meaning after_step see schema null Stage the folds are cut at (a step id or 'raw'), as data.split dim string "time" k integer required gap integer 0

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): n_folds (integer), folds (array).

docs.title: split.expanding_window — Rolling backtest (growing history)
docs.text:
Repeats the test at several points in time. Each time, the model trains on all the history up to that point, as in a real forecast.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: You forecast regularly and want a realistic estimate of the error; You need a gap between the training data and the test data because the data comes late.

Avoid it when: Very short series.

Example: Six origins 4 weeks apart, a 1-week gap, horizons 1 to 8.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: plan (split_plan).

Parameter Type Default Meaning after_step see schema null Stage the folds are cut at (a step id or 'raw'), as data.split dim string "time" horizons array required Forecast horizons scored per fold step see schema null Periods between origins (default: max) gap integer 0 Periods between training and test (not scored) n_folds see schema null min_train integer 1 Fewest training periods a fold may have anchor end \ start "end"

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): n_folds (integer), folds (array).

docs.title: split.geo_holdout — Hold out markets
docs.text:
Keeps whole markets or stores out of the training data and tests the model on them. You can also test only their latest periods.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: You will apply the model to new markets; You want to read the result of a geo experiment.

Avoid it when: You only predict for markets that the model knows.

Example: Hold out 2 random markets, 5 times with different draws.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: plan (split_plan).

Parameter Type Default Meaning after_step see schema null Stage the folds are cut at (a step id or 'raw'), as data.split dim string "geo" groups see schema null n see schema null n_folds integer 1 seed integer 0 time_dim see schema null test_last see schema null include_pre_period boolean false

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): n_folds (integer), folds (array).

docs.title: split.holdout — One test period
docs.text:
Keeps one part of the data, usually the latest periods, to test the model.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: beginner. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: You want one quick, honest test.

Avoid it when: You want to know how stable the error is (use a rolling backtest).

Example: Hold out the last 8 weeks.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: plan (split_plan).

Parameter Type Default Meaning after_step see schema null Stage the folds are cut at (a step id or 'raw'), as data.split split object required

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): n_folds (integer), folds (array).

docs.title: split.nested — Tuning inside a backtest
docs.text:
Runs a second, inner backtest in each training window, so that you can tune settings without data from the outer test periods. The search.grid node tunes on the inner folds and scores on the outer folds.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: expert. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: You tune settings (orders, penalties) and want an honest final error.

Avoid it when: You do not tune settings.

Example: Outer: expanding window, 4 origins. Inner: expanding window, 3 origins.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: plan (split_plan).

Parameter Type Default Meaning after_step see schema null Stage the folds are cut at (a step id or 'raw'), as data.split outer object required inner object required

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): n_folds (integer), folds (array).

docs.title: split.purged_kfold — Purged cross-validation
docs.text:
Works like blocked cross-validation, but removes the periods immediately before and after each test block. Use it for results that cover several periods.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: expert. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: The results come from windows that overlap the test block.

Avoid it when: Plain forecasts.

Example: Five blocks, purge 2 periods before and embargo 4 after each test block.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: plan (split_plan).

Parameter Type Default Meaning after_step see schema null Stage the folds are cut at (a step id or 'raw'), as data.split dim string "time" k integer required purge integer 0 embargo integer 0

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): n_folds (integer), folds (array).

docs.title: split.rolling_origin — Rolling backtest (fixed window)
docs.text:
Repeats the test at several points in time. Each time, the model trains on the same length of recent history, so you can see if the error stays the same.

Runs in a sandboxed workflow_node run. Difficulty: intermediate. Typical runtime: instant.

Use it when: Old history is possibly not relevant now; You want errors at several forecast horizons.

Avoid it when: Little history (each fold needs a full window).

Example: Train on 104 weeks and test 1, 4 and 8 weeks ahead. Move 4 weeks and do this 10 times.

Inputs: data (dataset).

Outputs: plan (split_plan).

Parameter Type Default Meaning after_step see schema null Stage the folds are cut at (a step id or 'raw'), as data.split dim string "time" horizons array required Forecast horizons scored per fold step see schema null Periods between origins (default: max) gap integer 0 Periods between training and test (not scored) n_folds see schema null min_train integer 1 Fewest training periods a fold may have anchor end \ start "end" window integer required Training periods per fold

Result fields (nodes.<id>.<field> in conditions): n_folds (integer), folds (array).

docs.title: Search (search)
docs.text: Tries many settings and selects the best setting by a score.
